##### **EDITOR’S BIOGRAPHIES** 

**Rodrigo A. Abel** graduated from de University of Chile as Mining Engineer in 1976. He received the Juan Brьggen award from the Institute of Mining Engineers of Chile for his academic results. In 2001 he obtained a M.B.A. degree from the Adolfo Ibбсez University in Chile. He’s been working for more than 36 years in metallurgical plants, mainly in copper refining processes. In 1977, he started in CODELCO CHILE at the Salvador Refinery in Potrerillos, and in 1988 he joined to Las Ventanas Refinery, ENAMI and then CODELCO CHILE from 2005. During his professional career he has held different positions in process engineering, operations and management. He held the position of Refinery Superintendant from both refineries, Potrerillos and Ventanas. His main expertise in the copper industry includes fire refining, electrolytic refining and anodic slimes treatment. He has developed different projects that resulted in improvements and modernizations in the processes. He has presented papers in four Copper Conferences since the first meeting in Chile in 1987. He is now senior engineer at Las Ventanas Refinery. 

**Carlos E. Delgado** graduated from the University Catholic of North as Chemical Engineer in 1978. Years later, he continued his studies at the University Catholic of Chile obtaining his MBA in 2004. 

He has been working for more than 34 years in non-ferrous mining industry, in mining companies such as Codelco Chile, Chuquicamata Division - Andina Division - Corporative Center and Minera Las Cenizas Group, and more recently in engineering companies Tetratech and Hatch. During his professional career he has held different position such as Chief of Electrolytic Processes, Refinery Head Metallurgist, Director of Quality Development, Commercialization Director, HSEQ Manager, Continuous Improvement Manager, Operati

ve Planning Director, General Manager and Business Development Manager. His main background is in process improvements, health & safety, operative planning, strategical planning and organizational development. Nowadays he is an independent consultant focalized on business development and organizational consultancy.

### **PREFACE** 

Copper 2013 International Conference is the 8<sup>th</sup> version of the most important global meeting that brings together leading scientists, researchers, academics, and executives from different companies and organizations devoted to the areas of economy, copper processing, metallurgical extraction techniques; environmental compatibility; copper applications, copper recovery, and waste management and recycling techniques. At the same time, the challenges faced by different mining projects will be addressed. We appreciate the work and collaboration from colleagues coming from over 30 countries and representing more than 300 companies and institutions. 

Copper 2013 Conferences find their origin in the joint work conducted between the Chilean Institute of Mining Engineers (IIMCh) and the Metallurgical Society of the Canadian Institute of Mining, Metallurgy and Petroleum (METSOC). Since 2007, when the Copper Conference was held in Toronto, new co-organizer institutions have helped disseminate the results achieved by the Conferences while granting these a strong global character in terms of convening power, submittal of papers, and the generation of collaborative knowledge. We deeply appreciate the disinterested contribution from GDMB of Germany, MMIJ of Japan, and TMS and SME from USA. 

This time, the current global situation is not only a scenario where competitive prices are being realized but also where strong and serious uncertainties are being handled in connection with the global economy; energy and key resources prices. 

Globally, ore grades have declined to historically low levels and, therefore, the recycling and recovery of what used to be waste material, nowadays represent great opportunities for the overall development of new projects. Water uses in production processes and the solutions applied no doubt represent a source of knowledge for the community gathered at this venue. Likewise, new long-term and mid-term forecasts to be made in the future will certainly set their focus on eventual challenges and on mining and metallurgical development opportunities in the decades ahead. 

The total of 330 papers submitted in response to the original call will present the main changes to take place in metallurgical processes, as well as the state-of-theart techniques responsible for providing effective solutions to new challenges posed by metallurgical processes. The widespread interest generated by innovations, particularly in the area of pyrometallurgy will undoubtedly occupy a special place in the course of the Con

ference, thanks to the research and development of technological solutions conducted in countries like China, for example. _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ The 2013 Conference has issued 7 volumes of Proceedings containing all the papers and management initiatives presented in each of the 10 symposiums hosted by the Conference. Most of them have included new and amazing technologies that have permitted them to reach remarkable results in productivity and energy efficiency. The old refineries meanwhile, it has been permanently modernizing and expanding to face the challenge to reduce or contain operation costs. The Copper 2013 Symposium of Electrowinning and Electrorefining has received a solid and consistent response from the refiners around the world. The submissions come from researchers and academic of 15 different countries. Contributors of USA, Japan and Australia represent near the half of the papers presented. Twenty of the 48 papers presented in this chapter are from Electrowinning applications, 28 are related to Electrorefining´s plant practices. In each topic the papers have been grouped in the following themes: Fundamentals, Plant Practices, Electrode´s Properties, Electrolyte Purification and Environmental Issues, Simulation and Information Management. The papers in this volume show the advances achieved in using high current density at electrorefining processes, the electrolyte´s circulation and purification, the anodes quality at electrowinning processes and acid mist control in the operations. Also, a wide variety of new technologies are shown. The content of the papers demonstrate the continuous interest of the specialists to share their experiences so to improve their knowledge and to develop new ways to afford the challenge of obtaining a better cathode quality at a minimum cost. #### **ABSTRACT** 

World copper electrowinning tankhouse operating practices are surveyed and evaluated. Previous surveys have been carried out in 1995, 1999, 2001, 2002, 2003, and 2007. The survey analyses current data to identify trends and operating correlations. Examples of recent design and operational choices to improve safety and operator health, increase productivity, improve copper quality, and decrease electrical energy consumption are discussed. These include further installation of automated electrode handling systems, acid mist suppression systems, and catalytic coated titanium mesh anodes that operate at lower cell voltage. Most brown- and greenfield copper electrowinning projects continue to be developed in Central Africa. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_

#### **INTRODUCTION** 

Continuing from similar surveys carried out in 1997, 1999, 2001, 2002, 2003, and 2007 [1-6], global operating practice in copper electrowinning (EW) in 2013 is reviewed. The survey also contains unpublished data from 2010, where this is the most recent available information. Contributing operations include sites from the USA (8), Chile (10), Peru (2), Europe (4), and Africa (8). Trends in operating conditions and performance, as well as equipment design and process technology choices, are analysed. Issues of operator health and safety are receiving increasing attention. The detailed survey results are provided on the CD-ROM of the conference proceedings. 

There are fewer contributions to this survey compared to past experience. In addition to the more competitive nature of the industry, several operations (particularly in Australia) have shut down, while new, large operations currently commissioning or ramping up to full production in Africa and Europe declined to participate as their current performance is not representative of expected future performance. None of the Chinese operations participated in this survey. 

There are currently some 75 operations worldwide with cathode production above 10 000 t/a [7]. Chile still leads the world in number and size of EW operations. The largest of the plants that participated in the survey is Escondida, Chile (which produced 377 kt Cu in 2010, some 14% above nameplate design), while the smallest is Northam Platinum, a South African base metal refinery (424 t in 2012). Of the 32 plants surveyed, 30 operated below their nameplate capacities in 2012 (Figure 1). In North and South America, this is largely due to declining ore grades and the associated declining cathode production, while in Africa this reflects recently commissioned operations that are still rampi

ng up as well as the detrimental effects of widespread, sustained strike action during 2012. The majority of operations today purify their advance electrolyte by including a solvent extraction (SX) step ahead of EW, however, older base metal refineries, particularly, still electrowin copper directly from the leach liquor. The positive influence of SX on the electrolyte and cathode qualities is demonstrated. #### **TRENDS IN OPERATING CONDITIONS AND PROCESS PERFORMANCE** #### **Electrolyte Composition** With respect to the main components, copper and acid, the compositions of the advance and spent electrolytes used for the production of London Metal Exchange (LME) or New York Commodity Mercantile Exchange (COMEX) Grade A copper are very similar throughout the world. The main differences arise with respect to the impurity elements that are transferred to the advance electrolyte either by aqueous-inorganic entrainment from the pregnant leach solution (PLS) to the loaded organic phase or by co-extraction on the loaded organic phase in SX plants. In other parts of the world, cobalt is intentionally added to the electrolyte to improve anode life. The lower cobalt concentrations of African SXEW electrolytes reflect the rejection of cobalt in the PLS to the SX raffinate, compared to the higher levels seen in direct EW electrolytes. High levels of iron and manganese are also evident, due to the predominance of agitation leaching in these flowsheets, with consequent higher solids in the PLS and higher aqueous-in-organic entrainments in the upstream SX circuits. Amongst SXEW operations, iron levels are lowest in South America, which are _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 6 indicative of oxide leach operations and low entrainments of iron into EW from secondary and low-grade sulfide leach operations. South American operations also operate with lowest chloride in electrolyte, although they typically have the highest chloride contents in their PLS, indicating good SX design with w

ash stages and other entrainment reduction technologies. The direct EW plants operate at much lower electrolyte acidities because the spent electrolyte is typically returned to a leaching circuit. These plants are also able to operate at higher electrolyte temperatures, since there no risk of organic degradation in the absence of an integrated SX circuit. 

#### **Electrolyte Additives** 

#### <u>Cobalt</u> 

Except in Africa where the PLS contain significant cobalt and an adequate concentration reports to the advance electrolyte, cobalt is added, as the sulfate salt, to maintain a concentration of 80 to 250 mg/L Co in the electrolyte. Co<sup>2+</sup> promotes oxygen evolution, rather than lead oxidation, at the anode [8]. This stabilizes the PbO2 layer on the anode surface, minimises lead contamination of the depositing copper, and extends anode life [9]. A correlation between lead contamination of the cathode (which results from lead corrosion of the anode) and cobalt concentration in the electrolyte would be expected. As indicated in Figure 2, some positive dependence is observed, although it should also be noted that this effect can be counteracted by high current densities, high manganese or chloride concentrations, as well as by poor housekeeping. Most operations readily achieve a maximum lead contamination of the cathode of less than 3 ppm. Cobalt is not required for lead-free operations that use mixed metal oxide anodes.

#### <u>Smoothing and Grain Refining Agents</u> 

Smoothing agents promote the plating of dense, smooth copper deposits and minimize physical entrapment of electrolyte impurities. Guar gum, modified starches (polysaccharides), and polyacrylamides (typically added at 200 - 700 g/t cathode) are most widely used, since these are compatible with SX organics. Guar gum has traditionally been the standard smoothing agent for EW copper production but there has been a recent trend to lower cost smoothing agents. The oligosaccharide product, DXGF7, is finding increasing use in Chile and various other global operations, with particular benefits in reducing sulfur contamination of the cathode [10,11]. The direct EW operations employ thiourea and avitone, similar to the copper electrorefining industry. 

Most operations operate with 20 to 30 mg/L Cl in the electrolyte. Chloride ions act as grain refiners and promote the growth of dense, fine grained, low impurity copper deposits on the cathode. When using permanent cathode technology (stainless steel cathode blanks), the chloride concentration must be kept below 30 mg/L to avoid pitting corrosion at the top of the stainless steel blade at the electrolyte–air interface, which causes the depositing copper to stick and resist detachment [7]. Chloride typically occurs naturally in the electrolyte: Chilean operations with high con

centrations of chloride in their leach liquors include a wash stage in the SX circuit to prevent excessive transfer to the advance electrolyte. Some sites add HCl. #### **Electrical Parameters and Power Consumption** Table 2 and Figure 3 summarise the trends in cathode current density and reported current efficiencies as a function of the plant size and location. This technology facilitates automated cathode stripping, as well as the use of higher current densities and much lower manpower requirements [7]. Several smaller plants, mainly in Arizona and New Mexico, as well as old plants in Africa still employ copper starter sheets from electrorefined and electrowon copper. Average plating time is 7 days, giving an average cathode mass of 95 kg. Plating times vary from 3.75 to 14 days, depending on the current density employed. #### **Anodes** Most operations employ lead-alloy anodes. With the exception of Mutanda Mining (Democratic Republic of Congo, DRC), all plants with an upstream SX circuit use rolled Pb-Ca-Sn anodes in preference to cast anodes. Rolled Pb-Ca-Sn alloys remain the most common type of anode techno

logy used for copper EW, with only the direct EW plants preferring the use of cast Pb-Sb anodes. At the higher temperatures used in direct EW, the Pb-Ca-Sn alloy can recrystallize, leading to reduced strength and higher corrosion than the Pb-Sb alloy [12]. Regional differences in the composition of the leadalloy anodes are shown in Table 3. The average lifetime of lead-alloy anodes is reported as 6.9 years, with Salvador (Chile) and Northam (South Africa) reporting lifetimes of 10 years. Anode lifetime is affected by the current density and initial thickness of the anodes, but also significantly influenced by the manganese and chloride levels of the _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 10 electrolyte, electrolyte temperature, and care and maintenance of the anodes – including the frequency and duration of power failures (a major factor contributing to anode corrosion in Africa). Anode replacement decisions are indicated by increasing lead contamination of the cathode with anode age. Most cells are elevated approximately 1.3 m above the tankhouse floor to assist with cell draining and maintenance: in newer, lower cost designs, such as at Safford, cells are supported on the tankhouse floor.

#### **Acid Mist Control and Mitigation** 

An increasing awareness of the detrimental health effects of acid mist [15], as well as the associated corrosion cost, has led to the implementation of various monitoring and control measures and equipment innovations in recent years [16,17]. Plastic balls and beads on the surface of the electrolyte serve to reduce the intensity of bursting of the acid-containing oxygen bubbles released from the anode, while design of ventilation systems is critical to efficient removal of acid mist from above the cell surface.  There is an increasing use of hoods over copper EW cells, particularly in large, automated tankhouses, with the main suppliers being SAME (Chile) and Outotec (Finland). Cerro Verde (Peru), amongst others, uses a Nomad mat, a 3M product that covers the cell to collect the electrolyte mist but allows the oxygen to escape [18]. 

The use of acid-mist suppression agents is increasingly employed.  It is notable that natural products, such as those based on _Saponins_ species, are no longer used at any of the plants surveyed. These products degrade at current densities above about 250 A/m<sup>2</sup> . FC 1100 (supplied by 3M) is the reagent of choice at most operations. It functions by modifying the surface tension of the electrolyte, thereby reducing the energy with which the oxygen bubbles burst at the electrolyte–air interface.  It is also compatible with the organics employed in SX – an interfacial process that can be catastrophically disrupted by the presence of incompatible surfactants [16]. 

The accurate measurement of acid mist levels in a tankhouse remains problematic and difficult.  Local legislated threshold limits reported range from 0.47 mg/L in Chile to 1 mg/L in South Africa and Zambia, while individual plants (Los Bronces and Collahuasi, Chile) target as low as 0.2 mg/L on their specific sites. Of the plants responding, Mantoverde (Chile) measures acid mist most frequently at once per month, while most operations make this measurement only annually, typically at six positions in the tankhouse. The only standard method reported to be employed is OSHA Method ID113 (South African and Chilean operations) [19]. 

#### **EMERGING TECHNOLOGIES AND ADVANCED PROCESS CONTROL** 

As process intensification demands higher current densities, the difficulties of achieving electrode alignment and avoiding short circuits also intensify. One method by which this is overcome is by the use of a SELE frame in the cells [20,21], a system allowing accurate vertical alignment and spacing of

cathodes and anodes and eliminating the need for edge strips. This Chilean technology was implemented at Los Bronces, enabling current densities up to 460 A/m<sup>2</sup> to be achieved, and, more recently, has been installed at the Escondida Oxidos tankhouse. Another innovation contributing to the ability to successfully run at high current densities is the use of air sparging into the base of the cells. This assists with mass transfer at the cathode but also increases the necessity for acid mist control.  All of the BHP Billiton operations, as well as Codelco’s Gaby site, now employ air sparging. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

12 

Process control and automated monitoring systems are finding increasing application. Systems for wireless, online individual cell measurements of temperature, voltage, and current have been available for a few years. Hatch’s recently announced HELM Tracker™ technology [22] tracks and trends real-time current in individual electrodes and is presently being demonstrated at several tankhouses. Such systems allow rapid detection and mitigation of shorts and permit more uniform current distribution, which in turn improves current efficiency and energy consumption. 

The Hecker system [23] superimposes an alternating current on the direct current from the rectifier, which effectively causes periodic current reversal on the cathode. Dissolution will occur preferentially from areas with high electric field strength, providing a non-chemical mechanism for smoothing of the cathode deposit surface. 

#### **FUTURE OUTLOOK AND CONCLUSIONS** 

Although Chile currently dominates global copper production, it is likely that this region will be overtaken within the next decade by the African Copper Belt, comprising northern Zambia and southern DRC.  Significant projects have come on line in recent years and many operations are expanding. DRC examples include Kamoto Copper (250 kt/a capacity) currently ramping up from commissioning an SXEW circuit, Mutanda Mining (100 kt/a) with their EW7 circuit currently under construction, and the Tenke Fungurume expansion that will increase capacity to 220 kt/a. Major DRC projects include Roan Tailings (105 kt/a), Sinomines (80 kt/a), and Kipoi (50 kt/a). In Zambia, expansions of existing operations will increase Kansashi’s capacity to 150 kt/a and Chambishi to 60 kt/a. 

Occupational health and safety issues are expected to receive increased scrutiny and attention worldwide, leading to greater automation and better control and monitoring systems. There is currently a reluctance of many operations to make acid mist data available, due to perceived sensitivities concerning the labour force, but sharing of such information can assist in driving industry-wide improvements in measurement and mitigation. Although not in copper industry, the open and scientific approach to control and mitigating of acid- and nickel-containing aerosols at the Rustenburg Base Metal Refinery (South Africa

) [24] should be lauded and emulated. 

Increasing automation, the increasing use of current, voltage, and temperature monitoring systems, and anode developments are likely to dominate immediate equipment advances in copper EW.

#### **THE ROLE OF DISSOLVED IRON PRESENT IN COPPER ELECTROWINNING ELECTROLYTES: ITS INFLUENCE ON DEPOSIT QUALITY**

#### **ABSTRACT** 

The influence of dissolved iron present either as ferric ion, Fe(III), or ferrous ion, Fe(II), on the morphology, microstructure and crystallographic orientation of copper deposits has been investigated.  Experiments were conducted at 55°C in solutions containing 40 g/l Cu(II), 180 g/l H2SO4 and concentrations of Fe(III) and Fe(II) in the range 0 to 5 g/l. Additions of  Fe(III) as a single ion or in mixtures with Fe(III)  in concentrations up to 5 g/l transforms the basis-oriented reproduction (BR) type of copper deposits obtained in iron-free solutions into field- oriented texture (FT) type of deposits.  Addition of  Fe(II) as a single ion in concentrations of 3 g/l completely transforms BR type copper deposits obtained in iron-free solutions into unoriented dispersion (UD) type of deposits. Results of this study suggest that the modification introduced by the presence of iron dissolved in the electrolyte on the microstructure of copper deposits is mainly related to the intensity of the inhibition introduced by the presence of Fe(II) on the crystal growth process, even when iron is added as Fe(III).

#### **INTRODUCTION** 

Dissolved iron, either as ferrous or ferric ions, is ubiquitously present in copper electrowinning electrolytes. Its presence mainly arises from undesired incorporation of dissolved iron contained in the PLS solutions due to contamination arising from lack of selectivity and/or inefficient separation in the solvent extraction process. 

The presence of dissolved iron lowers the current efficiency at the cathode as the fraction present as ferric ion is reduced in the cathode. Factors which determine the extent of current efficiency in a certain plant include current density, iron concentration, temperature and agitation degree, and their effect have been studied and quantified by several authors [1, 2]. 

The influence of dissolved iron on the characteristics of copper deposits has been also investigated. Copper electrodeposits obtained at 300 A/m<sup>2</sup> , Cu 37 g/l , H2SO4 152 g/l , 40 °C showed a more crystalline and compact deposit when the concentration of Fe(III) was increased from 1 to 2 g/l  [3].    The presence of iron has also been reported to have an effect on the crystal orientation of the copper deposit.  Concentrations of 0.5 g/l Fe(II)  or 0.5 g/l of Fe(III) altered the peak heights  for the planes (111) and (200), while the one of the plane (220) decreased  [4] . Copper electrowinning studies in electrolytes containing LIX64N have shown that this organic affects the crystallographic orientation and surface morphology of the deposit when there is 2 g/l of Fe(III) in the electrolyte [5].  Recent studies on copper nucleation from copper electrowinning ele

ctrolytes on glassy carbon have shown that the presence of dissolved iron, mainly as Fe(II),  increases the  nuclei density on the substrate about 5 times [6]. 

The present work presents a study of the influence of dissolved iron on the morphology, microstructure and crystallographic orientation of copper deposits. The results provide a further understanding of the specific influence of Fe(III) and Fe(II) in the electrocrystallyzation process.

#### **EXPERIMENTAL** 

Copper electrodeposition experiments were conducted in a 5 l electrochemical cell immersed in a thermostatic water bath at 55 °C.  A lead plate was used as an anode and a 316 stainless steel plate as a cathode. The stainless steel plate was covered with an isolating material so that only an area of 5 cm x 5 cm was left free for deposition on the side facing the anode.  The electrolyte, which contained 40 g/l Cu<sup>+ 2 and 180 g/l H2SO4,</sup> was prepared dissolving AnalaR grade copper sulfate and sulfuric acid in distilled water. Iron was added as AnalaR grade ferric and ferrous sulphate in order to prepare electrolytes with different concentrations of Fe(III) and Fe(II) ions. Copper deposits were obtained by applying a current density of 300 A/m<sup>2</sup> during  24 hr, which produced a deposit of about 1 mm thickness. Copper concentration in solution was maintained constant during the experiment  by periodic  additions of copper sulfate. The formed electrodeposits, after being washed, dried and weighed, were subjected to metallographic, SEM and X-ray analysis.

In the case of experiment 8 which initially contained  only Fe(II), the decrease in current efficiency with respect to the blank experiment can be related to the building up of ferric ion concentration during the experiment due to partial oxidation of Fe(II) in the anode.

#### **CONCLUSIONS** 

The addition of dissolved iron in copper electrowinning electrolytes either as Fe(III), Fe(II) or combinations of both ions, modifies the microstructure of copper deposits with respect to the one obtained in

iron-free electrolytes. 

Additions of dissolved iron as Fe(III) or mixtures of Fe(III)/Fe(II)  in concentrations up to 5 g/l transforms BR type copper deposits obtained in iron-free solutions into FT type of deposits. 

Addition of dissolved iron as pure Fe(II) at concentrations of 3 g/l completely transforms BR type copper deposits obtained in iron-free solutions into UD type. The crystallographic orientation of these copper deposits becomes very close to the one of random copper. 

The modification introduced by the presence of  dissolved iron on copper deposits growth patterns is mainly related to the inhibition intensity of Fe(II). 

The modification introduced by the presence of iron dissolved in the electrolyte on the microstructure of copper deposits is mainly related to the intensity of the inhibition introduced by the presence of Fe(II) on the crystal growth process, even when iron is added as Fe(III).

#### **ABSTRACT** 

Copper electrowinning and electrorefining are very effective methods of industrial electrochemistry. These processes have been carried out without substantial fundamental modifications for a pretty long time. For instance industrial copper electrowinning and electrorefining processes are carried out on industrial scale as current-controlled processes. Review of literature data shows that the fundamental understanding of copper electrodeposition processes from industrial electrolytes is not sufficient. Although, the industrial copper electrodeposition is a very complex multi-ion process realized in concentrated electrolytes with migration, convection and diffusion as mass transfer modes, most of the published theoretical and experimental copper electroreduction studies are carried out in diluted electrolytes of relatively simple compositions and the theoretical approach of diluted electrolytes is used to analyze the results. Consequently, many conclusions concerning industrial copper electrorefining and electrowinning processes which are considered as general are valid only in the case of current-control electrolysis and/or for diluted electrolytes. Potential is the primary parameter of electrolysis to determine the electrochemical reactions which might undergo at the electrode. In the present paper some basic (theoretical and experimental) aspects of patented potential-controlled electrolysis in copper industrial electrolytes as a new method of copper electrorefining and electrowinning are presented and discussed.

#### **INTRODUCTION** 

Copper electrowinning and electrorefining are very effective methods of industrial electrochemistry. These processes have been carried out without substantial fundamental modifications for a pretty long time. For instance industrial copper electrowinning and electrorefining processes are carried out on industrial scale as current-controlled processes. Review of literature data shows that the fundamental aspects of copper electrodeposition processes from industrial electrolytes are not sufficiently studied. It should be noted that one of the fundamental differences between current- and potential-controlled copper electrodeposition processes is related to the fact that current density is the measure of the electrochemical process rate. Thus, the current-controlled (e.g. galvanostatic) process is the one where constant rate of electrochemical reaction is impose

d, regardless of what processes occur. Potential is the driving force of an electrochemical process and its value is the primary parameter to define what electrochemical reactions might occur (or what electrochemical reactions might not occur which is especially important for electrowinning process with electrolytes of low copper concentrations). 

Potential-controlled electrolysis has been a subject of studies directed by P. Los and his co-workers to recover metal nanoparticles and powders from copper industrial electrolytes and by-products. This was subject of a large number of publications [1-14] and in ref. [6] the following statement has been presented in Conclusions: 

„Finally, on the basis of the obtained results (high purity of deposited copper from industrial electrolytes) potentiostatic electrolysis with convective diffusion conditions at flat electrodes (not ultramicroelectrodes) should be studied as a potential option to industrial, galvanostatic electrorefining of copper. Particularly, further studies regarding the quality of the copper cathode electrodeposited potentiostatically should be carried out. In this case, the usage of copper cathodes (as in tradition electrorefining process) is preferable.” 

Since then numerous experimental and theoretical studies have been carried out by P. Los and co-workers on laboratory, pilot and industrial scale of potential-controlled copper electrorefining and electrowinning processes. It should be noted that publications concerning potential-controlled electrolysis in copper industry are concerned uniquely with manufacturing of (sometimes impure) copper powders and dendrites. Current publication is the first in a series where the results of laboratory scale experimental investigations are discussed. 

It is well known that either in the industrial or laboratory copper electrorefining the current density distribution is not uniform when dc current is applied to the electrolytic cell. In the first place in the industrial cell there is a variation in the average current density at different cathode – anode pairs [15]. However, even more important is the non-uniform current distribution at a single cathode. Numerical analysis of copper electrodeposition in diluted copper sulphate and sulfuric acid aqueous solution shows [16, 17] high level of nonuniformity of current density along the cathode in the case of rectangular electrolytic cell. Proper understanding of the copper electrolysis is not possible without taking into account a natural convection at the electrodes resulting from the buoyancy forces. In this case “an appropriate treatment of the coupling of fluid flow and multi-ion transport is required” [16]. According to [16] at the initial stages of copper electrodeposition diffusion and migration are the dominating ion-transport phenomena. Due to the electrochemical reaction (e.g. copper electrodeposition at the cathode and copper dissolution at the anode in the electrorefining process) the buo

yancy force becomes dominant and causes the electrolysis to achieve the quasi-steady state. In fact, the steady-state could not be achieved without natural (or forced) convection neither in potential-controlled nor current-controlled electrolysis. In the case of 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013_ 

_Santiago, Chile_ 

29 

these complex coupled transport phenomena the influence of the non-electroactive electrolyte components of the industrial electrolytic solutions should be accounted for. Namely, one should take into account the influence of the formation of the space charge distribution in the vicinity of the electrode which might affect the thickness of the local diffusion layer [18]. According to [19] the influence of the migration of indifferent electrolyte on the buoyancy forces should be analysed properly, too. Consequently, the concentrations of non-electroactive ions may have strong effect on the value of the limiting current density [20]. This effect is very important in the case of the copper electrorefining where concentrations of nonelectroactive ions change considerably with time of the process. Finally, the effect of the surface roughness of the electrode (and especially of the cathode) is practically ignored in the theoretical and experimental studies concerning copper electrowinning and electrorefining. Knowledge of the real or electrochemical surface area of the electrode [21] is crucial to understanding any heterogeneous electrochemical process as it is pointed out by the IUPAC [22] publication: 

“Comparison of experimental data with theories or of experimental results for different materials and/or from different laboratories to each other is physically groundless without normalization to unit reel area of the electrode surface. Different methods have been proposed to normalize experimental data specifically with solid electrodes.” 

As it was pointed out by A.J. Bard [23] the electrode roughness might be different depending on the time scale of the process i.e. it might be different for double layer charging and mass transfer processes. 

Obviously, the uneven distribution of current density at the cathode causes local (nonuniform) distribution in the potential. Other important reasons of  the non-uniform potential distribution and its changes with time of the current-controlled i.e. currently conducted industrial electrorefining process are: 

- crystallization of copper sulfate at the anode 

- production of compact, adjacent to the surface of the electrode, anode sludge layer 

- adsorption of organic  inhibitors on the surface of the anode 

- changes in real surface area of the cathodes and anodes 

- variation in the distance  between the cathode and the anode 

Uncontrolled change in the copper electrolysis potential in time and space (i.e. local) of the electrolytic bath can result in many adverse processes leading to obtaining the copper cathode of lower quality. Consequently, the natural choice of the industrial proces

s especially, at high current densities electrowinning and electrorefining is the patented [7] potentialcontrolled copper electrolysis process.

#### **CONCLUSIONS** 

Copper electrowinning and electrorefining are complex multi-ion processes realized in concentrated electrolytes with migration, convection and diffusion as mass transfer modes. Literature review shows that there are surprisingly small number of theoretical and experimental publications dealing with concentrated electrolytes and especially, with industrial copper electrolytes. In the present paper it has been shown that current-potential dependencies of steady-state currents or potentials registered at electrolyte identical with industrial electrolyte at copper cathode for the cases of current-controlled and potentialcontrolled copper electroreduction processes are different. Especially, in the region of mass transport control i.e. in the region of high current densities and overpotentials current-control (galvanostatic) process might be accompanied by the potential peaks which may cause codeposition of arsenic and other impurities. This conclusion has been confirmed by SEM/EDS studies of the cathodes after a 5 minutes electrolysis. Due to highly uneven current distribution at the copper cathode this phenomena might occur locally influencing the purity and structure of the cathode, particularly at higher current densities. Laboratory experimental results show that the potential window for obtaining pure copper at the cathode is much wider in the case of potential-controlled in comparison to current-controlled electrolysis. 

Presented results show that for high current densities copper electrorefining and electrowinning processes the method of choice is a patented [6, 27] method of potentialcontrolled electrolysis. Potential is a driving force of electrolysis and by fixing its value at the electrode one might control the purity and structure of the product even at the very low concentration of copper in industrial electrolytes. In the case of other parameters changing in the industrial potential – controlled copper electrolysis current density (i.e. the rate of the 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013_ 

_Santiago, Chile_ 

38 

process) should follow such changes rather than the potential. This way possible codeposition of the cathodic by-products might be avoided. FEM primary current distribution simulations show that more uniform current distribution is obtained for potential-controlled process. 

Finally, the ambiguity of the usage of the first Fick law to estimate the thickness of diffusion layer in the copper electrolysis from concentrated electrolytes was shortly discussed.

#### **MANGANESE AND REDOX POTENTIALS IN CU EW PLANTS** 

G. Zarate 

_Anglo American Chile Pedro de Valdivia 291, Santiago, Chile_ 

#### **ABSTRACT** 

The information on redox potential and its relationship with manganese, iron and chloride concentrations in the electrolyte has been reviewed for several SX-EW plants and published elsewhere. The objective was to verify if the published recommendations to maintain redox potential under control were met, namely: 

- A minimum Fe:Mn ratio of 8:1 or 10:1. 

- A minimum 1 g/l of total iron. 

- A Fe<sup>+2</sup> :Mn ratio of 6:1. 

It was found that, in general, only one of these recommendations was partially met and that the redox potential was highly dependent on the combine

d effect of chloride and iron concentration in the electrolyte. The highest redox potentials, above 900 mV, are obtained at chloride concentrations between 35 and 50 ppm when iron concentration is below 1 g/l. In order to maintain redox potentials below 800 mV, at these chloride concentrations, the iron concentration should be above 1.5 g/l. 

This information has been updated, including the nitrate concentration in the electrolyte, which effect in the redox potential is even more significant. 

The data analysis carried out, as well as the conclusions and recommendations obtained, are discussed in this paper. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

42 

#### **INTRODUCTION** 

In Chile there are several heap leaching-SX-EW plants processing copper oxide ores, copper sulfide ores or copper mixed ores. Most of the ores contain manganese as copper wad in variable proportions, depending on the ore being treated. Accordingly, the manganese content in the ore can be quite variable, ranging from less than 0.01% up to 1%, and as a result the manganese concentration in the pregnant leach solution (PLS) can vary from 0.1 up to 15 g/l. 

Therefore, the occurrence of significant concentrations of manganese as manganous ion, Mn<sup>+2</sup> , in copper leach solutions feeding SX plants is becoming increasingly common. However, the literature about manganese effects on an industrial scale is sparse. Only CodelcoChuquicamata in Chile [1] and Girilambone in Australia [2] have published some information about manganese problems in their SX-EW plants, although the presence of manganese in electrolyte solutions in EW operations around the world is well known [3]. 

At chilean operations, the manganese concentration in the PLS is quite variable as mentioned above. As a consequence, the manganese concentration in the electrolyte is also highly variable, ranging from less than 0.01 up to 0.5 g/l [4]. 

#### **REVIEW OF MANGANESE EFFECTS IN COPPER SX-EW** 

An analysis of the manganese problems in copper SX-EW by Miller [2] lists some of the main problems as reduction in the extractant loading capacity and extraction kinetics, chlorine generation in electrolytic cells, stainless steel cathode pitting corrosion, accelerated anode corrosion, and precipitation of amorphous MnO2. These problems are caused by the high oxidation potential of Mn<sup>+7</sup> , which could be generated by the highly oxidative environment of EW cells particularly during the early weeks of plant operation, when no electrolyte bleed is being utilized due to low iron concentrations in both PLS and electrolyte. As a result, the electrolyte redox potential increases from a normal level of 400 mV to as high as 900mV (the reference electrode is not mentioned). 

According to Soderstrom [5], from Cytec, at a high enough redox potential the oxime is degraded. It is stated to be highly concerned at 800 mV and no question of oxime degradation if the potential ever approaches 1,000 mV (reference

silver/silver chloride). 

Tjandrawan et al [6] concluded that permanganate is unstable in the presence of Mn<sup>+2</sup> ions and thus it will only be observed in the electrolyte at low concentrations of manganese ions under which conditions it is metastable. On the other hand, Mn<sup>+3</sup> ions are unstable except in very concentrated acid solutions and disproportionate in MnO2 and Mn<sup>+2</sup> . 

The effect of manganese on lead anodes has been summarized by Ellis [7], of RSR Technologies, as follows: 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

43 

- Manganese can react with the stable PbO2 corrosion layer on the anode surface making it unstable, less dense, less adherent, and susceptible to shedding. It causes MnO2 to build up in the layer according to 

#### MnSO4 + PbO2 = PbSO4 + MnO2 (1) 

- The PbSO4 is converted back to PbO2, but it is now deposited in loose layers which are easily spalled off causing contamination of the copper cathode. 

Tjandrawan et al [6] concluded that this is the likely mechanism according to their results. 

The measures conventionally used to keep manganese under control focus on reducing PLS entrainment in the loaded organic and maintaining manganese as Mn<sup>+2</sup> . In the first case, PLS entrainment can be reduced by using coalescers and/or washing stages and by reducing crud generation. 

In the second case, two techniques are applied to maintain manganese as Mn<sup>+2</sup> , the most common being the use of Fe<sup>+2</sup> oxidized by permanganate, according to reaction: 



High levels of Fe<sup>+2</sup> (or total iron) need to be maintained to obtain low levels of Mn<sup>+7</sup> . The published recommendations in this respect are, however, not clear cut: 

- A minimum ratio of 8:1 or 10:1 (assumed to be Fe:Mn) is necessary to keep manganese effects under control [2]. 

- A minimum of 1 g/l of total iron is necessary to prevent high redox potential levels in the electrolyte [2]. 

- For an operation with 2 g/l iron, the maximum safe level of manganese is 200 mg/L, which means a Fe:Mn ratio of 10:1 [2]. 

- A Fe<sup>+2</sup> :Mn ratio of 6:1 is necessary to keep redox potential under control [8]. 

The second technique to keep manganese under control is limited to the use of either sulphur dioxide or hydrogen peroxide. Since peroxide can strongly attack the extractant it is unsuitable. SO2 at low dosages is suitable. Girilambone has reported its use in a copper system to obtain rapid reduction of permanganate ions in the electrolyte inventory [2].

ify if the published recommendations to maintain redox potential under control are met, namely: 

- A minimum Fe:Mn ratio of 8:1 or 10:1. 

- A Fe<sup>+2</sup> :Mn ratio of 6:1. 

- A minimum concentration of 1g/l of total iron 

It has been found that, in general, only one of these recommendations is partially met and that the redox potential is highly dependent on the combined effect of chloride or nitrate and iron concentration in the electrolyte. The highest redox potentials, above 1000 mV/SHE, are obtained at chloride concentrations between 35 and 50 ppm when iron concentration is below 1 g/l. In order to maintain redox potentials below 800 mV/SHE, the iron/chloride concentration ratio should be above 35. 

Redox potentials higher than 1000 mV/SHE are also obtained when nitrate concentration is higher than 100 ppm and iron concentration is also below 1 g/l. 

It has also been found that there is no a significant effect of the manganese concentration in the redox potential, except at very low concentrations (<10 ppm). Even though, the redox potential at this concentration is below 800 mV/SHE. 

As there was no information during the early weeks of operation of each plant, it was not possible to confirm if the redox potential reaches more than 900 mV at very low iron and manganese concentrations, as it is mentioned in one of the references. However, this problem can be easily solved by including an iron sulfate addition system, as it has been done in Plants 1, 2 and 9.

#### **MASS TRANSPORT TO CATHODES IN THE ELECTROWINNING OF COPPER** 

Michael J Nicol, Suchun Zhang, Allan Kwang Loon Ang _Murdoch University, Perth, W. Australia m.nicol@murdoch.edu.au_ 

Alessandro Fiorucci _Industrie De Nora, Milan, Italy_ 

#### **ABSTRACT** 

Mass transport of copper ions to the cathode during the electrowinning of copper is important in determining the optimum current density in order to achieve deposits of acceptable physical and chemical quality. The results of pilot scale tests using full size cathodes and anodes (both lead-calcium-tin and titanium mixed metal oxide, MMO) is described. In these tests, silver ions have been used as a tracer in order to determine local mass transfer coefficients to 16 sections of each cathode. The current distribution as measured by the mass of sections of cathodes was found to be uniform with a slightly greater current density towards the bottom of both types of anodes. There is no discernible difference in current distribution between the anode types. Measurements of silver mass transport to the cathodes during electrowinning with the various anodes have shown that it is slightly lower but more uniform when operating with MMO than lead anodes.Mass transport is greatest in the uppermost regions of the cathode and, in the case of lead anodes, lowest about one quarter of the cathode height from the bottom. Mass transport increases with increasing current density and also slightly with increasing flow of electrolyte. When account is taken of the different conditions ans scale of measurement, the results agree with previously published data obtained using half width and smaller electrodes and cells. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

52 

#### **INTRODUCTION** 

Mass transport of copper ions to the cathode during the electrowinning of copper is important in determining the optimum current density in order to achieve deposits of acceptable physical and chemical quality. It is well known that the physical and chemical quality of copper cathodes deteriorates as the current density increases above about 350 A/m<sup>2</sup> under normal electrowinning conditions of 35 g/L copper in the spent electrolyte at 40<sup>o</sup> C. Higher current densities can be achieved only by increasing mass transfer using, for example, air sparging or by increasing the temperature and concentration of copper in the electrolyte. 

Previous studies aimed at the quantitative measurement of mass transport to copper cathodes under electrowinning conditions have been conducted in laboratory or pilot cells with cathodes which are not of commercial production size. Thus, the earliest paper [1] described the use of a silver tracer in the measurement of local mass transfer coefficients in a full height but half-width cell and the silver ion mass transfer coefficients increased by about 80% from the bottom of a cathode to the top when operating without agitation at a current density of only

180 A/m<sup>2</sup> at 25<sup>o</sup> C in a solution containing 25 g/L copper. Recirculation of the electrolyte through jets in the bottom of the cell resulted in significantly increased mass transfer to the cathode at the bottom but only a relatively small increase at the top which was probably due to the increased current density of 230 A/m<sup>2</sup> . Laser-Doppler anemometer measurement [2] were used to estimate the mass transport coefficients for copper at cathodes of height 190 mm and width 95 mm in a cell operated at 50<sup>o</sup> C and 200 A/m<sup>2</sup> in an electrolyte containing 50 g/L copper and 165 g/L acid. The coefficient increased from 12x10<sup>-4</sup> cm/s at the bottom to 31x10<sup>-4</sup> cm/s at the top of the cathode. 

The study reported in this paper extends the previous investigations using the silver tracer method to map mass transport to full size cathodes operated in a pilot plant under typical electrowinning conditions with both conventional lead alloy anodes and mesh metal-metal oxide anodes(MMO). 

#### **EXPERIMENTAL** 

The full scale pilot cell in the Murdoch University pilot plant facility consist of a 800L rectangular cell (active volume 750L) fabricated from FRP which is designed to accommodate 5 full size 1m<sup>2</sup> electrodes. The cell is fed by gravity from an agitated 200L pre-heater tank in which the temperature is controlled to 40<sup>o</sup> C.  The outlet from the cell feeds a 200L agitated regeneration tank in which cupric oxide powder can be continuously fed to make up the electrolyte to the desired acid and copper concentrations. The outlet of this tank feeds a large 3000L holding tank from which the electrolyte is pumped at an adjustable flowrate back to the preheater tank. The electrolyte enters the cell through a manifold in the bottom of the cell and exits through an overflow weir. A removable plexiglass cover over the cell was connected to a dedicated aqueous scubbing system which allowed for measurement of the rate of acid mist generation in the cell. A photograph of the plant is given in Figure 1 and of the top of the cell in Figure 2. 

The electrolyte contained 180 g/L sulfuric acid, 1.5 g/L iron and 65 ppm cobalt. No chloride was added as this would have interfered with the silver ion tracer. In all experiments, two cathodes and one anode were used in the cell. Copper was

MMO anodes (two mesh types with the same coating but slightly different mechanical structure) were DSA<sup>**®**</sup> anodes provided by De Nora.

#### **CONCLUSIONS** 

In this first experimental study of mass transport to the cathode during the electrowinning of copper using comercial size anodes and cathodes, several conclusions can be drawn 

1. The mass distribution as measured by the mass of sections of cathodes was found to be uniform with a slightly greater mass towards the bottom of both types of anodes. There is no discernible difference in the mass distribution between the anode types. 

2. Measurements of silver mass transport to the cathodes during electrowinning with the various anodes have shown that it is slightly lower but more un

iform when operating with DSA<sup>**®**</sup> than lead anodes. 

3. As expected, mass transport is greatest in the uppermost regions of the cathode and, in the case of lead anodes, lowest about one quarter of the cathode height from the bottom. 

4. The values of the mass transport coefficients agree with previously published values when the differences in conditions and cell size are taken into account. 

5. Mass transport increases with increasing current density and also slightly with increasing flow of electrolyte.

#### **INTRODUCTION** 

Sustainable development is an evolving concept that emerged in the 1980’s in response to a growing realisation of the need to balance economic and social progress with concern for the environment and the stewardship of natural resources. The idea has been defined as using, conserving and enhancing the community’s resources so that ecological processes on which life depends, are maintained, and the total quality of life, now and in the future, can be increased. 

In an attempt to further contribute to this on-going work, this

paper proposes a framework of sustainability indicators for the electrowinning industry and it uses it to qualitatively compare the SELE Technology against the conventional technology used in EW. 

#### **Electrowinning Process** 

The copper electrowinning process is the final stage in hydrometallurgical copper extraction. Throughout this process, copper ore is heap leached with sulphuric acid, concentrated via solvent extraction and electrodeposited into copper cathodes in electrowinning cells. The chemical composition of the electrolyte fed to the cells is between 48-40 g/L of copper, 140-180 g/L of sulphuric acid, 0.5-1.5 g/L of iron, less than 30 mg/L of chlorine and between 30-80 mg/L of manganese [1]. 

Electrowinning cells are rectangular ponds equipped mainly with stainless steel cathode plates and anodes composed mainly of lead. They are connected so as to form a circuit through which an electric current is passed between electrodes. Current efficiency ranges from 82% to 92% where energy efficiency losses are primarily associated to short circuits and the development of undesired products as a result of side reactions. For an EW plant with a production level of 180 000 ton/year the energy consumption achieves 75 MWh that is, a specific energy consumption of 2000 kWh/ton approximately. Thus, electrical energy is an important cost factor in copper EW plants [2]. 

#### **SELE**<sup>**®**</sup> **Technology** 

The SELE technology was developed to enhance the EW process in several aspects. It is made of several modules designed to work independently from one another or synergistically all together. Each module solves a particular process problem. The centre piece of the technology, ‘the core’, provides spatial confinement for the electrodes and when used in conjunction with the other modules it becomes a management tool for the production of copper cathodes. 

The following modules can be added to the core to better the overall copper deposition and the tankhouse environment. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_

#### <u>Electrolyte Distributor</u> 

Use of the electrolyte distributor module allows the fluid feed along the electrowinning cells at precise locations improving the copper ion transfer uniformity to the depositing surface. 

#### <u>Sparger</u> 

By forcing air through micro-porous hoses, small air bubbles are fed to the electrowinning cell from below the electrodes whose main objective is to reduce the boundary layer between the cathode surface and the electrolyte bulk. Additionally, the agitation produced by the air bubble homogenises the electrolyte concentration. 

#### <u>Acid Mist Confining</u> 

This module embodies an array of structures coupled as a system that promotes the efficient capture of the acid mist generated during the copper EW process. In addition, this technological innovation provides mist confinement and extraction during the sowing and harvesting of cathodes, as well as reduces heat los

s from the cell electrolyte. 

#### <u>Permanent Anodes</u> 

The use of permanent anodes decreases energy consumption and solid waste generation in EW process. The core is the perfect cradle for the permanent anodes because on one hand it prevents handling scratches of the anode surfaces and on the other it prevents short circuits during de EW process that damage permanently this type of electrodes. 

When the SELE Technology is implemented as a whole, that is with all its modules, a vast number of technical advantages over those exhibits by conventional technology - defined by electrowinning cells, equipped with anode spacers, cathodes edge strips, wishbone busbars, and cell-attached electrolyte manifold - appear. 

#### **EXPERIMENTAL AND DISCUSSIONS** 

#### **Sustainable Development** 

It has been proven difficult to encapsulate sustainable development in a short, punchy definition, which is also precise and unambiguous. This is reflected in the fact that there is no internationally agreed definition of what is meant by sustainable development. A number of general statements of broad principles have been made and have been widely accepted, but it has been left to nations, organizations and individuals to come up with more precise definitions [3, 4]. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_

Sustainable development indicators translate sustainability issues into quantifiable measures of economic, environmental and social performance aiming ultimately to help address key concerns. One approach is to use a single indicator or a composite indicator while another approach is to define a set of indicators of sustainability which are reported over time [3]. 

#### **Measuring Sustainable Development** 

#### – <u>Ecological Footprint Single Indicator</u> 

This concept has become a popular benchmark for sustainability. The ecological footprint measures how much biologically productive land and water are required to provide the resources consumed and absorb the waste generated by human population, taking into account prevailing technology. As it only concentrates on the use of resources, it is not a measure of overall sustainability and should be considered alongside of other social and economic indicators [5]. 

#### - <u>Environmental Sustainability and Performance Indices Composite Indicator</u> 

The Environmental Sustainability Index attempts to define and standardise measures of sustainability to enable comparison between nations. The indicators fall into five broad categories: environmental systems, environmental stresses, human vulnerability to environmental risk, social and institutional capacity to respond to issues, and global stewardship. 

The Environmental Performance Index (EPI) records performance against targets for 16 specific indicators in six policy categories – environmental health, air quality, water resources, productive natural resources, biodiversity and habitat, and sustainable energy – and two overall dimensio

ns of environmental health and ecosystem vitality [6]. #### Sets of Indicators – Over Time Performance Sustainable development is envisioned as the simultaneous satisfaction of a number of policy objectives – social, economic, and environmental. Therefore, one approach to measure progress in achieving sustainable development is to develop a set of indicators that shows progress in meeting such policy objectives. However, it is difficult to interpret a set of results and conclude if sustainable development has been achieved or to decide how to weight the importance of individual indicators with a single measure in time. On the other hand, tracking the progress over time of a set of indicators can provide a trend illustrating whether _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 65 development is becoming more or less sustainable. The choice of indicators will depend in part on the definition of sustainable development that is used and also on the availability and ease of indicator data collection. #### **EW Issues Identification** Since the identification of relevant issues that capture the specific characteristics of each type of industry, is crucial in the development of indicators the identification of sustainability issues must be done by considering all activities in the supply chain from ‘cradle to grave’. A flow diagram of the life cycle for mineral products and facilities was developed by Azapagic [7]. In it, the principal stages and stakeholders involved in this industry are depicted. #### **INTRODUCTION** 

De Nora DSA<sup>®</sup> anodes - well known in the electrochemical industry - are made of a titanium structure coated with a proprietary and patented Mixed Metal Oxide (MMO) layer consisting of precious metal and valve metal oxides. Since their introduction in 1960, DSA<sup>®</sup> anodes have gradually replaced technologies not considered environmental-friendly [1], replaced lead anodes in processes such as the production of copper foil [2-3] and are established as a viable alternative to the chemicals used for water disinfection [4], both for industrial and municipal water, as well as swimming pool maintenance.[5] Additionally DSA<sup>®</sup> anodes are found in electrogalvanizing of steel with zinc, printed circuit board manufacture, surface finishing and many others applications [6-7].

#### **The structure** 

The DSA<sup>®</sup> anode structure is designed for a current density of 500 A/m<sup>2</sup> , low ohmic drop (≤ 50 mV) and with a twenty year operating life which allows four recoating cycles. The structure, (Figure 7) comprises of: 

1. Two DSA<sup>®</sup> screens activated with a novel MMO (mixed metal oxide) coating tailored for the Cu EW application 

2. Ti clad Cu rods, for good current distribution & mechanical support of DSA<sup>®</sup> screens 3. Ti cups, to protect the conductive copper core from exposure to the electrolyte 4. Ti C-profiles, used as spacers in order to allow multiple recoating cycles (every 5 years) without exposing the copper core of the rods to guarantee anode planarity 

5. Hanger bar, as per Cu EW industrial practice 

The connection of the Ti clad copper rods to the hanger bar was made by brazing, in order to allow for high specific current feed (1 kA total current – 333 Amps per rod). The joint between hanger bar and Ti clad rod was sealed to prevent crevice corrosion phenomena, a typical weak point for other type of mechanical couplings. The other joints were either TIG or resistance spot welded to give good current distribution on the DSA<sup>®</sup> surface.

#### **Dendrite mitigation & monitoring system** 

A problem in Cu EW processes is the formation of nodules or dendrites on the cathode surface, which can decrease copper quality/purity. In addition, if the dendrite reaches the anode, it leads to short-circuiting events, decreasing the plant’s current efficiency and affecting the copper production. Although several systems to guarantee anode-cathode spacing are available on the market and leveling agents (also referred to as inhibitors) are used to decrease dendrite growth, at present there are no state-of-the-art technologies able to avoid short circuits in Cu EW cells. 

As the formation of dendrites is an operational issue related to the cathode and the electrolyte solution not controlled by the anodes, De Nora’s goal was the development of a system able to limit the effect of a short. With this scope, specific studies were conducted, stimulating dendrite growth and investigating the effect on the DSA<sup>®</sup> anode. A test campaign was carried out in a transparent Cu EW pilot cell installed in Milan; a 0.15 m<sup>2</sup> electrode pair was used, tracking the current flowing to the anode and the cathode. The tests

were performed at a fixed potential in order to reach the desired current density and then deliberately seeding a dendrite on the cathode surface, as seen in Figure 10 left. Tracking the dendrite during its evolution was challenging, the contact of the dendrite with the anode can be seen in Figure 11 at 0:04 minutes, the peak current at 0:07 minutes represents the point at which the current interlock cut the power to the cell. The corresponding damage to the DSA<sup>®</sup> anode structure is seen in Figure 10 right. 

A patent pending dendrite mitigation system (DMS), has been developed. The system, complete with the sensor, allows detection of the presence of a dendrite and halts it before it reaches the anode surface, allowing the plant personnel to take action in reasonable time. The DMS system protects the De Nora solution and its components from damage caused by shorts and also prevents the decrease in current efficiency which is typical during the shorting event.. The DMS is coupled with a new monitoring system designed and provided by Infotrol S.L. (De Nora’s partner), capable of measuring the inflowing current and detecting short events for each individual anode.

#### **ABSTRACT** 

This paper presents the preparation, characterization, and performance of a novel oxide coated titanium anode for copper electrowinning. The anode consists of an amorphous mixture of RuO2 and Ta2O5 formed on a titanium substrate by thermal decomposition of a precursor solution containing Ru (III) and Ta (V). The oxide coating comprises nano RuO2 particles which are uniformly dispersed in amorphous Ta2O5 matrix; it is like a sea-island hybrid structure. This novel anode gives some excellent properties for use in copper electrowinning (Cu EW). Oxygen evolution on the an

ode occurs at a low overpotential so that the cell voltage of Cu EW is much reduced by 700 mV compared to lead alloy anodes and is 160 mV lower than the oxide coated titanium anodes with amorphous IrO2. Some unwanted side reactions such as deposition of PbO2 are suppressed on the anode, which usually occurs on lead alloy or IrO2-based anodes. The patents of this smart anode technology are licensed to Republic Alternative Technology, Inc. (Ohio, USA) from Doshisha University (Kyoto, Japan) for commercialization with the registered trademark, MSA<sup>®</sup> .

#### **INTRODUCTION** 

Copper electrowinning (Cu EW) is a hydrometallurgical process to produce a high purity of copper, in which a sulfuric acid aqueous solution containing Cu<sup>2+</sup> is electrolyzed with a cathode and an anode. Electrowon copper is deposited on the cathode, and oxygen evolution occurs on the anode, of which a typical material is lead alloy, because lead dioxide formed on the alloy surface works for oxygen evolution and for a long time by suppressing high rate dissolution of lead alloy in such an acidic media. A titanium electrode coated with some platinum group metal oxides is also well known as an oxygen evolution anode in acidic aqueous solutions and the examples of the oxide coatings are a mixture of iridium oxide (IrO2) and tantalum oxide (Ta2O5) and a composite oxide comprising ruthenium (IV) and titanium (IV) (RuxTi1-xO2; x is usually 0.3). These noble metal oxide coatings give a low overpotential for the anodic reaction compared to lead alloy anodes, so that the anode potential and the cell voltage of electrowinning are reduced. The reduction of electric energy consumption is a significant issue for electrowinning industry, and the cell voltage reduction is needed to realize more energy-efficient processes. Another issue is also indicated from environmental perspectives; _i.e._ , an improvement in electrowinning plant environment by eliminating hazardous byproducts and wastes. Such byproducts and wastes include lead oxide, manganese oxide, and acid mist. 

One of the authors of this paper (MM) aimed and investigated to reduce oxygen evolution potential in acidic aqueous solutions and to suppress the byproducts on the anode, and finally invented a new class of oxide coating based on an amorphous IrO2-Ta2O5 mixture in 2003 [1]. This invented coating successfully demonstrated that oxygen evolution potential shifted more negative so that the cell voltage was reduced and no PbO2 was deposited in acidic CuSO4 solutions containing PbSO4 [2,3]. Amorphous IrO2-Ta2O5 coatings were further applied in electrowinning processes, and it was found that the cell voltage was significantly decreased and the anodic deposition of MnOOH or CoOOH as well as PbO2 was inhibited on not only amorphous IrO2-Ta2O5 coatings but also amorphous RuxTi1-xO2 coatings [4-14]. 

The anode technology for electrowinning has been further developin

g by our group and RuO2-Ta2O5 coated titanium electrodes produced by thermal decomposition have showed superior performance than lead alloy or amorphous IrO2-Ta2O5/Ti electrodes as oxygen evolution anode. In this paper, we report the preparation, characterization, and performance of the amorphous RuO2-Ta2O5/Ti electrode for copper electrowinning. The performance is compared to those of lead alloy or IrO2-Ta2O5/Ti electrodes. 

#### **EXPERIMENTAL** 

#### **Anode Preparation and Characterization** 

RuO2-Ta2O5 mixed oxide coatings were prepared by thermal decomposition on a titanium plate (1 cm x 5 cm x 1 mm), which had been degreased in acetone and etched in oxalic acid solution (10 wt%) at 90<sup>o</sup> C for 1 hour. Thermal decomposition was carried out by 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

87 

painting the precursor solution, which was made by dissolving commercially available RuCl3 and TaCl5 into 1-butanol containing 6 vol% HCl, dipping the titanium plate into the precursor solution, drying at 120<sup>o</sup> C, and finally calcined at a temperature in 260<sup>o</sup> C to 500<sup>o</sup> C. This painting to calcination process was repeated to make RuO2-Ta2O5 layers, which were crystalline, less crystalline, or amorphous phase, depending on the calcination temperature. The crystallographic structure of the oxide coating was characterized by X-ray diffraction (XRD) with CuK  radiation (Rigaku, Ultima IV). Surface morphology was observed by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) using a ZEISS Model ULTRA55. 

#### **Electrochemical Measurements** 

Electrochemical measurements were performed with a conventional three-electrode cell comprising a KCl saturated Ag/AgCl reference electrode and a platinum plate counter electrode or a two-electrode cell using a copper plate as the cathode. The working electrode or the anode were RuO2-Ta2O5/Ti electrodes, of which the geometrical surface area was 1 cm<sup>2</sup> (1cm x 1cm). For comparison, amorphous IrO2-Ta2O5/Ti electrodes [9] and commercially available Pb-5%Sb alloy electrodes were also used as the anode. The electrolytes used in the measurements were H2SO4 solutions with and without CuSO4. All measurements were done with a potentio/galvanostat (EG&G, Model 263A) controlled by electrochemical analysis software (EG&G, Model 270), and the electrolyte was held at 40<sup>o</sup> C without stirring.

#### **ABSTRACT** 

Lead-based anodes are the dominant technology for electrowinning process in sulfatebased media (e.g. copper, nickel, cobalt, and manganese). The lifecycle of electrowinning anodes is dependent upon electrowinning tankhouse operating conditions and maintenance of the anodes including cleaning and straightening. This presentation will focus on the operational aspects of maximizing the utilization of Lead electrowinning anodes.

#### **INTRODUCTION** 

Lead-based alloys are the primary anodes used in electrowinning from sulfate-based aqueous systems. Lead anode technology has evolved over the years migrating from pure lead and lead-antimonial alloys to the present day lead-calcium-tin alloys for copper electrowinning and lead-silver alloys for zinc electrowinning [1]. Also, the anode technology has migrated from cast microstructure to mechanically deformed, rolled, microstructures in search of improved mechanical properties and higher corrosion resistance that rapidly produces a protective oxide coating [2-4]. Although great strides have been made in the development of new alloys and production processes [5], the industry still has unresolved issues related to untimely corrosion which limits anode life and may lead to higher contaminant levels in the metal being produced. The comments in this work, though directed toward copper electrowinning, can be extended to similar phenomena i

n other metals electrowon from sulfate media (i.e. Zn, Ni, Co, Mn). #### **Phenomenology** The fundamental efficacy of lead-based anodes is dependent on the properties of PbO2 [6]. In fact, lead anodes are used predominantly in sufate-based electrolyte systems because of the protective ability of PbO2. In particular, the protective, adherent α-phase, which is the brown PbO2 layer closest to the anode surface, isolates the lead from the corrosive electrolyte. It is composed of rhombic, large, closely packed crystals. The β-phase of PbO2 which is black in color is the interface between the protective α-PbO2 and the electrolyte as shown in Figure 1. It is composed of tetragonal, fine, loosely adhering, needle-shaped crystals. The transformation of α- PbO2 to β-PbO2 is marked by formation of PbO, Pb(OH)2, PbSO4, and other complex sulfates as reaction intermediates. The mechanism of electrochemical oxidation of lead to lead dioxide in sulfuric acid is discussed in detail by Pavlov and Dinev [7]. α-PbO2

Figure 1- Lead Anode Corrosion in Sulfuric Acid _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 97 The oxidation of a lead anode is therefore determined not by the reaction rate of lead with sulfuric acid but by the mass transport of the ions participating in the reaction through the electrochemical layer. The rate of oxidation decreases drastically with the increase in the thickness of the layer and is prevented almost completely if the corrosion layer does not dissolve, flake-off or become porous [8]. This mechanism renders the lead anode virtually inert in sulfate media, and the main reaction on the outer surface of the β-PbO2 layer becomes the electrochemical decomposition of water into molecular oxygen. Therefore, the concentration gradient in the oxide layer becomes the main driving force for lead anode oxidation. The selection of the phases is dependent upon the generation of oxygen from the electrolytic decomposition of water, equation 1. The first stage in lead oxidation in the presence of oxygen is the formation of lead monoxide (PbO) and lead sulfate (PbSO4). As the anode potential increases, the surface layer of PbO/PbSO4 transforms to Pb(OH)2, followed by conversion to the insulating, tetragonal PbO, and then finally to PbO2 at still higher potentials. As seen in the electrochemical layering diagram (Figure 2), it is necessary to maintain an anode potential above 1.77V to maintain the protective α-PbO2. Unless the anode potential is consistently maintained above this value, the protective, adherent α-PbO2 converts to the loosely adherent β-PbO2 that flakes off and causes cathode contamination.
