Given a very high purity material we find that the grain boundary areas corrode significantly faster than the rest of the grain. The desire to minimize grain boundary corrosion by a balance of alloying element selection and microstructural design allows the grain boundary area to be engineered. However, operational issues can lead to unexpected corrosion behaviors which we will discuss moving forward. #### **General Corrosion** When a lead-based anode is exposed to a sulfate-based electrolyte, a thin film of PbSO4 is formed instantly. As soon as power is switched on, oxygen is evolved at the anode. The thin film of lead sulfate is then converted to β-PbO2. Upon further oxygen evolution, oxygen diffuses through β-PbO2 to form α-PbO2. The exact process during the oxidation of lead anode is determined by the structure and composition of the anode layer which, in turn, is determined by the electrode potential as indicated in Figure 2. To produce the lowest lead content in the copper cathodes, lead anodes should be cleaned periodically to remove the loosely adherent portion of β-PbO2. The objective is not to remove all the β-PbO2 layers, but only the non-adhering layers with a pressure water wash. The typical surface of a cleaned lead anode in use with the adherent α-PbO2 is shown in Figure 3. In order to increase the functional life of the anodes, it is extremely important not to damage the brown, adherent, protective α-PbO2 layer during anode cleaning by being overly aggressive. Figure 3- Hard, dense, adherent α-PbO2 (brownish color) _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 99 #### **Chloride Corrosion** While 20-30 ppm Cl- in a copper electrowinning electrolyte is helpful for grain refining/leveling of the cathode deposits, higher chloride concentrations (>30 ppm) increase corrosion of the Pb anodes due to the formation of soluble PbCl2 and other Pb-chloride complexes. Pb-chlorides are relatively more soluble than PbO2 or PbSO4. A steady state concentration of 55-60 ppm chloride in the electrolyte is too high, and a concentration above 100 ppm Cl- in the electrolyte is highly deleterious for the anodes. High chloride levels in the electrolyte also enhance the corrosion of stainless steel cathodes. Chloride also reacts

with any MnO2 on the anode surface to form MnCl2. Higher levels of chloride (200-300 mg/l) are tolerated in zinc electrowinning because the much higher levels of manganese in the electrolyte form a thick, protective layer of MnO2. 

Chloride corrosion is highest at or above the solution line because the higher oxygen concentration at the surface enhances the formation of Pb-chloride complexes. Organic burn, discussed later in this paper, exacerbates the solution line chloride corrosion due to the reactions below. 



In order to increase the functional life of lead anodes, it is imperative to keep chlorides levels in the copper electrowinning electrolyte to 20 – 30 ppm. 

#### **MnO4- Ion Corrosion** 

Copper electrowinning solutions often contain some manganese. Problems related to manganese in the electrolyte have been discussed by Miller [10] and Hughes et al [11]. Once Mn<sup>2+</sup> – gets into the electrolyte from the pregnant leach solution (PLS), it is oxidized to MnO2 and MnO4 . The MnO4<sup>~~-~~</sup> ions attack the protective lead oxide directly producing voluminous layers of PbO and Pb(OH)2 and amorphous MnO2 as intermediate products rather than PbO2. These layers do not adhere to the anode and flake off. Anode cleaning is very important to remove these layers to maintain low power consumption. Cifuentes et al [12] investigated the effect of various impurities in a copper electrowinning electrolyte on the rate of corrosion of lead anodes and found that manganese was the only element not to diminish the corrosion rate of lead anodes during current interruptions and precipitate significantly on the anode surface. They also concluded that the deleterious effect of manganese on the corrosion rate of lead anodes is more significant during normal tankhouse operation than during current interruptions. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

100 

Manganese reacts with stable PbO2 corrosion layer on the anode surface as illustrated in Figure 4 making the PbO2 layer unstable. This results in a less adherent surface oxide layer susceptible to shedding and causes MnO2 to build up on the anode/electrolyte interface. 

MnSO4 + PbO2  PbSO4 + MnO2 



The PbSO4 is converted back to PbO2 but is now deposited as larger, softer, lighter loose layers. These layers are also easily spalled off causing contamination of the copper cathode. The main effect of the increase in anode corrosion is cathode contamination with lead from occlusion of the PbO2 flakes. Particles settling on cathode can also contribute to dendritic growth of nodules. 

In order to increase the functional life of lead anodes, it is important to control the manganese content of the electrolyte to < 40 ppm. Addition of 100-200 ppm cobalt to the electrolyte helps in minimizing the deleterious effects of manganese corrosion. By decreasing the oxygen overpotential on lead anode, cobalt in the electrolyte promotes oxygen evolution in preference to manganese oxidation. Other measu

res to control manganese in copper electrowinning electrolyte are discussed in detail by Miller [13].

#### <u>Hanger Bar Corrosion</u> 

The main reasons for hanger bar corrosion are: 

- a. Intimate contact of the electrolyte with the hanger bar: The electrolyte level is sometimes raised to overflow the electrolyte in order to float off the entrained organics and mitigate organic burn issues. Electrolyte can also seep up to the hanger bars through the mist control foam or plastic balls by capillary action 

- b. Reaction of precipitated copper sulfate with protective lead. 

- c. Penetration of the electrolyte between the copper hanger bar and the cast-around.

#### - (a) <u>Electrolyte Hanger Bar Contact</u> 

If electrolyte is allowed to come in direct contact with the hanger bars as shown in Figure 5, copper will react spontaneously with H2SO4 to form CuSO4.5H2O. The exposed portion of the copper hanger bar between the end of the lead covering and the attachment to the bus bar is corroded rapidly. 

To increase the functional life of lead anodes, it is therefore important not to immerse the hanger bars in the electrolyte and not to allow the level of plastic balls or the mist suppressant foam to be within 3-4” of the hanger bars. 



Figure 5- Corrosion of Hanger Bar due to Immersion or Seepage 

#### (b) <u>Corrosion by Copper Sulfate</u> 

In covered copper tankhouses, acid rains down constantly on the anodes. As shown in Figure 6, copper reacts with sulfuric acid to form cupric sulfate (CuSO4.5H2O). But, what is not obvious is that cupric sulfate reacts spontaneously with lead to form cuprous sulfate [Cu2(SO4)2].

#### (c) <u>Electrolyte Penetration</u> 

This type of corrosion is illustrated in Figure 7 and is most prevalent in covered copper tankhouses. Corrosion penetrates into the area between the lead covering the bar and the copper bar creating a significant amount of copper sulfate. This results in a great expansion of volume to be constrained by the lead casting on the hanger bar. It expands and causes lead to bulge out as the amount of copper sulfate increases. Localized and independent corrosion cells are set up beneath the lead causing the copper to be corroded rapidly. 

Any plastic lifting devices being bathed in acid, as in covered tankhouses, become conductive and form a corrosion cell between the exposed copper and the lead coating. In a traditional cell house, where the acid mist is controlled by the addition of balls or mist suppressing foam, the plastic would be an insulator. In covered cells, the anodes, cathodes, and plastic lifting devices are bathed in acid mist which condenses on the cell covers. The lead will not be corroded, but the copper can be attacked even b

eneath the lead surface. 

In some cases the plastic can contact the cathode as it is not only a lifting device, but also a spacer. When the plastic is coated with acid and it contacts the cathode, a small current can be generated between the anode and cathode along the surface of the plastic lifting device. This small current can corrode the copper bar of the anode as well as accelerate the cell reaction beneath the lead covering of the anode. 

In order to combat this type of corrosion in covered tankhouses and prolong anode life, the hanger bar needs to be completely coated with lead. In this case, when the plastic lifting lugs are also used as spacers, there will be no corrosion of the anode bus bars. This is because lead forms a PbO2 layer or a PbSO4 layer on the surface which passivates it and prevents further corrosion.

#### **Solution Line Corrosion: Organic Burn** 

Solution line corrosion is often mistaken as weld corrosion where the weld line in welded anodes corresponds with the solution level. Solution line corrosion, such as shown in Figure 10 is observed on rolled/slotted and cast anodes where a weld line is absent. 

Although animal glue and thiourea are used as leveling agent and grain refiner, respectively, in copper electrorefining, they are not typically used in copper electrowinning because of their deleterious effect on the organic phase in solvent extraction [14]. Therefore, guar in concentrations of 1-5 ppm is used as a leveling agent in copper electrowinning. The degraded derivative of guar can accumulate in the electrolyte and can reach dangerous propor

tions, especially if concentrations significantly greater than 1-5 ppm are added. Besides, there can be carryover of organics into the electrolyte from solvent extraction. Organics rise to the surface due to density differences and cause solution line corrosion and can sometimes, literally burn at the solution line. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

105 





Figure 10- Corrosion at Solution Line by Organics 

Solution line corrosion occurs by the following mechanism. 

_Formation of free radicals_ 





These surface active polar molecules concentrate at the aqueous- organic interface at the solution line and react with the protective PbO2 as follows [15]. 

_Free radical attack on protective α-PbO2 to form unprotective PbO_ 



_Reaction of PbO with H2SO4 to form PbSO4_ 

PbO + H2SO4  PbSO4 + H2O (11) 

Recall that formation of PbSO4 is the first step in the sequence of reactions leading to the formation of protective α-PbO2. 

Since no alloy currently exists that can protect the anode, the only suitable action is to prevent organics from entering the tankhouse. In order to minimize organic burn, the organics from the solvent extraction process must be removed from the electrolyte before it reaches the tankhouse. Column flotation, sand filters or scavenger cells can be used for this purpose [16]. Electrowinning cells should be split into scavenger and production cells to minimize organic carryover from the Solvent Extraction Purification Plant [17]. Improved mixer-settler design enhances the distribution of the dispersion exiting the mixer and minimizes organic entrainment. In the case of settlers it is essential to provide for sufficient floatation time to float the organics. Other means employed on the tankhouses include scrubbing and scavenger cells as well as surface “vacuuming”. None of these methods are ideal as anodes will be exposed to organic attack, even if it is only the anodes in the scavenging section of the tankhouse. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

106 

Other solution line or near solution line corrosion mechanisms have also been observed in nickel tankhouses where anode bags are used. Anode bags prevent rising oxygen dispersion resulting in acid mist and PbO2 flakes being carried upward. The area above the solution line is wetted by acid mist. Since there is no electrical contact with the cathode through the electrolyte, there is insufficient positive potential to form the protective PbO2 layer. The rising PbO2 flakes act as an oxidizer of Pb while the acid forms PbSO4. The latter is partially soluble and does not protect the anode. 

#### **Uneven Electrode Spacing** 

The electrode spacing should be as consistent as possible. Figure 11 indicates that this is not always the case in a tankhouse. The inter-electrode spacing in copper tankhouses is usually about 4” (10 cm). Below this spacing, the risk of shorts due to electrode alignment and dendritic growth of nodules becomes unacceptable. If a

dendrite touches the anode, the protective PbO2 gets overheated, is softened and spalls off under conditions of intense turbulence caused by oxygen evolution. This process is autocatalytic and blows holes through the anode. 

The potential of the electrowinning cell is the sum of respective half-cell reaction potentials as well as the ohmic drop in the electrolyte, busbars and other competing electrochemical reactions. The ohmic drop in the electrolyte is a function of the electrode spacing, ionic mobility, and concentration of the species in solution and current density. Nonuniformity in electrode spacing affects power consumption and determines plating quality. 

Therefore, to increase the useful life of lead anode and to decrease power consumption, it is important to maintain uniform anode-cathode spacing and monitor and eliminate the shorts as soon as they are formed.

#### **Ineffective Anode Design** 

Anode design is a crucial yet often overlooked or undervalued aspect of anode life optimization. Anode design is an important consideration in cathode plating efficiency. The anode hanger bar was moved closer to the solution line in an effort to minimize the size of the lead anode. When this is not taken into consideration with the design of the anode hanger bar, various modes of anode damage follows owing to both corrosion and mechanical mechanisms. 

Corrosion stems from the exposed copper bar’s proximity to the electrolyte level as well as to the presence of hoods for acid mist control. The captured acid mist runs down the hood and drops onto the exposed copper bar. With effective design, protection is extended to protect such vulnerable areas of the hanger bar. Figure 12 demonstrates the “evolution” of anode hanger bar encapsulation design from left to right. In addition to improvements on hanger bar design, the use of epoxy sealants at the vulnerable ends of the lead encapsulation has also been successfully tested and implemented. 







Figure 12- Progressive evolution in hanger bar design 

With mechanical damage the electrolyte is carried in the acid mist and enters the space between the copper bar and the protective lead encapsulation. Expansion upon crystallization of the ions in solution forces the lead away from the copper bar. This process becomes iterative resulting in the eventual demise of the anode as in Figure 13.

#### **Temperature Fluctuations** 

The lead anodes should be protected from temperature fluctuations of the electrolyte. Due to differences in the coefficients of thermal expansion between the lead anode and PbO2 on the surface of the anode, a rapid drop in electrolyte temperature of about 10 C may produce spalling of the PbO2 layer from all the anodes in a tankhouse simultaneously. Electrolyte temperature fluctuations o

f a few degrees are not uncommon in tankhouses in desert areas but a sudden cold weather front can result in electrolyte temperature fluctuations of 10 C or more especially in open tankhouses. An electrolyte heating system is therefore recommended to prevent rapid fluctuations in temperature. 

#### **Addition of cobalt** 

The main purpose of cobalt addition to the copper electrowinning electrolyte is to depolarize the oxygen evolution reaction on a lead anode. This decreases the oxygen evolution overpotential, and results in savings in power consumption. Cobalt also protects the lead anode from corrosion and the solution, i.e. cathode copper from lead contamination. The oxide layer in the presence of cobalt is very thin and dense. The adsorbed Co<sup>2+</sup> ions on the lead anode hinder the penetration of oxygen into PbO2 lattice thus decreasing the rate of PbO2 formation. In other words, cobalt promotes the evolution of oxygen from the anode surface rather than the corrosion of the anodes. Cobalt concentrations of 100-200 ppm are common in copper tankhouses around the world, and the exact level of cobalt in an electrolyte is dependent on the manganese content and the current density. Based on our experience, at a current density of 300 amps/m<sup>2</sup> , a cobalt content of 120 ppm or more may be required to produce low lead content cathodes. The adsorbed cobalt ions seem to harden the PbO2 on the anode surface and make it less subject to spalling. As the current density is increased, the cobalt content should also be increased. The optimum level of cobalt in the electrolyte should be determined experimentally for a particular tankhouse. Once determined, care should be taken to ensure that the cobalt content of the electrolyte is maintained at the specified level particularly in the presence of manganese in solution. 

The build-up of iron in the copper electrolyte results in a loss of current efficiency due to the Fe<sup>2+</sup> /Fe<sup>3+</sup> redox reactions at the cathode and anode respectively. In order to control the iron content, a portion of the iron-rich electrolyte is periodically bled. However, cobalt is also lost from the system with the bleedstream electrolyte. A drop in the cobalt content for several days may cause the cobalt to desorb from the anode surface, soften the flakes, and increase the lead contamination of the cathode. Therefore, cobalt must be metered in continuously to the electrolyte to replace the cobalt that is lost through the bleed. Cobalt is a significant operating cost to the copper SX/EW operation. 

#### **SUMMARY** 

The different types of corrosion processes affecting lead anodes discussed above are by no means exhaustive but represent a vast majority encountered in practice. In spite of this, lead alloys are the preferred material for electrowinning anodes from acidic sulfate solution because they are insoluble and have the ability to form a protective PbO2 layer. They are corrosion 

_Proceedings of

Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

109 

resistant, economical and have an acceptable operating voltage. There are alternate anode technologies out there but none can compete economically with lead anodes. Moreover, limited, long-term industrial test work has been carried out with the alternate anodes to prove their technical, practical and commercial viability. 

Rolled Pb-Ca-Sn anodes are used widely in copper electrowinning. They are strong, have a particularly high corrosion resistance, good form stability, and they have a low potential drop between the hanger bar and the lead sheet. The electrochemical performance of lead anodes is independent of whether they are made from primary or secondary lead. If the anodes are maintained properly according to the broad guidelines discussed in this paper, we can expect an optimum functional life.

#### **OPERATION OF ALTERNATIVE ANODES AT CHINO SXEW** 

S. Sandoval, R. Garcia, T. Neff, and N. Schnebly _Freeport-McMoRan Mining Company 4521 U.S. Highway 191 Morenci, USA Scot_Sandoval@fmi.com_ 

#### **ABSTRACT** 

In 2006, the Freeport-McMoRan Copper & Gold Inc. (FCX) Technology Center in Safford, Arizona undertook research to develop an alternative anode (AA) for copper electrowinning.  An anode development lab was established that included bench-scale electrowinning cells as well as accelerated life testing cells.  In 2008, the Chino electrowinning plant was fully converted to the new FCX anode becoming the first copper electrowinning plant in the world to exclusively utilize non-lead anodes.  A 15% electrowinning voltage reduction was achieved.  Cleaning of electrowinning cells for lead sludge and addition of cobalt to the circuit for stabilizing lead anodes were discontinued.  Lead content of copper cathodes measured less than 0.3 ppm. 

This paper describes operational results and findings with alternative anodes at Chino over the ensuing years.  Chino has exhibited higher than expected current efficiency, measuring 93% at 3.7 g/L iron in electrolyte.  Chino is operating without heat retention balls on the cells and achieves low acid mist with only small additions of FC1100. Use of Cyquest 900, a polyacrylamide, as the cathode smoothing agent has allowed Chino to operate with over 300 ppm Mn in electrolyte without depositing Mn on the AA surfaces.

#### **INTRODUCTION** 

It was reported in 2010 [1] that FCX’s Chino (New Mexico, USA) SXEW plant had fully converted to an alternative anode (AA) developed at FCX’s Technology Center in Safford, Arizona in cooperation with Republic Alternative Technologies.  The anode was comprised of a copper hanger bar, multiple

conductor rods attached to the hanger bar, and expanded titanium mesh screens attached to each side of the conductor rods.  On the outside of each titanium mesh screen was deposited a catalytic coating developed by FCX. 

The motivation for the work was to decrease operating cost by lowering electrowinning cell voltage and by eliminating the need for cobalt additions to electrolyte (for decreasing lead anode corrosion rate).  In addition removing lead anodes from the circuit also removed lead contamination from copper cathode and the need to regularly remove lead sludge from EW cells. 

The catalytic coating consisted of an under-layer of crystalline Ir/Ta Oxide and a top-layer of amorphous Ir/Ta Oxide (Figure 1). The under-layer provided for the targeted lifetime of the coating under oxygen evolving conditions in copper electrolyte.  The top-layer together with the under-layer met the targeted voltage reduction of 15% versus a lead anode.  Shown for the coating displayed in Figure 1 (from bottom to top) is the titanium substrate, the crystalline under-layer, and the amorphous top-layer. On the very top is a coating applied for analytical purposes. 



Figure 1- SEM micrograph of catalytic coating on titanium anode substrate 

The Chino conversion took place in 2008 after about two years of bench and pilot-scale development.  A key to the development was establishing a small Anode Lab at FCX’s SXEW Test Facility located in Morenci, Arizona.  The lab operated continuously using plant copper electrolyte from Morenci’s Modoc SX plant.  It was necessary to operate with plant electrolyte in order to optimize the AA coating in terms of voltage performance and also in terms of lifetime performance in a copper electrolyte. 

Since 2008 Chino has been operating without lead or cobalt in the SXEW circuit.  This paper reports on operational findings with continuous operation of AA.

#### **RESULTS AND DISCUSSION** 

#### **Current Efficiency** 

Upon conversion to AA and with double-double electrode contact furniture, tankhouse current efficiency increased by 2% as shown in Figure 2.  Figure 2 displays the switchover from the west tankhouse, which utilized lead anodes with single electrode contact cell furniture, to the east tankhouse, which utilized AA with double-double electrode contact furniture.  After the switchover the west tankhouse was shut down.  The combination of AA and double-double electrode contacts proved beneficial in terms of current efficiency performance.  A double-double electrode contact system is important in combination with AA because of the lighter weight of AA compared to lead anodes.  The Chino double-double contact system consisted of a notched round main bar with rounded-top rectangular equalizer bars. The notch on the main bar provided two pressure-point contacts for each electrode hanger bar.

to east tankhouse 

Figure 3 shows that current efficiency continued to measure in the 93-94% range at 3.5-3.7 g/L Fe in electrolyte.  Using a model developed in collaboration with University of Utah [2] a current efficiency of 92-93% was predicted for Chino operating conditions of  269 ASM current density, 3.5 -3.7 g/L Fe (2.5-2.7 g/L Fe<sup>3+</sup> ), and 35 g/L copper in electrolyte at 32<sup>o</sup> C electrolyte temperature (i.e. Chino does not utilize an electrolyte heater).  This model does not take into account short circuits which occur in the Chino tankhouse which decrease current efficiency, and indicates that Chino is exceeding current efficiency expectations by at least 1%. 

#### **Acid Mist** 

It was observed in the east tankhouse after conversion to AA that acid mist was lower than expected.  Acid mist measurements showed that Chino was 88% lower in acid mist than a comparable tankhouse.  The measurements were taken by setting up filter cartridge pumps over operating

#### **Manganese in Electrolyte** 

As noted above in Table 1 Mn in electrolyte typically was near or above 300 ppm at Chino after the conversion to AA, a level not normally operated in copper electrowinning.  If lead anodes were in use the 300 ppm Mn would accel

erate corrosion by depositing on lead anode surfaces which can lead to lead flaking. As shown in Figure 4 Mn deposition did not occur on AA anodes with increasing Mn concentration. 

A hand-held x-ray fluorescence (XRF) unit was used to scan AA anode surfaces.  Further investigation at FCX’s SXEW Test Facility showed that the Cyquest N-900 cathode smoothing agent used at Chino was responsible for preventing Mn deposition.  Cyquest N-900 is a polyacrylamide reagent.  A test was designed in which Mn was increased in Test Facility electrolyte and the effect of Cyquest N-900 measured.  Results are displayed in Figure 5. 

In this test Mn concentration in Test Facility electrolyte was increased to 100 ppm and simultaneously Cyquest N-900 addition was stopped.  Analysis by XRF showed that Mn deposition began without the presence of Cyquest N-900 and increased to a level of 16% Mn.  When Cyquest N-900 addition resumed the presence of Mn on AA surfaces disappeared.  The polyacrylamide smoothing agent served a double purpose, to smooth the copper cathodes and to maintain the AA surfaces free of Mn deposits.

#### **Anode Coating Performance** 

The wear rate of the Chino AA anode coating was monitored using in-plant XRF measurements.  Sample anodes were periodically removed from solution, rinsed with water, and allowed to dry.  A hand-held XRF unit was used to measure relative concentration of Ir remaining on the screen.  A plot of XRF measurements at Chino is shown in Figure 6. 

Three coatings were in operation in the tankhouse, labelled 1100-A, 1100-B, and 1200-C. Coatings 1100-A and 1100-B have performed about the same.  Coating 1200-C is on a better trend in terms of lifetime.  Coating lifetime was projected to be minimum 6 years based on accelerated testing in the Technology Center Anode Lab.  It appears that this forecast will be met with coating 1200-C exceeding expectations. 

As shown previously in Figure 1, the AA coating consists of an under-layer that is deposited on the titanium mesh substrate, followed by a top-layer that is the working surface of the coating (i.e. to evolve oxygen in the copper electrowinning cell).  The combination of the top-layer and the under-layer yield a 15% voltage savings as compared to electrowinning with lead anodes.  With continued operation the coating will wear as a function of oxygen evolution rate, or in other words, as a function of current density.  As the coating approaches the end of its useful life it is anticipated that the majority of the remaining coating will consist primarily of the under-layer, which is crystalline Ir/Ta oxide as compared to the top-layer, which is amorphous Ir/Ta oxide.

The crystalline Ir/Ta oxide coating operating alone in Technology Center’s Anode Lab produced a voltage savings of about 5% versus lead anodes.  It follows that as the coating is nearing required replacement voltage savings will decrease.  The crystalline under-layer is utilized as an insurance policy.  It is difficult to physically crack and will prevent unexpected failure of the anode that could lead to an interruption in copper production. 

Voltage savings after 5.5 years of AA operation at Chino was calculated to be 5% versus lead anodes.  This was determined by comparing older AA anode cells, measuring a cell voltage of 1.95 volts at 29,000 amps (256 ASM) and 32<sup>o</sup> C, to a newly installed AA cell, with a cell voltage of 1.80 under the same conditions.  The original measurements at Chino after conversion when the west and east tankhouses were operating together were 1.90 volts for lead anodes and 1.61 volts for AA (at 18,000 amps, or 159 ASM).  The west tankhouse was then shut down and all production shifted to the east tankhouse in which amperage was increased.

#### **SUMMARY** 

Freeport-McMoRan Copper & Gold Inc. (FCX) Chino SXEW plant (New Mexico, USA) has been operating with alternative anodes (AA) for about 5.5 years.  Because of the lead-free anode structure, Chino has operated without lead contamination of copper cathode, without cobalt additions to electrolyte, and without lead sludge cleaning and handling.  The AA coating is meeting lifetime expectations of minimum 6 years, and voltage savings after 5.5 years is measuring 5% compared to the typical operating savings of 15%. #### **INTRODUCTION** 

The paper emphasize the benefits of Electrolyte Soft Aeration in Cells, achieved in Pilot Test and Industrial Implementation in Electrowining Tankhouse, generating a significant impact in cathode production quality and specific consumption of energy. 

#### **GENERAL BACKGROUND OF ELECTROLYTE SOFT AERATION IN CELLS** 

For our objective of promoting continuous improvement of processes and putting in service the best industrial practices in the industry aimed to improve quality of production cathodes, the application of a new technology based on soft agitation of the electrolyte in the cells was evaluated, an innovation already implemented in national plants with good results. Work on this project was initiated in February, 2009, with the start of a Pilot testing program that was concluded with satisfactory metallurgical results after three months, and supported the recommendation of extending its installation to the entire Electrowining Tankhouse. 

The supplier ANCOR TECMIN S.A. has lodged in

the Industrial Property Registry of Chile its proprietary development of a soft electrolyte agitation technology based on an isobaric air diffuser structure for introducing air at low pressure in the form of micro bubbles into the electrolyte, whose technical description was reviewed by the Legal Department of Gabriela Mistral Division, validating its freedom for use. 

#### **FUNDAMENTALS OF ELECTROLYTE AERATION TECHNOLOGY IN CELLS** 

Soft agitation of the electrolyte inside electrowining cells favors uniformity of the mass transfer, cinematic viscosity and flow velocity throughout the entire cathodes surfaces, generating an homogeneous flat metallic deposit, exempt of preferential growths, and thus, without nodules nor short-circuits, enhancing overall obtainment of a copper chemical quality with minimum contents of Sulfur and Lead, main species whose concentrations determine cathode production inclusion in Grade “A” classification. 

#### **ADVANTAGES OF ELECTROLYTE AERATION TECHNOLOGY IN CELLS** 

The implementation of electrolyte agitation technology with controlled air diffusion in the cells constitutes an effective option to substantially improve the physical and chemical quality of electrowon cathodes on a sustained basis, through generation of the following effects: 

- Homogeneity of electrolyte concentration in the cathode-liquid interphase due to increased velocity of ion migration over the entire electrodeposit surface. 

- Reduction of the limit layer thickness.

#### **IS CELL VOLTAGE A RELIABLE INDICATOR OF  SHORTS OR POOR CONTACTS?**

#### **ABSTRACT** 

Measurements of cell voltages on several copper, zinc and nickel tankhouses have been made with a view to assessing the reliability of cell voltage as an indicator of shorts or poor contacts in electrowinning cells. In addition, simulations of current distribution in contiguous cells have been made using commercial electrical circuit simulation software adapted to the flow of current in electrowinning cells using the normal Walker configuration. 

The results of both plant measurements and simuations have revealed that the use of cell voltage as an indicator of the presence of shorts or poor contacts in electrowinning cells can be ambiguous. Both in the measured cell and in adjacent cells, erroneous conclusions can be drawn depending on the location of the voltage measurement. 

The important factors which determine the variations in measured cell voltages have been identified. It is recommended that operations make simple voltage measurements in a number of locations in a number of cells to establish the reliability of such measurements for their operations.

#### **INTRODUCTION** 

The ability to measure individual currents to cathodes and/or anodes enables operations to correct issues associated with poor current distribution in an electrowinning tankhouse.  However, currently there are no commercially available devices that can easily and accurately measure currents in all the anodes or cathodes of zinc or copper electrowinning tankhouses. Indirect methods have been in use for some time that enable plant personnel to detect “hotspots” in busbars and header bars using portable or cranemounted infrared cameras. However, as pointed out in two recent reports [2,3], these hotspots can arise from either a short circuit between the anode and cathode (which results in a higher current) and/or a poor contact of the header bar with the busbar (which results in a lower current but greater power dissipation in the contact).  More recently, several companies [4,5,6] have developed systems which monitor the voltage (and, in two cases, the temperature of the electrolyte) of each cell and transmit the data via a wireless signal to the control room. It is claimed that these cell voltages can be used to identify cells with poor current distribution due to either of the above defects. Thus, a lower (than average) cell voltage is interpreted in terms of

a short and a higher voltage in terms of one or more poor contacts in the cell. In one case, use of several such measurements at various points in a cell using segmented intercell bars has been claimed to provide more detailed information of the location of the problem electrodes within each cell. In previously reported [1] simulations of current distribution in tankhouses, it became apparent that the cell voltage will depend on the position in the cell where it is measured. This follows from the fact that the busbars in actual operation do not have zero resistance and therefore have small but finite and different voltage drops in sections between the header bars depending on the current flowing in the sections. Actual measurements taken in several operating tankhouses have confirmed this prediction and this paper will summarize the data obtained and will present simulations which will further illustrate the sources of these variations in cell voltage. #### **EXPERIMENTAL** As described fully in a previous publication [1], National Instruments Electronics Workbench Multisim 10 was used to construct and simulate the electrical equivalent of an electrowinning cell. The program handles the design and simulation of complex electrical circuits, which can include both standard and customised linear and non-linear devices. Circuits can be easily modified and the operating states can be measured and logged to determine voltages and currents at any point in the circuit. Measurements of cell voltages at the various tankhouses were made using a HP digital voltmeter and current through individual cathodes were measured using a clamp meter or a locally constructed hand held meter based on Hall effect transducers. For hypothetical zero busbar and contact resistances, the total cell current less that passing through the short would be distributed equally between all remaining cathodes and the cell voltage would be lower but the same at any point in the cell. This can be shown to be 1.936V for a short of five times the normal current density. However, the busbar does not have zero resistance and the data shown in Figure 5 was obtained by conducting simulations for different short circuit current densities. In this case, a busbar resistance of 1uOhm (between the header bars of adjacent anodes and cathodes) was used which is typical of the resistance of the triangular bars used in most copper electrowinning tankhouses. 

A low busbar resistance would result in the short “robbing” the remaining cathodes of current with those closest to the short passing lower currents than those far removed (ends) from the short.  This is apparent from the simulated voltage measured at cathode 16 as shown in Figure 5. Measurement of the cell voltage at the ends of the cell would give a lower voltage than that in the absence of a short due to the lower current density with the effect being greatest at the end closest to the short i.e. at cathode 1. The decrease in measured cell voltage at the ends of the cell would be expected to increase as the magnitude of the short increases as shown in Figure 5. Measured short circuit currents in copper cells are generally less than about five times the normal cathode current and, for the case shown in Figure 5, this will result in a lower (due to the short) measured cell voltages at the ends of the cell of less than 5mV.

#### **CONCLUSIONS** 

The results of both the actual plant measurements and simulated cell voltages have demonstrated that the interpretation of cell voltage as an indicator of the presence of shorts or poor contacts in electrowinning cells can be ambiguous in that both within the cell of interest and within adjacent cells, erroneous conclusions can be drawn depending on the location of the voltage measurement. The important factors which determine the measured cell voltages have been identified and it is recommended that operations make the desired simple voltage measurements in a number of locations in a number of cells to establish the reliability of such measurements for their operations. 

Unambiguous tracking of shorts and poor contacts will require alternative techniques such as those under development for actual current measurements in anodes or cathodes.

#### **ABSTRACT** 

In normal practice, the design of intercell contact bars (ICCB) for electrowinning is based on previously used designs or rules of thumb, rather than first principles. The major operating cost of electrowinning is power consumption. The ICCB is responsible for a significant portion of the power costs due to electrical resistance through the circuit. The electrical resistance of the ICCB system is comprised of electrode contact resistances and the bulk electrical resistance of the ICCB. The theory suggests that contact resistance is a function of electrode mass, whilst the bulk resistance is calculated using a function of cross-sectional area. ICCB’s are made from copper which is a high quality electrical conductor. The electrical resistivity of copper i

ncreases as temperature rises, resulting in an increase in the resistance through the ICCB electrical circuit. Electrical resistance also causes heat generation due to the Joule effect. By reducing the amount of heat that is generated it is possible to minimise the power consumption associated with the ICCB. This paper reviews several common ICCB configurations to determine their ability to reject heat and minimise the electrical resistance through the ICCB circuit.

#### **INTRODUCTION** 

Hatch is in the process of completing a study to compare a number of intercell contact bar designs currently available in the market for use in electrowinning and electrorefining plants. Previously Hatch has published an introductory paper discussing the calculation of the contact resistance between the intercell contact bar and the electrodes [1]. The different contact bar designs were discussed, and further work was identified to enable an improved comparison to be made. One of the items of further work was the impact that the ICCB thermal effects had on resistance and power consumption when subjected to various operating conditions. This paper explores these thermal impacts. 

Electrode contacts are established where the header bars sit on the ICCB. As current flows through the ICCB and these contacts are made, heat is generated due to the electrical resistivity of the ICCB and the contacts according to the Joule Effect. The header bars also generate heat as current passes through them. If the current is stable, these sources of heat will increase the temperature of the ICCB system to a steady value whereby the heat generated will be balanced by the heat loss of the ICCB system due to convection, radiation and conduction. 

It has already been established that most of the electrical resistance in ICCB systems is due to the contacts rather than the bulk of the ICCB copper and it has been concluded that the presence of continuously growing oxide films on the copper contact surfaces can increase contact resistance if the contacts are not kept clean [1]. The rate of oxide formation is also known to increase with temperature. 

This paper examines the thermal issues discussed above through computer aided modelling with plant measurements to validate the models. It considers the factors that govern the rates of heat removal as well as those that may lead to additional heat generation.

Each electrode is subjected to the ‘ideal’ scenario for the majority of its operation – ie. normal operating conditions. To reduce power consumption it would therefore appear advantageous to use the ICCB system that runs at the lowest average temperature under normal operating conditions as lower temperature results in lower electrical resistance. The modelling showed that the difference between the best and worst average ICCB temperatures is 2˚C. To increase an average ICCB temperature of 2˚C results in an increase in power consumption for the overall cell of 0.01% which is minimal. This suggests that in normal operation the thermal effects have little bearing on the power consumption of the ICCB system and is not a reason for selection of one ICCB system. In addition, the average operating temperature of the ICCB’s in normal operation appeared to be almost independent of the amount of exposed surface area. A small impact of reduced surface area due to insulator blocks (ie only 1 °C) is observed. _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 155 Any ICCB system must be able to function when, and after, an extreme event such as a short circuit occurs. The additional current and subsequent heat must not damage either the ICCB or any of the surrou

nding components. 

The results did not demonstrate a relationship between exposed surface area and the maximum temperature for the extreme scenario. The presence of insulator blocks had little impact. 

The modelling showed that the notched ICCB’s maximum cathode temperature for the extreme scenario situation is at least 12% lower than that associated with any other ICCB studied. However its anode temperature is higher than the triangle and dogbone ICCB’s. This is considered to be due to the fact that  two line contacts are generated when the cathode contacts the notched bar which results in splitting of the current flow and heat. This allows the heat to be drawn away from the cathode into the bulk material of the ICCB more quickly. There is also more bulk ICCB material close to the line contacts for the notched ICCB which aids heat dissipation. However, the contact points are closer to the anodes than they are for the dogbone and triangle bar ICCB’s which may be responsible for the notched bar’s higher anode contact temperatures. 

The spool assessment placed the heat generation at between the notched ICCB cases and the triangle bar and dogbone cases. This result is surprising given the use of the spool ICCB for high current zinc EW cells. As discussed previously [1], the spool has the advantage (shared with the notched bar) that it generates sheer on the ICCB surface and thus self cleans the contact surface. This fact may be responsible for its success in high current applications. 

One key item that needs to be kept in consideration is that this analysis was completed on the basis that each ICCB had the same volume of copper. If for a given application, one ICCB could utilize more copper than another, this would impact which design would be most effective in reducing the normal operating temperature and the maximum temperature seen in the ICCB during a short circuiting event. 

#### **CONCLUSIONS** 

This paper investigated the performance of intercell contact bars when subjected to both the ideal current situation and the extreme situation of a short circuit. This work followed on from a previous paper [1] that investigated the electrical resistance of the intercell contact bar network. The following conclusions can be drawn: 

- An FEA model was developed and validated using both a more sophisticated CFD model and site data. 

- In normal operation the thermal effects have no significant impact on the power consumption of the ICCB systems, assuming ideal contacts, and on the choice between ICCB systems.

- The notched ICCB appears the best system at keeping the ICCB temperatures low when a short circuit occurs while the triangle bar and dogbone systems appear worse at keeping temperatures low. 

- The spool bar has intermediate contact temperatures but this may be advantaged in practice by its self cleaning properties. 

- Utilising insulator blocks have little impact on thermal perform

ance of ICCBs.

While this work has continued the exploration into getting a better understanding of the important components of intercell contact bar systems, and the positives and negatives of the common designs available, the following needs to be undertaken to obtain a better understanding of the intercell contact bar network: 

- An analysis of how artificial bar cooling impacts performance and to determine the cost effectiveness. 

- More literature and practical testwork on film resistance and oxide film impacts is required particularly with respect to the importance of contact shear and contact weight/pressure. This increase in resistance may lead to a review of this thermal analysis to confirm that the conclusions listed are still valid.

- An assessment of cost impacts of the ICCB systems incorporating the differences in capital cost of the various systems as well as operating costs.

#### **ABSTRACT** 

In electrowinning (EW) and electrorefining (ER) operations, the detection of short circuits and poor current distribution has been a very labour intensive reactive operations task. The Hatch HELM _tracker_ ™ system measures and records the current flow of every cathode and/or anode in real time and presents this information to the operators through an interactive display clearly indicating the existence of shorts, poor contacts, and any uneven current distribution. It also provides operators with help with prioritisation to allow efficient correction of current distribution issues. Expected benefits include increases in current efficiency, and thus reduction in operating costs and/ or increases in production, as well as reduction in electrode damage due to shorts. 

Hatch has been demonstrating the robustness and performance of the HELM tracker system through trials at commercial copper EW and ER plants includ

ing at EW facilities operated by Freeport-McMoRan (FCX), with assistance from the company’s management, technology and operating personnel. This paper includes some observations and outcomes from these trials as well as technical advances from other trial locations. The technology is almost ready for commercialization and the paper describes the business case for installing the HELM tracker system in copper EW applications indicating the financial payback of the system for this particular application.

#### **INTRODUCTION** 

In electrowinning (EW) and electrorefining (ER) operations, it is common to experience problems with electrode currents that are too high (short circuits) and too low (poor contacts). These problems cause reductions in the current efficiency (CE) and profitability of the plant. In order to improve profitability, Hatch has developed a new technology, HELM _tracke_ r™, which is able to measure the current passing through each electrode in the tankhouse in real time and draw immediate attention to poor current distribution problems. The HELM _tracke_ r™ system has been in development for more than 10 years and is currently in the final stages of commercial trials. These trials have been outlined in previous papers [1,2]. 

This paper provides a description of the HELM tracker™ system and how it can be installed in a variety of cell configurations. A financial analysis of the expected benefits of the HELM _tracker_ technology in helping plants achieve lower costs and higher revenues is also presented. The paper concludes with a discussion of some performance verification results. 

#### **DESCRIPTION OF HELM TRACKER** 

The HELM _tracker_ system allows real time measurement of current flow in every cathode and/or anode in electrolytic tankhouses. The system requires no electrical or physical contact with electrodes, and can be robustly retrofitted into existing plants. The system has a sensing bar that is mounted in each cell either underneath or on top of the cathode header bars. 

HELM _tracker_ identifies and displays the magnitude and exact cathode location of current distribution problems such as short circuits and poor contacts. The system also assists operators with priorities for fixing the problems. Display screens can be installed in the control room and/or in places around the tankhouse and access is also possible via handheld devices. Additional functionality allows detection of the exact time of harvesting for each cell, providing useful data for plant floor operations, as well as for individual cell CE assessment. The system’s data can be integrated with an existing plant information system or tank house control system as an addition to the installation. 

There are a small number of alternative sensing methods used for EW and ER operations [3,4,5]. These include infra-red imaging, cell voltage monitoring, gauss meters and individual electrode current measuremen

t devices such as clamp meters. These devices have been compared and contrasted with HELM _tracker_ previously [1,2] and their relative disadvantages described. The system is capable of providing a number of financial benefits depending on specific plant design and performance: - The early detection and remedying of shorts and bad contacts will increase CE. - Operators can spend less time working in the tankhouse searching for faults, and can spend more time rectifying them. This may reduce labour requirements. - Fewer or shorter duration shorts and bad contacts mean that deposition of metal on the cathodes will be more

uniform which may reduce scrap and decrease inclusions in product metal, affecting sale price.

- In electrowinning plants utilising more expensive titanium mixed metal anodes, the HELM _tracker_ system's earlier detection of shorts will mean that less damage is caused to the anodes, thereby prolonging their life. 

- Dendrites (uneven protruding growths) can damage electrode bags and other cell dividers. The early detection of shorts may reduce damage and operating costs. 

- Plants may be able to reduce electrode spacing and thereby increase plant capacity with minimal capital investment if they have instant information about short circuits. 

In the analysis below, the financial benefits of installing the HELM _tracker_ technology associated with just the first point listed above are determined, where increases in CE lead to increased production and/or reduced power consumption. The benefits associated with the other points are more difficult to quantify and may vary significantly in different plants and for this reason no attempt has been made to quantify benefits. 

#### **Current Efficiency Improvements** 

CE is a measure of the proportion of the current passed through an electrolytic cell that actually delivers the primary purpose of the cell, for example, plates out copper in copper EW or ER. It is an important metric for all tankhouses. Increasing CE will reduce the power consumption of a plant where the tankhouse is not throughput limited, or produce additional metal for those plants that are tankhouse limited (operating at maximum capacity). 

Depending on the electrolytic system, the factors that affect CE vary, but for copper EW the main factors include [6]; iron in the electrolyte; short circuits; uneven current distribution including bad contacts; stray currents; other impurities. 

Of these, iron is commonly found in copper electrolytes at levels that are known to significantly impact CE [6]. It is also Hatch experience that shorts and uneven current distribution can be major impacts but that other causes are generally minor. As mentioned, improvements in CE with the HELM _tracker_ system are expected to result from the reduced time to rectify shorts and bad contacts made possible via real time monitoring of currents. Thus the HELM _tracker_ system is expected to lead to reduction in power costs or increases in production, if shorts or bad contacts are a significant cause of reduced CE in a plant. 

#### **Data Inputs and Methodology** 

Data from a 2010 survey of copper EW operations [7] have been assessed to develop a realistic estimate of the improvements in CE resulting from installation of the HELM _tracker_ system. Surveyed plants without the following data were omitted from calculations:

Las Parcelas 5490 Santiago, Chile_ #### **ABSTRACT** This paper is focused to chilean experiences on design, manufacturing, maintenance and operation of high current controlled rectifiers for copper SX-EW and refinery plant. It concern with new copper or “greenfield” projects and with the re-engineering of existing transformerrectifiers or “brownfield” projects. The paper deals with parameters for the design, boundary conditions, current control, protection criteria, harmonics mitigation, maintenance and spare components, focusing to the most important requirements of this type of equipment: reliability and high efficiency. Finally, from the authors experience, this paper recommends some aspects of technical specification and characteristics for the future projects. #### **ABOUT TRANSFORMER-RECTIFIER CALCULATIONS FOR A TYPICAL SX-EW COPPER PLANT** In this Section a method used by the authors to calculate a transformer – rectifier system for a given SX-EW copper plant is presented. necessary| #### **ABOUT THE DIGITAL CONTROL OF HIGH CURRENT RECTIFIERS** In an analog control system, the controller consists of traditional analog devices and circuits, which are principally linear amplifiers. The first control systems were analog because it was the only available technology. In the analog control system, any change in either set point or feedback is measured immediately, and the amplifiers adjust their output (to the actuator) accordingly. In a digital control system, the controller uses a digital circuit. In most cases, this circuit is based to an industrial computer or microprocessor or microcontroller. The digital controller executes a control program that repeats over-and-over (each repetition is called an iteration or scan). The program instructs the digital controller to read the set point (reference) and sensor data and then use these numbers to calculate the controller output, which is sent to the actuator of the plant. The program then loops back to the beginning and starts over again. The total time for one pass through the complete program may be less than 500 µsec. The digital system only “looks” at the inputs at a certain time in the scan and gives the updated output later, as it is shown in Figure 3. If an input changes just after the computer looked at it, that change will remain undetected until the next time through the scan. This is fundamentally different than the analog system, which is continuous and responds immediately to any changes, according to the time constant response. However, for most digital control systems, the scan time is so short compared with the response time of the process being controlled that, for

all practical purposes, the controller response is instantaneous. It is very well known that a continuous waveform can be perfectly represented by a limited number of discrete samples, as long as the samples are taken at greater than two times the highest frequency component in the continuous waveform.

The physical world is basically an “analog place.” Natural events take time to happen, and they usually move in a continuous fashion from one position to the next. Therefore, most control systems are controlling analog processes. This means that, in many cases, the digital control system must first convert real-world analog input data into digital form before it can be used. Similarly, the output from the digital controller must be converted from digital form back into analog form. Next Figure 4 shows a block diagram of a digital closed-loop control system. Notice the two additional blocks: the digital-to-analog converter (DAC) and the analog-to-digital converter (ADC). Also, it can be observed that the feedback line is shown going directly into the controller. #### **ABSTRACT** 

Acid mist is an undesirable and costly by-product of copper electrowinning (Cu EW), damaging to the health of people working in the tankhouse as well as corrosive and dangerous for all the metal parts in the plant. De Nora’s mission is to provide safe and environmentally friendly electrochemical technology. The De Nora solution is built around DSA<sup>®</sup> anodes, with an integrated anode-frame structure and a permeable separator skirt and a de-misting box, which captures the acid mist at the source – the interface between the electrolyte solution and the atmosphere. The De Nora solution will allow an EW plant to operate with an unprecedented low level of atmospheric acid mist, providing extra added value in safer Cu EW tankhouse operations. This paper describes the innovative acid mist containment system - an integral part of the De Nor

a solution - and the related benefits obtained by confining the oxygen micro-bubbles in an enclosed space. Significant improvement in operating practice, new areas for costs savings and environmental benefits generated by the De Nora solution will also be presented.

#### **INTRODUCTION** 

Copper Electrowinning or Cu EW (1), is an important component of electrometallurgical technology.[1-2] The anodic reaction of Cu EW is oxygen evolution (2), the release of the anodic oxygen bubbles at the anode results in carry-over of electrolyte in the form of acid mist in the tankhouse atmosphere. The mist is harmful to the plant personnel and requires the use of personal protective equipment (PPE), the acid mist can also damage the tankhouse, building and equipment. 



The most common practices for minimizing the acid mist release comprises of (i) the use of a mechanical barrier e.g. layer(s) of hollow plastic spheres / or polystyrene spheres which float on top of the electrolyte (ii) a chemical method e.g. by the use of chemical additives in the electrolyte which interfere with the mechanism of the collapsing bubbles when they emerge from the electrolyte bulk. (iii) acid mist capture hoods or other ventilation systems above the cells.[3] 

Even if the acid mist concentration in the tankhouse complies with existing standards, it is expected to become unacceptable in the near future, as the trend with new environmental and workplace legislation becomes increasingly challenging. A definite improvement of the workplace atmosphere might be obtained by turning to the gas confinement equipment which is installed on the chloride based Nickel EW plants: there the chlorine evolving anodes are assembled with bags for the containment of chlorine gas, collected in a top box and collected under vacuum and utilized in the leaching process. 

The objective of the De Nora solution is to avoid such gas handling as used in Ni EW and provide a DSA<sup>®</sup> anode structure which is able to confine the oxygen bubbles by means of a skirt and to collect the bubbles into a top box (see Figure 1).[4] Inside the demisting-box the acid mist is separated into the acid and oxygen components; the separated acid electrolyte phase is returned to the cell (Figure 2). Oxygen gas released from the cell will have a lower acid concentration complying with present and future standards for workplace and environmental safety.[5-6]

#### **EXPERIMENTAL** 

The De Nora development of the acid mist abatement can be split into three steps, that is the lab testing of ideas, the pilot confirmation of the lab results and final scale-up and evaluation in industrial ce

lls. The lab testing was conducted in a full height (1m) narrow width (15cm) Cu EW cell with cathode area of 0.15 m<sup>2</sup> as shown in Figure 3. 

The test cell in Milan, Italy was set to have an inter-electrode gap of 38 mm, the operating conditions were chosen to represent a challenging industrial Cu EW process with a cathodic current density of 450 A/m<sup>2</sup> . The copper concentration was kept in the range 40 – 50 g/liter, sulfuric acid in the range 170 - 190 grams/liter. Leveling agents such as DXG-F7 (a mixture of guar gum and poly acrylic acid) were injected close to the cell inlet at 1 ppm. An equivalent flow rate of 200 liter hr<sup>-1</sup> m<sup>-2</sup> , temperature in the cell was maintained at 50 to 52 °C.

The De Nora solution uses a cloth skirt to confine the anodic oxygen and channel it upwards to the de-misting box. In standard Cu EW the anodic oxygen bubbles provide the main electrolyte mixing due to gas-lift. The objective of this test series was to detect any changes in the copper cathode deposit when the oxygen bubble gas-lift effect is altered or decreased.

#### **RESULTS** 

The testing of the De Nora solution has been intentionally performed in different cells under a wide range of operating conditions in order to investigate the effect of mass transport and any impact on the deposit morphology; as a matter of fact, each and every tankcell have a specific flow pattern linked to its peculiar setup (e.g., feed with/without manifold, specific flow to tank, etc.) that affects the boundary layer on the cathode surface and eventually the quality of the deposited copper. 

The first result obtained applying the De Nora solution in an electrochemical cells was the current efficiency (C.E.), calculated by measuring the cathode mass. In an EW test with an electrolyte feed rate of 200 liter/(hour · m<sup>2</sup> ) and a total iron concentration of 1g/litre, the C.E. for the bare DSA<sup>®</sup> anodes was 94.2% and with the De Nora solution was 96.8%. The introduction of a gas separator in the liquid removes the gas bubbles from the bulk electrolyte and also removes the mixing effect that enhances mass transport on the cathodic surface. The high current efficiency obtained shows that the local current density is below the limiting current density for copper transport to the surface, and also suggests that the discontinuity between anode and cathode surfaces can have a positive impact on the Fe<sup>2+</sup> /Fe<sup>3+</sup> shift reaction that is one of the main causes of loss of C.E. in Cu EW cells.[7] 

Copper deposits obtained in the presence and absence of the gas capture skirt have been analyzed, Figure 5 shows cross-sectional micrographs of cathodes obtained (i) with a PbCaSn anode in a full-scale industrial pilot cell, (ii) the 0.15m<sup>2</sup> cell with a bare DSA<sup>®</sup> anode and (iii) the 0.15m<sup>2</sup> cell with a DSA<sup>®</sup> anode and a gas capture skirt. The punched cathode samples had a comparable morphology, independent of the presence or absence of the gas capture skirt. This result reinforces the concept that the use of a gas confinement skirt does not affect the local current density on the cathode up to the point where the limiting C.D. is reached, which is one of the most important variables for the structure and quality of the deposited metal.

#### **INTRODUCTION** 

Copper electrowinning is a standard technology used by the industry to recover copper as cathodes mainly. From its origin electrowinning cells have used parallel electrodes which have shown to be a very efficient way to use the space. Main differences are found in Interelectrode Distance (75mm – 108 mm), Design Current Density ( 150 A/m2 to 415 A/m2), Cathode Plating Area (0.60 m2 – 1.2 m2 per side), Anode Thickness ( 6 – 12 mm), Anode Alloy Material (PbSb – PbCaSn), Type of Cathode (starting sheet of stainless steel blank), etc. Some hardware improvements in anode insulators, anode guides, edge strips, among others, complete this relative modest list of modifications respect of the original cell concept and hardware. 



Figure N° 1: Electrowinning Cell Assembly with Parallel Electrodes 

Therefore the limit for improving productivity **<u>using parallel electrodes</u>** has been mainly Current Density and little has been done at industrial scale to go beyond such limit, except the introduction of the flow distributor at Magma Copper in the early 1980’s and Air Sparging, most recently at Minera Spence and others in this decade. 

A second component of the current tankhouse technology limitations which requires attention is acid mist. The anodic evolution of oxygen at the anode surface, catalysed by the presence of PbO2, forms gas bubbles which wetted with electrolyte containing sulphuric acid ( and copper) burst above the electrolyte bath generating acid mist. Regulations are being modified with some countries already demanding compliance of very strict limits, such as Norway where acceptable level of acid mist in the environment is 0.3 mg/Nm<sup>3</sup> (breathable fraction). However, the European Community has recently recommended a new limit of 0.05 mg/Nm<sup>3</sup> as thoracic fraction. Due to the difficulties in measuring this concentration in any individual, the recommendation is to limit such level to the equivalent breathable fraction of 0.1 mg/Nm<sup>3</sup> . In practical terms, for the copper electrowinning process it means to capture the emissions entirely.

Diffusion is a molecular transfer process produced by the concentration differences existing in the solution. Convection is a transfer process by which the dissolved material is borne along by the hydrodynamic movement of the liquid. Migration is the transfer of the ions under the influence of the electrical field in the solution. The total flow, i.e. the number of copper moles transported per second through a unit area, for example one square centimetre, is equal to the sum of the different flows: migration, convection and diffusion. For parallel electrodes, only the components perpendicular to the electrodes are of interest. #### **AN INVESTIGATION OF MODIFIED POLYSACCHARIDE AND POLYACRYLAMIDE ON PLATING POLARIZATION AND SURFACE ROUGHNESS IN COPPER ELECTROWINNING** 

Tyler Helsten Department of Metallurgical Engineering University of Utah 135 South 1460 East Salt Lake City, UT, USA 84112 

Michael S. Moats Materials Research Center Department of Materials Science and Engineering Missouri University of Science and Technology 1400 N. Bishop Rolla, MO, USA 65401 moatsm@mst.edu 

#### **ABSTRACT** 

Recently, the use of modified polysaccharides and polyacrylamides has been reported as smoothing agents in commercial copper electrowinning operations.  Very little published data exist on the fundamental behavior of these compounds in copper electrode

position.  In this study, the polarization behavior and surface roughness of short term deposits grown in the presence of a modified polysaccharide, a polyacrylamide or a 50/50 mixture of guar and modified polysaccharide in synthetic copper electrowinning electrolytes are reported.  The polyacrylamide demonstrates classical behavior in that polarization increases with increasing concentration which correlates to a smoother deposit.  The modified polysaccharide and combination of guar and modified polysaccharide did not exhibit classical behavior in that increasing concentration did not affect polarization but also resulted in smoother deposits. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

208 

#### **INTRODUCTION** 

Essentially all of the world’s refined copper production occurs through electrodeposition; either in electrorefining or electrowinning [1]. The utilization of organic smoothing agents is critical to these operations’ abilities to produce high purity product with minimal energy consumption. 

The organic compounds used differ between copper electrorefining and electrowinning. In electrorefining, a combination of glue, thiourea and optionally Avitone are used to produce dense smooth cathodes [2]. In electrowinning, traditionally guar products have been used [3]. The choice of guar in electrowinning instead of glue relates to reports that glue causes phase disengagement issues in solvent extraction. 

Recently, the use of modified polysaccharide and polyacrylamide has been reported in commercial electrowinning tankhouses [4-5] as a replacement for guar.  The modified polysaccharide was reported to produce a denser cathode deposit at a higher consumption (g organic/tonne cathode) but an overall lower cost.  The polysaccharide was reported to produce high quality cathode along with the removal of MnO2 from coated titanium anodes. 

The electrochemical and smoothing behavior of modified polysaccharide and polyacrylamide in copper electrowinning has received very little attention in the open literature.  Moats and Derrick [6] indicated that a modified polysaccharide (Hydrostar<sup>®</sup> ) had no measurable polarization effect on copper electrodeposition in room temperature synthetic electrolytes using a galvanodynamic method similar to that used by Adcock [78] to examine zinc electrodeposition. Polyacrylamides in copper electrowinning were investigated by Vereecken and Winand [9] and Fabian et al. [10-12].  Vereecken and Winand reported changes in cationic polyacrylamides resulted in modifications to the copper cathode structure without causing a change in the overpotential.  They indicated that the deposits were not as good as those produced with guar.  Fabian et al. examined polyacrylamides that were activated. They reported smoother deposits than those produced with guar. 

In this study, we continued the work started by Moats and Derrick [6].  A galvanodynamic method was again utilized to measure the nucleation potential of coppe

r on a substrate and the growth or plating potential of copper.  The effects of electrolyte and electrolysis parameters similar to those used industrially in copper electrowinning tankhouses were examined.  Then the surface roughnesses of one hour electrodeposits were examined. The main goal of this research was to investigate the polarization and smoothing behavior of commercial smoothing agents - a modified polysaccharide, a polyacrylamide and a mixture of guar and modified polysaccharide.

#### **EXPERIMENTAL** 

#### **Materials** 

All experiments were performed in 1 L cylindrical lipped cells. Each cell was covered with a plastic lid that had access ports to insert one working electrode (either 316L stainless steel or copper plate with 1.8 cm<sup>2</sup> exposed area), one counter electrode (a 2.5 cm X 2.5 cm IrO2-Ta2O5 coated titanium mesh attached to a grade 2 Ti rod for electrical contact) and a reference electrode (Ag/AgCl saturated with KCl, 0.2 V vs. NHE). <u>All potentials are reported versus this reference electrode. The anode-cathode</u> spacing was 2.7 cm. A thermometer was also inserted to monitor temperature. Temperature was controlled within +/- 1<sup>o</sup> C by inserting the cell into a water bath.  The electrolyte was not externally agitated. 

Working electrodes were prepared using 316L stainless steel and copper blanks. Prior to each experiment, the blanks were prepared by grinding sequentially with 120, 320, and 600 grit silicon carbide paper to obtain a uniform surface for copper deposition. After polishing, each cathode was washed with DI water and rinsed with acetone.  Each cathode was masked with chemical resistant non-conductive tape, leaving the top centimeter uncovered for electrical connection. Then, a plating area (1.8 cm<sup>2</sup> ) was carefully cut-out using a template. Additional tape was applied to insure solution contacted only the plating area. 

For each experiment, one liter of synthetic electrolyte was prepared.  All chemicals were analytical grade and used without further purification.  Source chemicals were copper sulfate pentahydrate, sulfuric acid, and sodium chloride. De-ionized water was used in all experiments. While copper, chloride, and organic concentrations were examined, sulfuric acid concentration was kept constant at 180 g/L for all experiments. The modified polysaccharide (MP), polyacrylamide (PA), and guar were provided by industrial partners and used as received. The organics were pre-dissolved in water and added one hour prior to the experiment starting.  Chloride concentrations are listed as the added concentrations.  The analytical grade chemicals contain small quantities of chloride and thus the actual chloride concentration is likely slightly higher than the values reported. 

#### **Electrochemical Methods** 

Two electrochemical methods were employed to

evaluate the electrochemical and smoothing behavior of additives in non-agitated synthetic copper electrolyte. The methods were galvanodynamic (e.g. galvanic staircase method) and galvanostatic (e.g. copper electrowinning). 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

210 

#### <u>Galvanic Staircase</u> 

For galvanic staircase experiments, current was supplied and potential was recorded by a Gamry PCI4/750 potentiostat/galvanostat using VFP 600 software. Linear galvanodynamic ramps developed by Moats and Derrick [6] were employed. The first ramp increased the current density from 0 to 12.5 A/m<sup>2</sup> over a period of 1500 seconds. The second ramp increases the current density from 12.5 A/m<sup>2</sup> to 600 A/m<sup>2</sup> in the next 100 seconds. The last ramp returned the current density back to 0 A/m<sup>2</sup> in 750 seconds. 

#### <u>Electrowinning</u> 

One hour electrowinning tests were performed to produce samples for surface roughness measurement. Constant current was supplied by a Gamry PCI4/750 potentiostat/galvanostat operated in galvanostat control.  Current values were recorded once every 30 seconds during each experiment.  Up to four cells were connected in electrical series.  Each cell was monitored for cell voltage using an ADAM data acquisition module.  The cell voltages were recorded using Tracer DAQ software.  Cell voltages were recorded every second during each experiment and reviewed to insure the experiment proceeded as expected. 

After each experiment, cathodes were weighed for deposit weight after removal of the masking tape, rinsing with DI water and drying.  The plated copper was examined to insure that plating occurred only in the non-masked area. The weight of the copper deposits were compared with their respective duplicates reassuring the experiments were reproducible. 

Deposit surface roughness was analyzed using an optical profilometer without removing the copper deposit from the substrate. The roughness was measured using a Zygo NewView Optical Profiler. The objective was set at 5X with a zoom of 1X. The scan length used was 150 µm bipolar (34 seconds) at a FDA resolution of high and min mod % at 0.001.

#### **CONCLUSIONS** 

The effect of several electrowinning process variables were examined on the nucleation and plating potentials from the galvanodynamic staircase method and surface roughness of one hour electrodeposits.  The nucleation potential appears to be primary governed by the substrate on which copper deposits.  The plating potential was most affected by copper concentration, temperature, current density and polyacrylamide concentration.  Chloride, modified polysaccharide and MP/guar mixture concentration had no measurable effect on plating potential in this study. 

Increasing chloride concentration, temperature and current density produced rougher deposits.  Increasing any of the additive concentrations decreased the surface roughness.  No correlation existed between surface roughness and any of the potentials measured by the galvanic staircase method.

Many of these trends support previous research.  However, the mechanism by which leveling occurs without appreciable polarization should be investigated further. Additionally, care should be given to the exact organic specie being evaluated as not all polyacrylamides appear to act the same.
