#### **ELECTROLYTIC TANKHOUSE ACID MIST CONTROL – MEETING STRINGENT WORKER EXPOSURE LIMITS AND EMISSIONS TARGETS** 

Dr. Andreas Siegmund and Amandeep Randhawa _Gas Cleaning Technologies, LLC 4953 N. O’Connor Road Irving, USA 75062 Siegmund@gcteng.com_ 

#### **ABSTRACT** 

SX/EW operations are commonplace due to their lower operating costs.  However, one of the undesirable consequences of this operation is the evolution of acid mist in the electrowinning step in the process.  This acid mist creates a significant worker exposure hazard, results in corrosion to building and equipment requiring excessive maintenance, and presents an environmental concern when discharged to the atmosphere. Therefore, addressing these concerns is key to meeting tighter hygiene and environmental regulations.  This paper presents a summary of the process techniques to minimize acid mist formation, and the engineering methods used in evaluating tankhouse vent

ilation systems including the use of Computational Fluid Dynamic (CFD) modelling to optimize ventilation systems. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

226 

#### **INTRODUCTION** 

During the electrowinning process of non-ferrous metals such as Copper, Cobalt and Nickel, a considerable amount of Oxygen gas is generated at the inert anode. While the formed oxygen gas bubbles can be beneficial for mass transport effects of ions within the electrolyte, the bubbles grow and rise to the surface of the electrolyte. Due to the buoyancy force of the oxygen bubbles they burst free at the solution surface liberating highly acidic droplets into the tankhouse atmosphere forming airborne sulfuric acid mist which is highly corrosive to the tankhouse equipment, a major environmental concern and poses a health and safety risk for the operators. Time weighted average and short term exposure limits have been established by the Occupational Safety and Health Administration in most countries to minimize this serious health hazard. For example, the Chilean regulations require acid mist concentration to be less than 0.55 mg/m<sup>3</sup> . 

Therefore, it is necessary to take adequate measures through the implementation of process controls, mechanical physical barriers, chemical surfactants that decrease the surface tension of the electrolyte, and alternative anode technology producing smaller bubble sizes, to modify the way the oxygen bubbles burst at the surface of the electrolyte, and / or the installation of effective ventilation systems. There have been many process control solutions implemented to minimize or eliminate acid mist formation and a summary of these methods is provided. More recently, computational fluid dynamic model (CFD) has been developed as an effective tool to supplement conventional engineering calculation methods typically used in the design of fume capture hoods and overall building ventilation systems. CFD provides a means to quantitatively predict the fluid flow behaviour in and around equipment and structures, accounting for fluid dynamic, heat release, and other physical effects. For tankhouses, CFD can be utilized to predict the ventilation patterns and contaminant migration path within the tankhouse and calculating the acid mist concentration pattern within the tankhouse. Different ventilation scenarios to control emissions in the tankhouse can be compared and evaluated to achieve an optimized design that meets the regulatory exposure limits. 

#### **PROCESS CONTROL MEASURES** 

The size and the burst mechanism of the oxygen bubbles have a significant impact on the generation of acid mist.  Studies have found that the bubble size ranges from 33 to 278 μm with a mean size between 65 and 68 μm independent from the employed current density.  However, the total amount of generated bubbles increases linearly with higher current densities, which increases proportionally the amount of generated acid mist [1]. 

Various process an

d operating parameters can have a direct impact on the formation of the oxygen bubbles in the electrolyte and acid mist evolution from the cells.  These include electrolyte temperature, current distribution and the Lead oxide layer on the anodes. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

227 

#### **Electrolyte Temperature** 

Operating the electrowinning process within an optimum temperature range is necessary to maintain acceptable electrolyte viscosity to minimize acid mist formation. 

It is preferred to operate a Copper electrowinning process at a temperature between 44 – 48 °C.  Higher temperature not only promotes anode corrosion but also lowers the viscosity of the electrolyte.  The latter has a direct impact on the buoyancy of the oxygen bubbles. 

#### **Current Distribution** 

A common problem in the electrowinning industry is that of maintaining a uniform current distribution among the electrodes in each cell throughout a tankhouse.  Uniform power distribution is becoming more and more important in the industry striving for better energy utilization and optimized physical and chemical deposition qualities.  Unbalanced power distribution also results in higher localized current densities and a higher localized acid mist formation. The implementation of a preventive maintenance program measuring current distribution and temperature assists in an early detection of non-uniform power distribution in order to take early corrective actions. 

#### **Anode Conditioning and Handling** 

The stability of the Lead oxide layer is essential for proper anode performance and has an impact on acid mist generation. 

New rolled Lead-Calcium-Tin anodes, the standard anode used for Cu-EW, need to be “conditioned” to work properly.  It is desired that the anode rapidly forms an adherent and stable Lead oxide layer on the surface.  During that “conditioning” period an increased oxygen evolution is observed at the anode during which a potentially higher acid mist formation can occur.  Different measures to pre-treat new anodes such as sandblasting exist and are applied in the electrowinning industry to substantially shorten this “conditioning” period. 

To produce the lowest Lead content of the cathodes, any anode should be cleaned periodically to remove the number of loosely adhering PbO2 flakes from the anode surface.  The anodes should be taken out from the cell and cleaned with pressurized water to remove the loosely adhering flakes.  The cleaning process should not remove the PbO2 layer to bare metal otherwise it will need to be regenerated through another “conditioning” process.  The surfaces of anodes should not be scraped or polished after the Lead oxide has formed.  The time interval between cleaning the anodes is governed by the anode current density, the electrolyte temperature and Manganese content of the electrolyte and various at each individual tankhouse. For Copper electrowinning, the anodes should be cleaned every 3-6 months depe

nding on the Manganese content, the operating parameters and the employed anode alloy and type. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

228 

#### **PHYSICAL BARRIERS** 

Polyethylene balls, suction hoods, mats, brushes and wipers, chemical reagents and forced ventilation are examples of many measures implementing mechanical barriers to reduce acid mist formation in the tankhouse atmosphere. Qualitatively, the use of chemical reagents such as FC-1100, Mistop, Dowfroth, and alkylated ethoxylates has been rated as the most effective method of suppressing acid mist [2]. 

#### **Demisting Balls and Beads** 

Hollow plastic balls are widely used in the Copper electrowinning industry to control acid mist. Most plants are using hollow, app. 19mm diameter polypropylene balls in combination with another acid mist control method.  These polypropylene balls are stacked in 2 – 3 layers and float on the electrolyte surface. Other plants are using polyethylene or HDPE as the material of choice for smaller 9.5 mm balls or 5 mm beads.  They are stacked only in two layers but the measured air-borne acid mist concentration is reportedly low. 

The balls represent a physical barrier for the oxygen bubbles to freely rise to the electrolyte surface and burst at the interface electrolyte / atmosphere liberating acid aerosols. Smaller ball / bead sizes have a higher packing density and it seems that this increases the resistance for the bubbles to pass through.  The buoyancy of the oxygen bubbles significantly reduces while passing through the dense ball / beads layer.  Many bubbles lose their drive and burst at the liquid surface with much less energy, thus ejecting smaller electrolyte droplets with less force.  The acid mist aerosols are partially already caught within the layers. 

#### **Anode Cap Control** 

Several inventions have been made where a multi-element cover system is applied below the electrode hanger bars and above the surface of the electrode bath.  These covers are evacuated in the freeboard below the cover and above the bath at a rate exceeding the stoichiometric ratio, mist generation and evaporation rate. 

One patented invention [3] has each individual electrode cap element mounted to the anodes by corrosion resistant bolts and nut fasteners.  The primary anode cap is made from semirigid non-conductive material such as dual hardness extruded polyvinyl chloride.  The caps each include a tapered eave spanning to the cathodes forming a substantially air tight seal immediately after the cathodes are inserted into the cell.  The eaves are sufficiently flexible to maintain a conformable seal at the cathodes but to allow the Copper plated cathodes to be both harvested and inserted.  On the underside of the anode caps, adjacent the ends of the eaves, are so-called “drip lips”, which protrude downwards to and towards the bath.  These drip lips cause the acid aerosol condensate to fall into the electrolyte before reaching the cathode in order to

prevent etching of the stainless steel.  At the respective tanks sides, a system of shingle-like, overlapping flexible plastic strips form a substantial air tight seal. At the respective cell ends, covers are provided at both the electrolyte inlets and outlets. Ventilation is performed at the outlet end through a wetted weir.

A similar system has been developed and commercialized under the name LateralVex [4].  It is based on the same multi-component cover principle but utilizes flexible, bend covers and a lateral inner duct ventilation system.  The flexible covers are assembled onto the top of the lateral ventilation ducts and sag towards the cell center as shown in Figure 1.  This arrangement permits the condensated acid mist to run towards the cell center before the droplets fall back into the electrolyte. The interstices underneath the covers and above the electrolyte are ventilated through an integrated lateral duct system installed along the sidewalls of the cells.  The system has and still is being tested at several smelters in Chile. Another major benefit of this system is that it allows for continued extraction of acid mist while the cells are being harvested, which is not possible with many other hood designs.

#### **Brushes** 

One plant is successfully using brushes installed around the anodes to scrub the acid mist carried by the oxygen. It is claimed that brushes are filtering the moisture and solid particles; however, the oxygen is passed through the brushes. The brushes are easy to install and they can be retrofitted into an existing plant. Simple maintenance is necessary to spray wash all sediments back into the cell which is done during spray washing of the electrical contacts. Cathode corrosion between the brush and the electrolyte level is not apparent.  In addition, it is claimed that the brushes provide a heat blanket reducing heat losses and evaporation. 

#### **Mist Suppression Agents** 

The addition of many chemical compounds has been investigated in the past as agents for acid mist suppression.  Some of these compounds are very effective in reducing the bubble surface tension resulting in less energy on the surface of the oxygen bubbles, which in turn reduces the amount of acid ejected from the electrolyte. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

230 

One potential problem is that the large amounts of foam generated through the lowered surface tension can trap oxygen on the surface of the electrolyte as well as organic resulting from the entrainment of circuit organic.  This organic has a substantial amount of kerosene fraction that can become flammable in the presence of high oxygen atmosphere at the air/electrolyte interface and foams can ignite if there is a spark. 

FC-1100 is the current industry standard chemical additive for mist suppression.  FC1100, or in one extent its predecessor FC-100, is used by a majo

rity of plants.  It has been shown that at the optimal concentration for FC-1100 is 8-10 ppm concentration.  Testing indicates that there is a sharp decline in surface tension from over 63 dynes/cm down to about 43 dynes/cm at 10 ppm concentration [2]. FC-1100 also has extremely low-foaming characteristics even at higher concentrations of 50 – 100 ppm. Higher concentrations will however result in a larger cross-flow to the Solvent-Extraction process (SX) and an increase of slurry tailings in the SX while having negligible effect on surface tension. 

Other classes of suppressants have been synthesized and investigated.  Some promising results have been achieved with the new mist suppression agent EnviroMC 1000, an alkylbetaines compound.  The reduction in acid mist for these additives is relative to their capability to reduce the surface tension of the electrolyte.  Tests have shown that these compounds also result in a sharp decline in surface tension at up to 10 ppm concentration, some with results similar to FC-1100 [2]. However, commercial operation had to be abandoned due to instability of the suppressant. 

To a lesser extent, foaming chemical additives have been used in electrowinning systems. Mistop, Dowfroth, and alkylated ethoxylates are foaming agents that reduce acid mist by trapping the oxygen bubbles and impeding the ejection of mist. 

Mistop is a surfactant of natural origin.  Mistop contains triterpenic saponins derived from the Chilean quillaja tree.  The product is non-toxic, and poses no risks to the environment or to tankhouse operators.  Mistop was tested at laboratory and pilot plant scale, and is currently used industrially at one plant in Chile. 

#### **Hoods** 

It has been reported that mechanical or physical barriers alone are not sufficient to obtain acceptable levels of acid mist concentration, particularly at high current densities of 400 A/m<sup>2</sup> [5].  The installation of hoods assures a significant reduction of acid mist to acceptable ambient conditions. SAME and SELE each have developed close capture systems that collect the acid mist near the source. 

SAME’s High Energy Hoods (HEH), shown in Figure 2, provide ventilation by adjusting the rate of extraction of the captured and collected acid mist and reducing potential electrode corrosion in the bar area.  The hood provides draft from the edge of the hood which prevents acid mist from escaping from the sides of the hoods.  The hood is a one-piece system with no moving parts that can be damaged when handling the hood during harvesting operations.

However, the installation of the SAME HEH system does not eliminate the release of acid mist during cathode harvesting since the hoods must be removed.  Therefore, the combination of demisting balls and chemicals is recommended in conjunction with the hood installation.  These hood systems also require special modification

SELE have developed a system similar to the LateralVex as shown in Figure 1.  One of the greatest benefits of the SELE system occurs during cell harvesting.  The harvesting operation can be made more efficient as there is no hood or cover over the cells that need to be removed before collecting the cathodes. The SELE system continues to provide ventilation during harvesting and the flexible covers provide some control of acid mist escape into the tankhouse environment after the cathodes have been removed.  However, there are significant issues associated with retrofit installation into existing cells.  This requires the cell to be off-line and some modifications to the utility, electrolyte and effluent supply system are necessary as are modifications to connect the gas off-takes to the common header. The SELE system also is highly dependent on the condition of the flexible cover and the seal it provides against the cathode and anode plates.  Since the draft is provided perpendicular to the natural updraft flow of the mist, there is potential of acid mist escaping from near the center of the cell.

Many Copper EW tankhouse have installed a manifold system to feed the electrolyte into each individual cell.  Typically, a ring type PVC pipe system is installed along the length of the cell wall, or in newer tankhouse it represents an integral part of the polymer concrete design. The manifold consists in many cases of a 2” PVC pipe with one-quarter inch holes drilled at a forty-five degree angle to the cell bottom aimed at the centre of each cathode.  Depending on the

actual electrolyte flow rate this might result in a strong laminar or even turbulent flow, which increases the force of the buoyancy.  The bubbles are bursting at the electrolyte surface with a higher energy rate generating more acid mist aerosols. 

A modified electrolyte inlet system was developed by METTOP [6].  The METTOPBRX-Technology is using a parallel electrolyte flow between the electrodes.  Special design nozzles govern the fresh electrolyte in an upward natural electrolyte flow in-between the individual electrode spacing (Figure 3). To improve the Copper deposit at the cathode further, some plants have implemented air sparging.  This additional forced convection system deliberately enhances the agitation of the electrolyte particularly at the lower portion of the anode, where the amount of generated oxygen bubbles is too small to provide sufficient agitation. Reported advantages are: 

- Higher current density operation 

- Improvement of the physical and chemical cathodic Copper deposit

#### **ALTERNATIVE ANODE TECHNOLOGY** 

Noble metal-coated electrodes have been tested for electrowinning applications for many years but their cost and limited service life have precluded their use in Copper electrowinning until recently. These anodes have a Titanium Substrate, which is coated with a catalytic layer consisting of an electrocatalyst.  The service life of the electrocatalyst, a combination of a platinum group metal as a metal oxide and a stabilizer, and electrochemical passivation effects by deposition of Manganese Dioxide during operation are the most limiting factors in its possible application. 

In a joint development, FMI and Republic have developed a DSA anode, which seem to be a promising alternative to the standard Lead alloy based anode [9]. This anode consists of a Titanium Substrate with an IrO2-Ta2O5 coating.  Meanwhile, FMI has completely converted two tankhouses (Chino and Miami) from Lead alloy anodes to this alternative technology because targets for voltage reduction (15%), coating lifetime projections (min. 6 yrs.) have been met. A FMI tankhouse in Chile is currently in the process of being converted. An additional positive ramification seems to be a substantial but not quantified reduction in apparent acid mist generation. It is assumed that this alternative anode creates much finer oxygen bubbles with less buoyancy force. 

#### **COMPUTATIONAL FLUID DYNAMIC MODELING** 

Despite the process improvements and advancement in technologies for acid mist reduction from the electrolytic operation, residual acid mist concentration within the tankhouse still pose a risk to worker exposure and deterioration of the building and equipment.  Secondary ventilation systems are most often necessary to improve conditions inside the tankhouse. 

A computational fluid dynamic model is an effective tool to supplement conventional engineering calculation methods typically used in the design of fume capture hoods and overall building ventilation systems.  CFD provides a means to quantitatively predict the fluid flow behavior in and around equipment and structures, accounting for fluid dynamic, heat release, and other physical effects. 

CFD analys

is is performed by developing a model of the system under investigation using a CFD package which enables the designer to create a model of the system divided into three-dimensional cells. Each cell within the model solves the fundamental equations (momentum, mass, and energy balance) for the specific conditions in the cell. Boundary conditions are entered for the model and the program solves the equations, simultaneously, for each cell in the domain. The program iterates until the entire domain obeys the momentum, mass, and energy balance criteria. The domain of the model can be as simple as a fume source and collection hood, or complex, such as a building and its surroundings to account for the effects of adjacent equipment, door openings, and external wind conditions. _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 234 CFD modeling for tankhouses can be developed to: - Evaluate and compare various hood system designs and configuration for optimal capture of emissions form the cell, - Evaluate and compare various scenarios and thereby optimize the secondary ventilation system design, - Predict the ventilation patterns and contaminant migration path within the tankhouse, - Predict relative mist concentrations within the tankhouse. Drawings and field observations are used to develop the geometrical configuration of the 3D model. CFD programs, such as CHAM’s Phoenics or ANSYS’ CFX, use this 3D model to develop a computational domain that can be used to solve the geometric and fluid dynamic properties of a particular application. #### **CONCLUSIONS** 

Many solutions like process controls, mechanical physical barriers, chemical surfactants and alternative anode technology have been implemented to reduce acid mist formation. Mechanical or physical barriers alone are not sufficient to obtain acceptable levels of acid mist concentration, particularly at high current densities. The installation of hoods and secondary ventilation systems are most often necessary to improve conditions inside the tankhouse. 

CFD can be used to provide valuable information on the relative performance of different hoods and secondary ventilation system configurations.  The end result from the CFD modeling is a system that is configured for optimal operation under the actual operation conditions meeting regulatory exposure limits for acid mist.

#### **ABSTRACT** 

Acid mist is a ubiquitous problem throughout all tank houses of the copper industry. Various approaches to alleviate the problem have been adopted by companies from chemical additives to hoods, but all with varying degrees of success. All of these really have been attempts to treat the symptom (acid mist) rather than the inherent problem and indeed many of these “band-aids” have proven both expensive and in some cases ineffectual. CSIRO has established a full size (width and height) transparent cell capable of simulating plant operating conditions (across the range currently used) and generating bubbles under very controlled conditions. With the use of sophisticated diagnostic analytical tools and in parallel to quantification of acid mist under each condition, it was possible to study all the operating variables independently for their effect on bubble size, bubble velocity and consequently acid mist generation. The early results of our consideration of the underlying factors contributing to acid mist generation will be presented.

#### **INTRODUCTION** 

Acid mist is a pervasive problem in electrowinning operations, and is receiving increasing attention due to a better appreciation of its adverse effects on human health, leading to tightening of regulations.  Despite the long history of this phenomenon, mitigation strategies tend to be rather ad hoc: a deeper knowledge of the underlying mechanisms is lacking.  This presents an impediment to the adoption of optimal technologies for further reduction in acid mist levels. 

It is well known that acid mist is formed from droplets ejected into the tankhouse atmosphere by gas bubbles busting at the electrolyte surface.  The gas is primarily oxygen evolved from the anode.  The nucleation is promoted by crevices and other inhomogeneities in the electrode surface [1-3].  More important to acid mist generation is to understand the factors controlling bubble size.  These include current density, electrolyte composition, surface properties of the electrodes, and electrolyte flow [1, 4 and 5].  Unfortunately, there is as yet limited understanding of the combined effect when all of these factors are considered. 

Once the bubbles detach from the anode surface, they rise through the electrolyte cell to the surface of the bath.  The more important phenomena occurring during this process are bubble growth that may be due to coalescence, and separately bubble growth or shrinkage depending upon bubble size and gas supersaturation in the electrolyte [6-8]. It is therefore important to consider the complete size distribution of bubbles. 

O

nce the bubbles reach the electrolyte surface they burst.  Droplets are created by two primary mechanisms: centrifugal acceleration of the retracting bubble’s pellicle and breakup of a capillary jet.  These processes have been better studied in the field of oceanography, where the research has revealed complex variations of the size, number, and ejection trajectory of droplets as a function of bubble size.  Apparently the droplet sizes vary widely, in a range of about 0.01 µm up to 100 µm or more, depending on the bubble size, and can be multimodal, with peaks at low, intermediate and high droplet diameters [9-14].  Many experimental studies are unable to measure such a broad range of sizes. 

Once the drops are airborne, their fate depends chiefly upon their size, the ejection trajectory, the relative humidity in the tankhouse, and the prevailing air currents. Larger droplets will tend to settle out first, and are more inclined to coalesce with other droplets along the way.  The smaller droplets are more pernicious.  Even if they are subject to some degree of evaporation, it will be the more volatile water that goes off, leaving an even more concentrated acid droplet in the air. 

There have been ongoing attempts to minimize acid mist exposure in electrowinning operations.  The methods used typically fall in two categories – acid mist dilution and capture.  Dilution relies on large air flows to turn over the air inside the tankhouse to dilute the mist [15].  Capture aims to trap or prevent the oxygen bubbles at 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

245 

source using mechanical means such as suction hoods, polypropylene balls and surfactants [16].  Each of these methods has been used individually or in combination on different operations.  Although these methods have helped reduce acid mist exposure, existing plant practice and variable operating conditions make control of acid mist in the tankhouse a challenge.  Variability in current density, temperature, electrolyte concentration, flow rate, additive concentration and electrolyte impurities can affect oxygen bubble properties which are of critical importance to the mechanisms for mist formation and therefore the amount of mist generated. 

CSIRO experience and capabilities particularly in computational and physical modelling affords a unique opportunity to carry out a study to understand the effects of variable operating condition on acid mist generation, with the ultimate goal of eliminating acid mist all together.  The first step towards this goal was the initiation of an industry multi sponsored 12 month project to establish the capabilities and expertise required to address some of the knowledge gaps highlighted above with respect to bubble and droplet characterisation as well as acid mist quantification to enable assessment of the impact of operational factors on the quantity of acid mist generated. #### **CONCLUSIONS AND NEXT STEPS** 

The capability that has been developed here has for the first time provided an opportunity to measure in-situ, the characteristics of bubbles and droplets with a resolution down to 1 µm.  Coupled with this capability is the ability to quantify the total acid mist produced under a given operating condition.  These combined capabilities provide an opportunity to create a baseline understanding of the key operating parameters that contribute significantly to acid mist generation in electrowinning.  Furthermore the techniques developed provide an ideal way to assess and compare the various acid mist

An extension to the multi-sponsored project is currently being offered and part of this phase will be to expand the range of operating parameters to be investigated on their impact on acid mist generation.  With the broader aim of acid mist elimination, a computational fluid dynamics (CFD) model will be developed to predict bubble flow within a cell and look at how changes to various operating conditions and designs affect the distribution of gas and bubble size within the cell.

### **ABSTRACT** 

The world’s first copper electrorefinery started production in 1869 at Burry Port in South Wales. Built within the Pembrey Copper Works which had commenced smelting operations in 1849, the new refinery was based on principles described in the British patents issued to J.B. Elkington in 1865 and 1869. Refining principles and practices pioneered there were key to the foundation of modern electro-refining practice in what is now a dominant international industry producing over 16 Mt of electrical grade copper annually. This paper explores the background to this pioneering application of the new, early 19th century, science of “electro-metallurgy” and examines its links to the contemporary decorative electro-plating industry and to the shortcomings of 19th century fire refining. The beginnings and early years of the Pembrey electrorefinery are briefly discussed in relation to the quality, applications and pyrometallurgy of copper at the time. More than a decade would elapse before the birth of the electrical age: the Pembrey refinery may be seen as one of its vital precursors

.

#### **INTRODUCTION** 

In the 1840s, the new science of ‘electro-metallurgy’, a term coined by Smee in 1841 [1], was being adapted to the decorative electro-deposition of silver in a thin, bright adherent coating that was evidently equal in appearance to traditional silverware [2]. Chief among innovative manufacturers of decorative objects who took up the new art of silver electro-plating was the acclaimed firm of G.R. Elkington and Co. of Birmingham, England.  The company, which vigorously developed all aspects of electro-metallurgy for the decorative trade, entered the field of ‘electrotyping’, a technique in which the surface features of a mould are copied on an electro-deposited copper layer which, when stripped off, can be used to reproduce an imprint of the mould. In essence, it is a form of casting by electrodeposition, invented in 1837 independently by Jacobi in Russia [3] and Spencer in England [4, 28].  Applications in printing on paper or cloth, for example, are selfevident, but the company, now Elkington, Mason and Co., developed the technique further to reproduce relatively massive decorative objects.  This became a very successful business: electrotype objects large and small produced by the company even featured in the Great Exhibition of 1851 in London [4]. It is therefore clear that by 1850, techniques to produce thick copper layers by electro-deposition on a mould wall had been perfected within the company.  This copper was known to be of very high quality [22]. 

The growing importance of copper in the company’s activities led, in 1849, to the establishment of a primary copper smelter on a green field site at Burry Port near Llanelli in South Wales, operating as ‘Mason & Elkington’, reflecting the different proportions of ownership. Subsequently, James Balleny Elkington (1830-1907), 3rd son of the company’s Birmingham-based founder, George Richards Elkington (1801-1865), began investigating the electrochemical recovery of copper as cathode from anodes of fire refined copper, probably with the help of the metallurgist Alexander Parkes. Although predated by electrorefining experiments elsewhere in Europe [5], there was an evident link to the company’s expertise in electrotyping. 

However, with little contemporary information available, the underlying purpose of the work remains open to question. Was the metallurgical objective to produce a purified anode material for electrotyping?  With access to the earlier work of von Leuchtenberg [6], for example, James Elkington would also have been well aware that the anode precipitate formed during electrotyping contained precious metals, notably silver, and might therefore be worth recovering as an end in itself. Indeed, Mason & Elkington were one of a small number of UK copper smelters to specialise in the smelting of argentiferous copper ores and had opened a silver refinery within their Pembrey Copper Works in 1853 to utilise o

ne of Parkes’s patents to recover silver [27], probably inspired by the company’s silver plating interests. James Elkington obtained two patents embodying the technology and procedures for a process of continuous copper electro-deposition from cast anodes on a commercial, industrial scale. The first, granted in 1865 [8], concerned the recovery of purified copper as cathode; the second, granted in 1869 [9], was additionally aimed at the recovery of silver as precipitate. Both patent specifications address the chemical shortcomings of _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 261 contemporary fire refining practice, but without comment on the relative costs of the two refining methods. In 1869, an electrolytic refinery was opened at the Pembrey smelter based upon the principles outlined in both patents [27]. 4 5

Elkington. #### **ELKINGTON’S PATENTS** The supply of refined copper for all applications, including its use as the anode material for electrotyping, depended on pyrometallurgical methods which had been _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 262 meticulously perfected in South Wales and elsewhere over a period of many years [14]. In Elkington’s time, thermodynamic analysis was in its infancy: copper pyrometallurgy relied largely on empirical knowledge and repeated batch processing in reverberatory furnaces to achieve chemical change, as exemplified by the Welsh process [14], and the composition of even the best quality product, ‘best selected’ copper, fell far short of the levels of purity tha

t would become possible by electrorefining [15]. 

In the South Wales industry of the 1850’s, the extractive pyrometallurgy of silver from the rich copper ores of the period was painstaking, costly and chemically inefficient, with high levels of silver retention in de-silvered copper [16].  Awareness within Elkington, Mason & Co of von Leuchtenberg’s discovery that silver could be recovered by electrolytic precipitation [6] would, given the company’s prowess in stateof the-art electrotyping, surely stimulate thinking on an electrochemical approach to copper refining that yielded silver (and in later times PGM’s). 

#### **First Patent 1865 – Copper** 

In the short preamble to his patent application, Elkington relates the principles of his invention for the treatment of reverberatory-refined copper as follows: 

“. . . the products [i.e. fire refined copper] . . . are . . . refined by magnetic or electric currents, by employing such metal products to be used as positive plates in a solution, by which the copper in these plates will be dissolved and deposited as pure copper on the surfaces in connection with the negative poles employed, whilst the other metals previously combined with the copper in the unrefined plates at the positive poles will be precipitated in forms or combinations depending on the solvent employed in the solutions.  In carrying out this invention, a series or succession of vats are used, and the electric or magnetic currents pass in succession through the series.”  (Note that the terms ‘anode’ and ‘cathode’ first appeared in 1833 [13] but were not used by Elkington). 

John Percy, the leading British metallurgist of the day, dismissed Elkington’s assumed claim to the originality of the electrochemical concept [17], citing the earlier work of von Leuchtenberg [6].  But he seems to have misunderstood.  The burden of Elkington’s patent lies in the proposed technology. To be more specific, and quoting from the text of his patent, Elkington proposed features of tankhouse practice listed below that are readily recognisable in any present-day electrorefinery, regardless of metallic species:- 

#### ● Anode arrangement: 

“. . . I cast such impure copper as it comes from the furnace into plates, say eighteen inches [~ 45.7cm] square and three quarters of an inch [19mm] thick, and with lugs projecting from their corners at one end.  These plates I place in troughs each sufficiently long to take two plates end to end, and I place three such rows of plates, or in all six positive plates in each trough, a space of say six inches [15.2cm]. The lugs on the plates rest on the ends of the trough and on a cross bar fixed midway of its length, which parts have strips of copper fixed on them . . . all in metallic connection, the one with the other”.

#### **Second Patent 1869 – Silver** 

The patent of 1869 takes the earlier patent as its starting point but is different in character, introducing specific claims, giving considerable detail on the proposed technology and conduct of the process, and addressing the recovery of silver. 

#### <u>Tankhouse Arrangement</u> 

Changes proposed in the physical arrangement of the tankhouse (‘ _dissolving house_ ’) may have been in response to experience with the precursor arrangement of fixed troughs.  For example: 

1.  The electrolyte is circulated by having a sloping tankhouse floor (at a slope of 1 in 24) to promote intermittent, manually controlled gravity flow between and within cells. 

2.  The sloping floor permits the accumulation of anode slimes in the cells to be flushed to collection tanks at the lower end. 

3.  The collection tanks, and others at the top of the slope, act as reservoirs supplying the banks of cells. Electrolyte is pumped between them to sustain cell circulation. But electrolyte treatment is still seen as a batch operation: the whole of the electrolyte in this now much larger combined system is to be replaced when iron contamination becomes unacceptable.

#### <u>Cell Operation</u> 

Gravity circulation through and between the lines of jars from the upper to the lower storage tanks, and the need to drain the system from time to time, required an intricate arrangement of  piped connections which were controlled by pipe clips: 

“. . . each [jar] has a hole in the bottom closed by a wooden plug, also a hole in the side 4 inches from the bottom, and another hole diametrically opposite to the first and 4 inches from the top.  The jars are set up level on the inclined floor with wooden wedges saturated with pitch.  The jars are connected together from the upper to the lower level of the room, each jar having a pipe passing out from it at the hole near the top, and entering the next jar below at the hole near the bottom. The connections with the jars are made with vulcanized India-rubber, and intermediate of the connections the pipes may be of lead and about half-inch internal diameter.” 

The flow within a jar was upwards, and the small bore of the connections would ensure a modest velocity within the jar.  The start-up and circulation procedures are described as follows: 

“The solution . . . is admitted to the uppermost jars and runs from jar to jar until those at the lower end of the building are filled. The electrolyte was to be circulated through the array of jars once every 24 hours, when it would also be pumped from the lower to the upper tanks.  When anode slimes built up to the level of the lower hole:

The jars would, presumably, then be replenished according to the start-up procedure. 

Elkington’s perception of the need for upward electrolyte circulation in the cell is the accepted norm today.

### **Commercial Considerations** 

#### <u>Silver</u> 

Elkington’s second patent [9] was clearly aimed at recovering silver from firerefined copper more effectively and cheaply than by contemporary pyrometallurgical methods, as well as producing refined copper free of the perceived ‘injurious effect’ of silver.  This effect is thought to relate to annealing temperature, which increases sharply with silver content up to approx. 500ppm Ag, or ~16 oz/tonne [21].  The high and variable silver levels occurring in fire refined copper could cause problems in cold working operations such as wiredrawing which might conceivably be minimized by having the consistent and lower silver levels found in electrorefined copper. 

The patent specification is quite carefully written to justify the treatment of blister copper,

preferably low in iron, of any silver content.  However, Elkington chooses to refer to the silver assay of the ore rather than that of the anode copper, probably reflecting the company’s experience in primary smelting and its long-standing interest in smelting argentiferous copper [27]. He distinguishes between low-silver ores where “. . . the quantity of silver is not such as to pay for the cost of [pyrometallurgical] extraction, but the process has nevertheless been necessary when copper of high quality is required . . .”, and “Ores containing a larger quantity of silver, say from eight ounces to the ton [250 g/tonne, or ~8 oz/tonne] and upwards . . .”. 

#### Elkington’s claims imply the following: 

● the silver in any ore can readily be recovered by electrolytic precipitation at marginal cost;  for copper ores low in silver (containing less than ~250g Ag per tonne or ~8 oz/tonne, say) which do not attract a silver premium, that silver is essentially ‘free’. According to Elkington, such ores would invariably have been treated for removal of silver during smelting so as to produce copper with acceptably low Ag content, even though the cost of Ag extraction might have exceeded the value of the silver, 

● Electrorefining offers a crucial benefit for silver where the cost of the pyrometallurgical process exceeds the value of silver recovered, 

● for copper ores high in silver (containing more than ~250g Ag per tonne, say) that could attract a premium,  the economic return on silver recovered by electrolytic precipitation is proportionately greater than that by the pyrometallurgical methods which would have been necessary to remove the silver before or during smelting, 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

270 

● a quality premium for copper from cathode is apparently chargeable no matter what the silver content of the ore. 

. 

Elkington’s claims were based upon experience of the smelting trade and the copper ore market of the time.  The apparent cost advantage of silver recovery by electrolysis would conceivably have led the company to seek silver-rich anode copper from external suppliers.  An ore containing, say, 6% copper, a typical minimum of the time, with a silver assay of ~250 g/tonne (8 oz/tonne) would yield anode copper containing roughly 4000 ppm Ag (4 kg/tonne, or 129 oz/tonne) of which perhaps 85% was likely to have been recovered by electro-refining in the Elkington period up to 1884. It is possible, moreover, that refining bought-in copper could have produced even higher yields by treating those selected for their high silver content. 

#### <u>Copper</u> 

In the mid nineteenth century, fire refined copper served market demands well, and there seemed little potential for the relatively ultra-pure copper that would emerge from Pembrey electrorefinery.  However, there were exceptions.  First, was the perceived need for a pure copper for electrotyping, which was at that time an important commercial activity. Second, fo

llowing the work of Thomson (Lord Kelvin) on the electrical resistance of telegraph cable [22], there was a clear need for high purity copper wire in the rapidly expanding telegraphy industry. Before the unforeseen dawn of the electrical age, this limited market for electrorefined copper must have been seen as a commercial challenge, and Elkington’s focus on silver recovery therefore seems entirely appropriate. 

#### <u>Pembrey Copper Works Electrorefinery post-1869</u> 

The jar-based layout was still in use in 1878 [23]. Not surprisingly, reaching “design” capacity was slow.  It is believed that initially a small number of jars was in use, and that by the early 1870s, production of refined copper was about 0.5 tonnes/week (29). In 1878 Percy reported an increased production of 6 long tons per week (~5.9 tonnes/week) [17], roughly half the output projected nine years earlier in Elkington’s patent claims [9].  This perhaps exposes the boldness of Elkington’s ideas.  The plant was acquired by Elliott’s Metal Co. in 1884, and by 1890 Elkington’s jars had been replaced by lead-lined wooden vats [24].  Under Elliott’s, copper output rose to about 135 long tons per week (~137 tonnes per week) and the weekly production of Ag and Au from anodes was 30,000 oz and 500 oz respectively [7], corresponding to a silver assay of 220 oz per long ton or 6,900 g/tonne anode copper. But, despite modernisation, the works began to decline later in the 1890s [25], no doubt due to the rapid expansion of copper smelting and refining in overseas mining areas and in locations closer to international markets [26]. The works closed in 1912 [27]. A detailed discussion on the evolution of the Pembrey refinery and the initial spread of copper electrorefining technology worldwide will be given in a forthcoming paper [29].

#### **CONCLUDING REMARKS** 

Within two decades of the commissioning of the Pembrey refinery, the electrical age had arrived and there was a relentlessly increasing demand for electrorefined copper. In parallel with but not apparently constrained by the Elkington patents, electrorefineries were soon established in continental Europe, the first thought to have been at Mansfeld, Germany in 1873. Dynamo technology was also advancing at this time and the capacity of the first refineries may have been limited in part by shortcomings in dynamo design. The technology of the new refineries was based upon rectangular vats as suggested in Elkington’s first patent, not the jars specified in his second [25].  The first electrorefinery in the US, commissioned in 1883 at Newark, New Jersey followed the European lead: electrorefing subsequently spread rapidly in North America and elsewhere (perhaps a little delayed in the US by the energetic marketing of Lake copper) to the extent that by 1903 there were at least 30 electrorefineries operating throughout the world with a combined annual output of about 250,000 tonnes [

25], of which 85% was produced in the US.  In 2012, combined world output was over 16 M tonnes produced by more than 50 refineries distributed across six continents.

#### **INTRODUCTION** 

Decopperizing the bleed electrolytes at copper refinery tank houses in their “Secondary” and “Tertiary” Liberator Circuits has been an area which requires significant improvement and advancement in the refineries around the globe. Electrowinning of Copper from these circuits is either in the form of impure copper cathodes or highly impure copper powder with high content of Arsenic and other metals. These cathodes then have to be sent back to the smelters leading to extra costs and handling. Decopperization of this corrosive electrolyte in conventional liberator cells generates a potentially hazardous working environment and the produced copper will be in the form of impure arsenic bearing copper powder posing severe handling issues. This technical paper focuses on replacing of the conventional Liberator circuits with advanced emew® cells to provide the following advantages: 

- 1) Production of coherent, harvestable and high purity copper cathodes even at very low copper concentration 

- 2) Technology which can provide safe working environment 

- 3) Achieving higher purity for copper cathodes with high the overall efficiency of liberator circuit 

- 4) Reducing man hours per tonne of production 

#### **CONVENTIONAL LIBERATOR AND EMEW®** 

Single Cell arrangement of the conventional liberator circuit is shown in figure 1. Due to plannar nature of the cathode/anode and low flow/turbulance there always exists a “Zone of Depletion” which effects the purity of the target metal in the conventional cells. Thus, even with the high concentration of Copper there is always occurrence of impurity adherence. The emew® cell comprises of a stainless steel pipe with ABS (or other suitable material) plastic end caps. As depicted in figure 1, the anode is located in the center of the cell while the inside surface of the pipe is the cathode. The metal being recovered is plated onto a removable/reusable starter sheet pressed against the inside pipe surface. In conjunction with a high electrolyte flow this cylindrical arrangement of the anode/cathode provides a significant increase in mass transfer which enables selective deposition of the metal such as Copper. Thus the most wide reaching application for the emew® technology in this area lies in complete replacement of the Liberator circuits on new projects, or expansion and/or refurbishment of installed facilities.

#### **RESULTS AND CONCLUSIONS** 

Successful pilot plant trials were performed with Aurubis Hamburg personnel conducting the trials. During each deposition cycle, which lasted up to 120 hours, the emew® cell was easy to operate on a continuous basis. The cell however can also be stopped and started easily during this time period.

#### **INTRODUCTION** 

In the mining industry two widely used technologies exist for the electrorefining process: the conventional, which uses a starting sheet, and that of permanent cathodes. The conventional technology dominated the market without competition until the 1980s. However, the permanent cathode technology achieved a strong position in the industry in the early 1990s, as it allows operating at high current density (300 A/m2 – 340 A/m2), and since it is mechanized, and in many cases automated, it also has high productivity levels. This drove many refineries, drawn by the certainty of increased production, to a technological change.  Nevertheless, some conventional refineries that use starting sheets, such as Ventanas, have significantly improved their processes, establishing themselves as a competitive alternative to the permanent cathode technology, even at high current densities. 

The Ventanas Electrolytic Refinery is an example of the conventional technology since it uses a starting sheet and its production makes intensive use of manual labor, owing to low levels of mechanization. Ventanas is a custom plant that processes four types of anodes:

Ventanas, Codelco Teniente, H. Videla Lira and Anglo American. Each of these shows different performance, since they have distinct chemical characteristics. Reducing the spacing between electrodes requires a larger amount of starting anodes and cathodes and, consequently, a greater use of the preparation machines of anodes (MPA) and starting cathodes (MFCI). For that purpose conventional refineries normally have exclusive circuits for their production, requiring high physical and chemical quality of anodes, electrolyte with low impurity content, special addition of additives, and continuous maintenance of plates on which the deposit is produced. For that reason the process usually operated at the current densities of less than 270 A/m2. In the case of Ventanas the current density is at 235 A/m2. In 2008 there was a major fault in the transformer of the rectifier unit Nº 1 of the Electrolytic Refinery, which provides energy to the stripper circuit composed of sections Nº 1, 2, 7 and 8. Under the circumstances it was necessary to feed this circuit from the rectifier unit Nº 4, for which the continuous current had to be reduced from 20.8 kA to 15 kA (a normal operation parameter for said sheets), involving an estimated production loss of 2,700 t of cathodes per month. On the other hand, in August 2011 it was agreed to modify the system of liberator cells by continuing the operation only in the first stage and detaining the second and third stages. That is to say, the production of high quality cathode by electrowinning (EW) continues while the production of arsenic cathodes and arsenic slime has stopped. The growing complexity observed in the refined copper markets has encouraged the Ventanas Refinery to improve its competitiveness through innovative means of low-cost investment, high creativity and short introduction periods, which have allowed for a better application of its resources. In an increasingly competitive environment it is important to evaluate the adoption of new technologies from a practical point of view, which should comply with a costbenefit analysis. It is essential to maintain active employee participation by supporting creativity and ingenuity and preserving the correct operational practices. #### **THE HAMBURG TANKHOUSE OF AURUBIS AFTER FINISHING OF THE MODERNIZATION PROJECT** 

G. Leuprecht and R. Behlmer _Aurubis AG Hovestrasse 50 D-20539 Hamburg, Germany g.leuprecht@aurubis.com_ 

#### **ABSTRACT** 

The Hamburg tankhouse of Aurubis was built in 1989 and expanded in 1992. After more than 20 years of operation, the old lead lined cells had reached the end of their lives. During a 3-year program, 1080 old cells have been replaced by polymer concrete cells. The replacement was executed section by section during normal operation of the tankhouse. Each turnaround was completed during an anode cycle of 21 days. All steps will be described in this presentation. In parallel to the replacement program, longer cells with an increased number of anodes and cathodes were installed. This fact combined with the full utilization of the rectifier capacity has maintained an increase of cathode capacity to 416,000 m per year. Beside the change of the cells, some modifications into the handling systems were necessary. So t

he inlet and outlet conveyors of the stripping machines and the spacing conveyor of the anode preparation machine had to be adapted to the increased number of electrodes in the cells. Also a special construction of the crane bale was required for operating old and new cells during the conversion time. 

After the retrofit, the modernized tankhouse has increased its productivity and will be able to achieve the technical and economical demands for the next future.

#### **INTRODUCTION** 

Aurubis is the largest copper producer in Europe and the second largest producer of copper cathodes in the world. The company was formed after the acquisition of the Belgian Cumerio group by Norddeutsche Affinerie in 2009. Today Aurubis is operating 16 production sites in 11 European countries and North America with about 6,400 employees. It has become the largest copper recycler and rod producer in the world. It also is one of the world’s leading manufacturers of copper foil and flat rolled products and stands for a production capacity of about 1.3 million tonnes of different copper products. With a lot of efforts during the last decades, Aurubis is also one of the global leaders in environmental protection in the copper industry. 

Today Aurubis is operating 4 tankhouses in Hamburg, Olen, Pirdop and Luenen with a capacity of approx. 1.2 million tonnes of copper cathodes. All of these tankhouses are using the ISA-process. The Hamburg tankhouse was built in 1989 and is the oldest and the largest tankhouse amongst the Aurubis cathode production sites. 

After more than 20 years of operation and a production of nearly 7 million tonnes of cathodes, the original lead lined cells were at the end of their lives and had to be changed. Within Aurubis it is usual, that such expensive investments always have to be combined with efforts for an increased productivity and often with a rise of production capacity by applying the most modern technology. 

This presentation will describe the main improvements and the chronology of works during the realization of the project.

#### **CONCLUSIONS** 

After long 44 months 35 sections and 1,050 cells were replaced in a tankhouse, which was producing approx. 365,000 m of cathodes per year. During this time a big hole was walking through the plant, making the normal production work not easier and especially not

safer. But the whole tankhouse team and all the contactors did a good job, so that there were only 2 minor accidents and 20 first-aid treatments during the whole period with more than 100,000 working hours for replacement works. In total 5,300 m of you pipes have been installed and approximately 5,500 special shaped parts were incorporated into the new structure. 

1,300 m of old lead lining was recycled and about 2,400 m<sup>3</sup> of old concrete parts had to be removed. Approximately 7,000 m of polymer concrete was installed in the form of 1,050 cells. 

The 2 cranes were running a distance of 1,400 km for installing new beams and cells and removing old lead lining and old concrete parts. 

Summarized it could be stated, that the project organization worked excellent and even the very long duration of the project, did only cause minor disturbances to the normal production. The project was realized strictly in the planned time schedule and below the budgeted costs and therefore was a real success and a step forward. 

#### **SUMMARY** 

Aurubis has modernized its Hamburg tankhouse by replacing the original lead lined cells to polymer concrete cells. The program was started with the installation of a pilot section with longer cells for testing the behavior of the modified design. After excellent testing results the conversion of the other sections started in September 2009 and was finished October 2012. Since this time the tankhouse capacity increased to 416,000 m of copper cathodes per year. The capacity increase was realized by an increased number of cathodes and anodes per cell and the fully utilization of the installed rectifier capacity of 40 kA. The new capacity can be realized with the existing cranes and handling mac

hines. Only small modifications were necessary for adapting the equipment to the higher capacity. The productivity of the tankhouse was increased by the fact, that no additional workforce had to be implemented. 

With the realization of the replacement program the Hamburg tankhouse of Aurubis has made a very important step forward in competitiveness of copper cathode production and will be well prepared for the challenges in the future.

#### **ABSTRACT** 

In 2011, the first two electrorefining tankhouses using the METTOP-BRXTechnology went into operation – one producing cathodes out of ore and one out of secondary raw material. Both tankhouses show the possibility of achieving Grade A cathodes at a current density of more than 400 A/m² while maintaining a current efficiency of 97.0 – 98.5 per cent. 

After almost two years of operation it is now possible to directly compare the costs of the two-part tankhouse of Montanwerke Brixlegg AG. While half of the tankhouse is operated at standard current density, the other half is equipped with the METTOP-BRX-Technology. 

Basis of the technology is an optimized electrolyte feed system in each electrolytic cell. Even though the higher current density is directly proportional to the consumption of electrical energy, the overall operational expenditures keep the same due to the lower costs for bound capital. Furthermore, the higher productivity results in a smaller footprint of the tankhouse. 

The present paper gives a detailed insight into the additional costs and economic benefits when operating a tankhouse at high current densities. It shows the mathematical background of the calculation, as well as the result – the capital and operational cost savings when using the METTOP-BRX-Technology.

#### **INTRODUCTION** 

Increasing tankhouse capacity can generally be done in two ways: Either by increasing the cathodic deposition area (i.e., adding more cells or increasing the number of electrodes in the cell) or by increasing the current density. The former possibility is relatively cost-intensive, as new buildings and infrastructure are required, and sometimes it is not possible due to limited space and/or other restrictions. Increasing the current density is generally a matter of the actual electrical system but it is also limited as current efficiency and cathode quality tend to decrease with increasing current density, due to problems with both cathodic

deposition and anodic dissolution. Consequently, the current densities that are used in electrorefining are far below the theoretical limiting current density. 

According to physical and chemical laws, the only way to increase the current density in a way that ensures that the electrodeposition is still pure and that the metal sheets are smooth and of a high quality, is to minimize the diffusion boundary layer and/or to influence the electrocrystallization by an optimized inhibitor distribution. This can be achieved by increasing the flow directly at the cathode, for example by using a manifold inlet to achieve a parallel electrolyte flow and introduce the fresh electrolyte with the active inhibitors directly at the cathodes. 

METTOP has developed together with Montanwerke Brixlegg AG, Austria a new type of manifold inlet: the METTOP-BRX-Technology<sup>(1,2)</sup> . This technology uses a parallel electrolyte flow in the cell to achieve more homogeneous conditions in the cell, as well as to enable the use of higher current densities. The parallel electrolyte flow can be achieved by either using a Parallel Flow Device (PFD), namely a separate device that is installed in the cell, or a Parallel Flow Plate (PFP), namely an integrated system in the polymer concrete cell. 

#### **Parallel Flow Device** 

The core of the METTOP-BRX-Technology is a Parallel Flow Device (PFD) (Figure 1), which introduces the fresh electrolyte between each pair of electrodes (Figure 2a and b). Special positioning devices, so-called cathode spacers (Figure 3), provide an accurate electrode positioning, a defined relative position of cathode and nozzles. The nozzles, which are designed for each individual tankhouse, direct the fresh electrolyte in an upwards flow in front of the cathode surface, which only enhances the already existing flow resulting from natural convection. Therefore, the settlement of the anode slime is not influenced by using the METTOP-BRX-Technology. The PFDs are customertailored to guarantee optimum results for each specific tankhouse.

The effects of the parallel electrolyte flow are:

- Better temperature distribution in the entire cell 

- More homogeneous copper concentration 

#### **Parallel Flow Plate** 

The Parallel Flow Plate (PFP) is a combination of PFD and the cell: In new tankhouses – or when replacing cells in an existing tankhouse – the METTOP-BRXTechnology can already be integrated in the polymer concrete cells (Figure 4 and Figure 5). The main idea is to cast th

e cell in a way that the volume for the electrolyte distribution system is already included. Therefore, only a stainless steel front plate with nozzles and cathode spacers – the Parallel Flow Plate – is attached to the cell. Implementing PFPs minimizes the installation effort, as only the front plate has to be mounted. Furthermore, these systems can already be preassembled at the cell supplier and the customer can install the complete cells just like normal cells.

#### **ABSTRACT** 

This paper introduces the Parallel Flow Device (PFD) technology and production practices for high current density copper electrolytic refining. The technology has been successfully implemented for the first time on a large industrial scale, enabling the copper electrolysis current density to reach 420 A/m², thereby substantially increasing copper electrolytic productivity. Through this technology, a new level in copper electrolytic refining has been achieved.

#### **INTRODUCTION** 

Copper electrolytic refining technology, its process flow, and the associated equipment have improved greatly over the years since the first implementation in 1869. However, although the basic principle of this electrolytic process has not changed, achieving intensified, highly efficient, high-class, and energy-saving copper electrolytic refining has been an ongoing development goal. At present, there are two main production processes used in copper electrolysis: One is the traditional starting sheet – process with a current density of 220 280 A/m²; the second is the permanent stainless – steel cathode process with a current density of 280 350 A/m². An important means of improving the electrolytic productivity is to increase the current density. Therefore, all copper electro-refining plants are focused on increasing the current density to improve production capacity. 

In 2007, Xiangguang Copper finished Phase I of the electrolysis project, implemented to produce 200,000 tonn

es of cathode copper annually, and started production. The tankhouse, comprising 720 cells, was designed to operate at a current density of 280 A/m². In 2009, Xiangguang Copper began Phase II of the capacity expansion project and in order to further improve productivity, Xiangguang Copper decided to cooperate with METTOP GmbH, Austria. By adopting the – METTOP-BRX-Technology [1 2], optimized for a high current density, the productivity has been increased to 300,000 tonne/annum using the same number of cells (i.e., 720). In June 2011, this technology was put into operation. The current density achieved the guaranteed level of 385 A/m² in July of the same year. Subsequently, it was increased to 420 A/m² and has remained at this stable current density to date. 

#### **METTOP-BRX-TECHNOLOGY** 

#### **Basic Principle of the METTOP-BRX-Technology** 

It is well established that the most effective way to improve productivity during copper electrolytic refining is to increase the current density. However, increasing the current density is associated with certain problems, such as thickening of the electrolyte diffusion layer in the anode region and cupric ion depletion in the cathode region, which can result in a concentration polarization, anode passivation, and the formation of nodules on the cathode copper. To minimize or eliminate these issues, the cycling speed of the electrolyte should be greatly increased; however, an increased cycling speed decreases the sedimentation rate of slime in the electrolyte, resulting in a low purity electrolyte. Inevitably, the slime is a serious pollutant and thereby reduces the cathode quality, even making it hard to continue production.

The basic principle behind the METTOP-BRX-Technology is to minimize concentration polarization resulting from high current densities by modifying the electrolyte flow in the cell. More specifically, through the use of special devices the electrolyte flows into cells at a certain speed from one side of the cathode plate, enabling the electrolyte to flow upward, parallel to the cathode surface (Figure 1). When the electrolyte flows upward at high speed across the cathodes, enhanced natural convection is generated between the cathodes and anodes. With the electrolyte around the cathode region moving upward and the electrolyte around the anode region moving downward, the electrolyte flows in a circular motion (Figure 2). The upward movement of electrolyte around cathode region reduces concentration polarization and the downward movement of electrolyte around the anode region accelerates diffusion within the layer adjacent to the anode and increases slime sedimentation. The special device that the electrolyte flows through is called the Parallel Flow Device (PFD). The high-speed parallel flow of electrolyte also generates a more even temperature and concentration distribution, avoids concentration polarization and anode passivation

caused by high current density, and ensures good cathode quality, resulting in enhanced productivity. Figure 1 – Parallel upward movement of electrolyte _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 336 Anode

Figure 2 – Circular movement of electrolyte between the cathode and anode #### **Process Flow of METTOP-BRX-Technology** #### Process Summary The 720 cells are divided into 8 independent circulating systems that are uniformly distributed in the tankhouse and every 4 independent circulating systems share one circulation tank. The electrolyte in the circulation tank is heated up or cooled down to 65 °C and then pumped into the cells through the PFD installed on the cell side. The electrolyte enters the cell at the bottom of every cathode plate and then flows up parallel to cathode plate. At both ends of the cell there are overflows, through which the electrolyte returns to the circulation tank, thus forming a complete circulating system. To ensure purity of the electrolyte during circulation, a purification and filtration system is incorporated. The system includes two filter press pumps, one purification filter, and the corresponding piping, valves, and flow meters. Everyday a certain amount of electrolyte is pumped through the purification filter and then returned to the circulation tank to complete the filtration. When the anode and cathode plates are taken out, the liquid supernatant (i.e., 75% of the electrolyte in each cell) is put into the liquid supernatant tank and moved to the purification filter by a filter press pump. Subsequently, it is returned to the circulation tank and reintroduced into the electrolyte circulatory system. The slime (i.e., 25% of the electrolyte in each cell) is transported into a pit and allowed to settle by natural sedimentation. The separated electrolyte then flows into the liquid supernatant tank using a manual filter press and the separated anode mud is sent to the precious metals recovery process after going through an automatic filter press. #### **EXISTING PROBLEMS AND COUNTERMEASURES** 

1) Cell voltage and DC energy consumption are high **:** The cell voltage can be calculated using the formula: V=IR1+IR2+(EA-EK). It is well established that the cell voltage is directly proportion to the electrical current and when current density is 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

342 

420  A/m<sup>2</sup> , the average cell voltage is up to 0.44 V, nearly 1.5 times more than the average cell voltage of conventional electrolysis (i.e., 280 A/m<sup>2</sup> ). The DC consumption during electrolysis depends on the cell voltage and current efficiency, namely W=1000V/1.1852 η. Therefore, when high current density electrolysis is used, the unit consumption rises with rising cell voltage. When the average cell voltage is 0.44 V, the DC energy consumption for one tonne of copper cathode is up to 403.60 kWh, nearly 1.5 times more than the DC consumption for conventional electrolysis. This results in more electrical energy being transformed into thermal energy. The main countermeasure is continuous optimization of process parameters. For example, reducing the copper in the electrolyte as much as possible to decrease the cell voltage and energy consumption; improving purification and control of the electrolyte, decreasing As, Sb, Bi, Ni, Fe, Zn and other impurities in the electrolyte and the specific electrolyte resistance, thus decreasing the cell voltage and energy consumption; maintaining a lower acid content and lower additive level, and decreasing electrolyte resistance and viscosity. In addition, cell voltage and energy consumption can be decreased by using appropriate quality and shaped anodes. 

2) Copper cathodes are prone to getting pores **:** Since the circulation system has no overhead tank, the electrolyte is directly supplied to cells by the frequency conversion circulation pump. This can increase the probability of air being introduced into the closed electrolyte circulation system, for example if the pump malfunctions or there is air ingress through the piping. As a result fine bubbles can become distributed in the electrolyte. If the bubble level is low, it is manifest only on one side of the copper cathode close to the nozzle. However, with increasing levels, needle-shaped eyes are formed in the middle and upper part of the copper cathode. In the most extreme case the entire copper cathode surface can become affected by pores. To circumvent these issues, various devices can be installed to enable any trapped gas to exit the closed system. Additionally, adopting high-strength composite tubing and establishing good-tightness along with increasing the internal pressure in the tubing can prevent air entering into the circulation system from tube connections and other leakage points. 

3) High temperature electrolyte: Since the electrolyte is continually heated due to the large current, it retains this heat in summer even if nothing cov

ers the cell surface. As a result the temperature can reach over 70 °C, which exceeds the control range. The main countermeasure for this problem is to cool the electrolyte using water cooling. If the thermal balance is calculated for the Xiangguang Copper tankhouse with 720 cells, running at 420 A/m<sup>2</sup> , under an atmospheric temperature of 42 °C, an electrolyte temperature of 64 °C, and no coverage, an excessive heat of 9372600.23<sup>_KJ•h-1_</sup> needs to be balanced. If cooling with water, when the inlet water temperature is 34 °C and the outlet water temperature is 42 °C, the cooling circulation water needs to flow at 279 m<sup>3</sup> /h. If 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

343 

half the cell surface is covered, the water needs to circulate at 600 m<sup>3</sup> /h. Therefore, Xiangguang Copper introduced a water cooling system set at 600 m<sup>3</sup> /h to cool the electrolyte in summer when the weather is very hot. 

4) Stainless steel permanent cathodes bend easily and the insulation plate is prone to burn: Bent cathodes can result in short circuits occurring between the anode and cathode plates. During production at 420 A/m<sup>2</sup> , the cathodes can emit a considerable amount of heat in a short time. Under conditions where the hanger bars become red hot, the cathodes are prone to deformation, and the busbar insulators can burn. The main countermeasure to avoid these issues is to prioritize cathode maintenance. Additionally, performing regular inspections to detect short circuits is paramount to guarantee timely detection and proactively handle any malfunction. Utilizing the newest cell temperature and voltage detectors enables the group of cells with the short circuit to be identified and corresponding measures to be carried out. Thereby, the stress associated with process interruptions can be alleviated and the working efficiency can be enhanced. 

5) Anodes prone to passivate: A lot of slime particles occur in passivated copper cathodes, since impurities precipitate on the surface. Sampling tests have indicated that Bi can reach 0.0024 wt% in the copper cathode，a level 12 times higher than the amount in A grade copper. It is well established that passivation significantly influences the chemical composition of copper cathodes. 

Data obtained during operations at 420 A/m<sup>2</sup> have shown that peripheral – passivation rises if the anode contains 0.30 0.35 wt.% Pb. When the Pb levels reach – 0.35 0.45 wt.%, peripheral passivation can seriously increase. In cases where the anode – Pb content reaches 0.45 0.60 wt.% during the third cathode cycle the voltage can exceed – 1V, forcing the production to terminate. When the Pb content reaches 0.6 1.0 wt.%, – passivation arises in the second cycle and the voltage reaches 1 2 V. Under these circumstances it is quite difficult for the production to proceed normally. Intermittent power cuts and anode ramping carried out during electrolysis facilitate light pas

sivation; however, this does not seriously affect the anode. 

#### **CONCLUSION** 

Production practice has shown that the METTOP parallel flow technology is an advanced and highly effective copper electro-refining technique. It was successfully implemented during Phase II at Xiangguang Copper to generate increased current densities up to 420 A/m<sup>2</sup> , drastically enhance the electrolytic capacity, and has enabled copper electro-refining to reach a new level.

Operating the process at high current density requires qualified staff as well as high quality equipment, raw materials, process control, operations, and management. As long as these conditions meet the requirements, a guaranteed stably running process with high current density provides superior high-purity copper cathodes. 

In the future, Xiangguang Copper will further optimize the copper electrolysis technology based on high current density. In particular the focus will be placed maximizing production from low quality anodes, reducing the number of cathode cycles from three to two, realizing additional cell innovations, and further developing the electrolytic process to generate more effective, energy-saving, and environment-friendly copper production.

#### **ABSTRACT** 

At present, most SXEW and electrolitic copper refineries currently use permanent stainless steel cathodes, however, some of them still use starter sheets/traditional cathodes technology. As traditional technology plants, they require copper starter sheets for their final cathode harvesting. Stripping starter sheets manually is boring, tiring, unsafe and physically hard from the occupational health point of view. To reduce risks associated with manually stripping starting sheets, management at Ventanas decided to explore different alternatives; one of these was to automatize the process. MIRS designed and developed a Starter Sheet Robotic Stripping Machine (SSRSM) focusing in improving safety, occupational health and reduce hazards in the process. One SSRSM was commissioned at Ventanas during 2011. An industrial test to cover 50% of starter sheets production was carried out whose objective was to test functionality and performance while stripping in normal operating conditions. Test results were: effective throughput 160 plates per hour and stripping per

formance of 94%. The methodology consisted on full automatized stripping during the tests: to mix robotic and manually stripping wasn’t compatible with the operation. The complete system to reach 100% production incorporates a washing station and two laser scanners, one for sheets and another for base plate quality plus a starting sheet weighing station to sort them into different qualities. Because the SSRSM is robotic, it is compact and configurable so it adapts to existing layout and equipment. It is also capable of using different stripping strategies according to cathode quality.
