Electrorefining is the last step in copper production, be it in a refinery after smelting concentrates from copper sulphides or in an SXEW tankhouse after leaching and solvent extraction from oxides or leachable sulphides. Operating and Cost advantages of each method are beyond the scope of this document, but it is worth mentioning how difficult is for an existing operation to switch from one technology to the other. #### **Manual Stripping** 

Since its startup in 1966, Ventanas Refinery has operated with Starter Sheets technolo

gy, which are manually stripped. The starter sheet production has been both high quality, high performance, therefore it has not been feasible to justify moving to permanent cathodes technology. 

Manual stripping starts when operator strikes one side of the cathode with a knife in sheet’s upper corner, then grabs it and slides the knife along the upper edge. Finally operator grabs the partially stripped sheet weighing about 5kg (11 lbs) with both hands and strips it from the titanium base plate (Figure 1) and places it on a stack. 







Figure 1 – Starter Sheet Manual Stripping 

According to medical studies [3] regarding ergonomics of manual stripping, the function requires inadequate position of some sections of the arms. Furthermore, working stance is with upper body inclined, rotated and shifted sideways beyond recommended ranges. Biomechanical risk factors in forearms, hands and to a lesser degree in shoulders and vertebral column expose the operator to high risk of occupational illnesses. 

Management at Ventanas decided to explore altertnatives to avoid these illnesses and reduce the risks associated to manually stripping starting sheets: One of these was using robotics to automatize the whole operation.

#### **New Cathode Wash System** 

Every copper producer must obtain London Metal Exchange (LME) registration for their cathode copper. In order to receive and maintain this certification the cathode copper must consistently exceed strict specifications in both purity and wire drawing properties. 

The new wash system ensures the cathode has been completely cleaned of surface contamination; this will contribute to an overall improvement in the quality of cathodes produced by the tankhouse. We have designed the cathode washing system with a washing efficiency that approaches 100% removal of contaminants from the surface of the cathode copper. 

The cathodes are placed vertically into retaining “baskets” on a conveyor. The “baskets” are oriented at an angle of 45° from the conveyor axis, and at a sufficient spacing to allow direct spraying of water on both full faces of the cathode. This arrangement guarantees full access for the wash water spray and the best possible washing efficiency. 

The “baskets” are designed so that in the event that the copper prematurely separates from the blank, it will be maintained in position along with the blank and cannot fall into the wash booth. 



Figure 3: Cathode Basket

Cathode washing occurs continuously as the cathodes progress through a three stage wash booth containing 9 cathodes (Figure 4). The entire washing process is carried out with hot (70°C) water at 4 bar pressure.  Each stage utilizes the wash water from the previous stage in a counter-current manner.  This counter current design ensures that each cathode is rinsed with fresh water as it exits the wash booth. The position of the spray nozzles and their full conic jet flow angle ensures that the entire surface is properly washed, and that there are no “masked” areas that can retain impurities on the surface.  The counter current design ensures >99% removal of surface impurities with the minimum consumption of fresh water.

#### **INTRODUCTION** 

Copper tankhouse in Naoshima Smelter & Refinery has successfully been expanded in the capacity to 19,500 m-t/m by raising the current density of commercial cells and various modifications applied on both facilities and operation conducted by 2006.  Stable operation has, however, not lasted so long because the expansion has exceeded the capacity of liberator cells.  As a result, the elution of Cu and Ni into electrolyte caused the accumulation of these elements.  In order to produce the quality cathode and stabilize the operation, electrolyte must be maintained in an adequate range of the composition. 

In recent years, impurities level of copper concentrates has been increasing noticeably and recycling businesses has been enhancing greatly in Japan.  These business trends have raised the impurities level of anode, especially the level of 5b group elements.  The simultaneous dissolution of 5b elements causes the precipitation of arsenate crystals, such as BiAsO4 and SbAsO4, to form floating slime.  Since floating slime may serve as a starting point of the nodule on the surface of cathode, floating slime must be removed from the electrolyte. 

To cope with the subjects above, various modifications have been conducted and improvement has been definite on the cathode quality and operational results as well.  The present paper will describe the modifications those have been necessary to produce quality cathode, including the modification of liberators-cells operation, the introduction of on-site and automatic analysis and the expansion of filtration equipment. 

#### **MODIFICATIONS OF LIBERATOR CELLS OPERATION** 

In tankhouses operation, the accumulation of Cu, Ni, etc. in the electrolyte causes difficulties in the operation and influences adversely on the quality of cathode.  Bleeding several elements from the electrolyte is conducted in liberator processes.  The liberator process of Naoshima refinery is illustrated in Fig

ure 1. The electrolyte taken from the commercial cells passes the 1st liberator cells, the 2nd liberators cells, and then NiSO4production process. The 1st liberator cells extracts superfluous Cu eluted to the electrolyte as copper cathode. The 2nd liberator cells remove Cu, As, Sb, and Bi as slime which is recycled to the smelter. Since Ni cannot be electrodeposited in the liberator cells, it is crystallized out of the electrolyte flown out of the 2nd liberators cells by cooling and recovered as crude NiSO4. Finally, a part of the 2nd liberator cells are used for intensive removal of arsenic by the addition of the electrolyte of commercial cells. However, the capability in the conventional liberator cells process has been insufficient by the increase of cathode production in recent years. Coping with the subject, the function of 3 cells among 6 arsenic removal cells are diverted to Cu electrowinning as same as the 1st liberator cells when Cu concentration of the electrolyte is excessive. Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile 387 #### **SOLUTION** #### **Filtration system** #### Existing system Figure 4 shows existing electrolyte circulation system. Decantation tanks received electrolyte drainage with anode slime from the bottom of electrolytic cells, and settled for 90 minutes to separate anode slime particles from electrolyte. After settling, upper part of the electrolyte flew out to filters to remove suspended solids, which were fine anode slime particles. Filtered electrolyte was sent back to storage tanks and conditioning tanks and the filtration ratio for drainage part was 100%. However, ordinary electrolyte circuit did not have enough filtration capacity. There used to be filters at conditioning tanks, but the capacity was not large enough. Therefore, total filtration ratio of electrolyte was only 9%, the smallest in the PPC refineries. Because of the small filtering capacity, suspended solids concentration in electrolyte increased drastically and caused nodules on cathode surface, when current density increased at 300 A/m2 . Since controlling the suspended solid generation was so difficult, Saganoseki Refinery decided to install new filter systems to increase the filtration ratio to 100%. Figure 4 - Ex

#### <u>New system</u> 

Figure 5 shows new electrolyte circulation and filtration system in Saganoseki tank houses. Electrolyte filters were replaced with larger filtering capacity and located in series, so that the entire electrolyte from conditioning tank went through the filters on the way to the head tank. Current circulation and filtration capacity is 5.7 times of total electrolyte amount. Two new filters installed and started their operation in July 2009, and accordingly the suspended solid level in electrolyte reduced to 0.1 mg/L,. Because filters require the cleaning by NaOH in every several months, and then one filter has to stop for 36 hours, resulting in lower filtering ratio due to the cleaning. To avoid the situation, another filter was placed in parallel with the existing two filters in May 2011. Current system can operate at least two filters even in the cleaning period. 



Figure 5 - New electrolyte circulate system 

#### **Additive agent supply system** 

Saganoseki tank houses are using glue and thiourea as additive agents. The agents were dissolved together in two solution tanks and the solution was prepared in the previous day, so that the dissolved agents fed continuously to electrolyte at the conditioning tank. By this method, dissolved additive agents keep in solution tank for a long time, and the agents were decomposed before feeding to electrolyte. Furthermore, 

Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile 

389 

new question was raised after installing filters regarding the addition point. When electrolyte went through filters, additive agent is easily absorbed into filters and resulted in lower the agents’ concentration in electrolyte. Since the agents were fed from the top of the conditioning tank, it was likely to cause segregation in agents’ concentration. Therefore, there was a tendency to feed the agents superfluously, and end up with an adverse factor of the electric power consumption rate by a power surge. 

#### <u>Continuous dissolving and supply system</u> 

The addition point and the dissolution method of the additive agent have been changed in September 2009, to make the additive agents perform more efficiently in electrolytic cells. Figure 6 shows an improved electrolyte circulation flow including the addition point of the additive agent. The additive agents’ addition point has been changed to a head tank, to minimize the loss in a filter. And the continuous dissolution system has also been introduced to reduce the age deterioration effect in May 2011. When an additive agent dissolves, decomposition will immediately start and be difficult to maintain the additive agents’ effect in electrolyte. 



Figure 6 - New additive agent addition point at electrolyte circulation system 

To solve the above mentioned problems, new continuous dissolution system has been developed. This system has two hoppers, because Saganoseki

uses glue and 

Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile 

390 

thiourea for additive agent. The hopper size is designed so that those additive agents are supplied once in one or two days. Screw conveyers are placed at the bottom each hoppers. The screw conveyer has a function to weigh and feed the agents continuously. Water which is also measured is supplied continuously to the tank so that the additive agent concentration in the solution is maintained at the same level. The solution tank has a heating system and stirrer, to keep proper dissolving temperature and consistent concentration. The supply speed of additive agent is also controlled by pump rotation speed. Supply speed data are checked by flow meter and the data are fed buck to the pump rotation speed. Originally the system was designed at Tamano Refinery and modified to dissolve thiourea together in the system at Saganoseki.[1] 



Figure 7 - Continuous dissolving and supply system 

The dissolved additive agent is supplied to the head tank with the pump, and the pump rotation speed is controlled by the flow meter, installed at the pump discharge side. The additive agent solution is continuously supplied to the electrolyte at the set value. 

#### **OPERATIONAL RESULTS** 

New electrolyte filtering system started its operation in July 2009, and then suspended solid level in electrolyte reduced substantially, as shown in Figure 3. The short-circuit ratio has also been reduced and become stable after September 2009, when the new additive agent feeding system installed. Consequently, current efficiency increased to 98% and maintained at the level. However recently, there has been a tendency to increase the short-circuit ratio, and decrease the current efficiency to 97%. It is estimated that the increase of impurities in anodes can be a factor of declined current

efficiency, and we are taking several measures to accommodate the condition. It is also noted that the glue consumption has been reduced by about 30% after installing the new additive agent supply system. 

#### **CONCLUSION** 

After the introduction of the Waxless ISA permanent cathode system in 2006, Saganoseki experienced a sudden increase of short circuit ratio and a serious decline in current efficiency on the way to increase the current density. It was presumed that high suspended solid contamination and inadequate additive agents concentration caused the situation. The countermeasure were carried out subsequently, and resulted in achieving 97% current efficiency at current density 311 A/m<sup>2</sup> . 

Owing to the improvements, Saganoseki Refinery currently continues the stable and efficient operation as well as the adequate cathode quality. Saganoseki Refinery will be committed to improving its productivity and product quality.

#### **INTRODUCTION** 

Since December 2007, Onahama Smelter and refinery has operated the O-SR process in which the S-furnace of the Mitsubishi process is followed by two hearths of reverberatory furnaces in order to increase the capacity of copper concentrates.  The S-furnace has been introduced newly to treat copper concentrates which were treated in existing reverberatory furnaces and P.-S. converters in the original system, and to enhance smelting capacity.  The reverberatory furnaces have, then, been used to settle melts recieved from the S-furnace while enhancing the treatment of combustible wastes on the hearths.  Such enhancements at the smelter requested the tank-houses to increase the productivity more than 25%. 

The productivity of No.1 and No.2 tankhouses has been enhanced by the reinforcement of rectifiers with modifications of equipment.  The productivity of No.3 tankhouse has been enhanced by increasing the number of daily operation cells.  Since such enhancement has increased the load of impurities and cupric ions in the electrolyte, the operation of the secondary liberators have been resumed to cope with this issue.  Futhermore, the elements like copper, nickel, chloride have been controlled by monitoring assays with automatic flowinjection analyzer.  The present paper will describe these modifications and demonstrate that the modifications are attributable to quite stable operation and excellent cathode quality.

Ltd., Refinery Manager, 3-3382 Saganoseki, Oita-shi, Oita, 879-2201, Japan_ #### **ABSTRACT** Electrolytic copper contains, on average, 10 ppm silver as an impurity. This means copper smelters are losing a cash-cow product. Most of the silver included in blister copper anodes passes into the anode slime when electrolyzed, remaining in the elemental state. However, once a part of the elemental silver oxidatively-dissolves from the anode or from anode slime for some reason, because silver is more nob

le than copper then silver can co-deposit with the electrolytic copper cathode. In the present work, the dissolution behavior of silver from anode slime was examined using granular silver as a model of the slime.  We have shown that the silver dissolution is caused by dissolved oxygen in the electrolyte, and that thiourea and/or chloride ions as typical additives play a role in suppressing the silver dissolution by approximately one half. Moreover, it was found that the dissolution of silver was almost completely suppressed by galvanic contacting of the granular silver with less noble metals (Pb or Cu) immersed in the same electrolyte. This indicates that the use of a Pb or Cu lining at the bottom of the electrolytic cell can depress silver dissolution from the anode slime that settles to the bottom, reducing the silver loss to electrolytic copper.

#### **INTRODUCTION** 

Electrorefining is the final step of the copper refining process, in which the purity of copper is raised by successive anodic dissolution of blister copper (anode) into Cu<sup>2+</sup> ion (Cu ⟶ Cu<sup>2+</sup> + 2e) and reductive deposition of the resulting Cu<sup>2+</sup> ions at the cathode as electrolytic Cu (Cu<sup>2+</sup> + 2e ⟶ Cu). In this process, precious metals like gold and silver contained as impurities in the blister copper are recovered by their precipitation as anode slime. Raising the recovery rates of such precious metals increases the profitability of the whole process. Any precious metals lost into the electrolytic copper ( _i.e._ cathode) instead of passing into the anode slime, means to a loss of the precious metals as a final product. Today, the silver included in electrolytic copper, that is, the loss of silver is about 10 ppm [1] in most copper refineries in the world. If we could reduce this even to 5 ppm, it would lead to 1-ton more silver per year, in the case of a copper refinery producing 200,000 tons of electrolytic copper annually. Considering that the price of silver was 94.5 yen per gram in April 2013, this this would mean about 100 million yen (= 1 million dollars) profit increase for the plant. Although mechanical "inclusion" of suspended anode slime into the cathode can be a cause of the recovery loss, we considered that the electrochemical reduction of silver (Ag(I) + e ⟶ Ag) is the main reason for this recovery loss. The slime containing silver is heavy enough to precipitate easily to the bottom of electrolytic cells, so it is unlikely that the mechanical inclusion of anode slime causes the recovery loss of silver. If the metallic Ag in blister copper is dissolved as Ag(I) ion into the electrolyte instead of passing into the anode slime, Ag(I) ion will be reductively deposited at the cathode (electrolytic copper) because Ag is more noble than Cu. 

We thus assumed that a part of Ag really dissolves from the anode or anode slime and that the resulting Ag(I) ions are taken into electrol

ytic copper. To clarify the silver dissolution, we conducted an experiment based on the thermodynamic causes of it. In addition, we considered how to prevent it. First, we have investigated the effect of thiourea, an electrolyte additive, which can reduce the activity of Ag<sup>+</sup> aquo ions by complex formation with the thiourea and stimulate anodic dissolution. Second, we examined the oxidative dissolution of Ag accompanied by the reduction of dissolved oxygen in the electrolyte. Finally, in order to find a method to suppress the silver dissolution, we tried a galvanic contact of the silver with less noble metals such as Pb and Cu. The suppression effects in the presence of each additive (chloride ion, thiourea, glue) were also discussed. 

#### **EXPERIMENTAL** 

In the current copper electrorefining, the anodic potential is about +0.37 to +0.40 V vs. SHE (SHE = standard hydrogen electrode). According to the potential-pH diagram of Ag-H2O system (Fig. 1a), it seems unlikely that the metal Ag contained in crude copper dissolves by the anodic reaction at this potential. The activity of Ag<sup>+</sup> ion in equilibrium with elemental Ag calculated by the Nernst equation for (Ag<sup>+</sup> + e = Ag) at +0.385 V vs. SHE is 6.0 Ч 10<sup>-7</sup> , indicating that the amount of silver dissolved as Ag<sup>+</sup> ion, if any, is negligible. So, we concluded that the chemical components in electrolyte 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

421 

promote the dissolution of metal Ag. 



Figure 1– Potential - pH diagram of (a) Cu-H2O system and (b) Ag-H2O system at 298 K. 

The aqueous electrolytes used in copper electrorefining are typically copper sulfate, sulfuric acid, and additives such as chloride ion, a thiourea (TU; thiourea), and glue, in order to make the cathode surface smooth and uniform. Ag<sup>+</sup> ions form complexes with thiourea, through which the activity of Ag<sup>+</sup> ions is lowered and the potential of the reaction Ag<sup>+</sup> + e = Ag shifts in the negative direction. Thermodynamically, such a negative shift of the redox potential can enhance the anodic dissolution. In response to this, we plotted the equilibrium distribution of the silver-thiourea complexes and checked the change of Ag<sup>+</sup> ion activity by the complex formation. We also investigated the effect of thiourea on the anodic polarization behavior for Ag electrode using Cu sheet as a counter electrode. 

Since copper electrorefining is performed in an air atmosphere, the electrolyte contains dissolved oxygen. The concentration of the saturated solution is about 5 ppm when the bath temperature is 65 ℃. The potential-pH diagram of Ag-H2O system shows thermodynamically that oxidative-dissolution of Ag can spontaneously occur in combination with the reduction of dissolved oxygen (O2 + 4H<sup>+</sup> + 4e<sup>-</sup> ⟶ 2H2O). To verify the extent of the Ag dissolution in the presence of dissolved oxygen, we used silver grains (particle diameter

425-850 μm) as model of anode slime and immersed them in electrolyte aerated by the air or deaerated by nitrogen for a given length of time. After immession,the concentration of Ag<sup>+</sup> was measured by ICP atomic emission spectroscopy (ICP-AES) using a calibration curve method. 

Our experience shows that the more lead is contained in blister copper, the less silver is included in electrolytic copper. Taking a hint from this phenomenon, we supposed that, when metals less noble than Ag ( _i.e._ Pb and Cu) are in galvanic-contact with silver in the blister copper or anode slime, those metals will suppress the oxidative-dissolution of Ag by negative-shifting the rest potential of Ag. To verify the effect of such galvanic-contact, the above-mentioned dissolution tests for granular silver 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

422 

in the aerated electrolyte were also conducted for grains placed on a Pb or Cu sheet. After the immersion, the amounts of Ag dissolved were determined using the same method as described above. 

Conventional additives for copper electrorefining, such as chloride ion, thiourea, and glue, are used to make the surface of the electrolytic copper smooth and uniform. In addition, Ag<sup>+</sup> ions form poorly-soluble Ag2S and AgCl with S<sup>2-</sup> and Cl<sup>-</sup> ions, where the solubility products are 6.2 Ч 10<sup>-52</sup> and 1.8 Ч 10<sup>-10</sup> , respectively [2]. In this case, the S<sup>2-</sup> ions are provided by the decomposition of thiourea. So, the addition of thiourea and/or chloride ions could promote the formation of Ag2S and AgCl layers on the surface of silver grains, suppressing the oxidizative dissolution of Ag. We thus compared the dissolution behavior of granular silver with or without additives. After each immersion experiment, the surface of the granular silver was analyzed by EDX. In order to clarify the effects of the three additives, the immersion experiment was carried out with various combination of additives. 

For each experiment, we used an electrolyte containing sulfuric acid and copper sulfate solution (0.76 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> H2SO4 - 1.94 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> CuSO4, 65 ℃) without stirring.

#### **Effect of dissolved oxygen** 

As mentioned above, about 5 ppm oxygen dissolves in the electrolyte at bath temperature 65 ºC. In order to investigate the influence of dissolved oxygen on silver dissolution, 10 g of granular silver imitating anode slime was immersed in 300mL of electrolyte without additives at 65 ºC for 6, 24 or 48 hours. The concentration of Ag<sup>+</sup> ions determined by ICP-AES as a function of immersion time is shown in Fig. 4. With aeration by air (30mL min<sup>-1</sup> ), the amount of Ag particles dissolved increased with increasing immersion time. 



Figure 4– Concentration of Ag (I) in the solution as a function of immersing time at 338 K 

In contrast, the same experiments with N2 bubbling to remove oxygen from the electrolyte showed a remarkable fall in the amount of dissolution without oxygen. 

If the silver contained in blister copper or anode slime is in the metallic state, such oxidative-dissolution of Ag by dissolved oxygen becomes essential. If the silver is in a monovalent compound, such as Ag2O, the reaction of silver dissolution is a mere acid-base reaction. As for the blister copper, we checked the chemical state of Ag using X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (WPS). We cut small pieces of blister copper ac

tually molded for copper electrorefining at Saganoseki smelter. Samples were taken from both the mold-side and the side exposed to the air. Figure 5 shows the XPS Ag 3d spectrum for the sample from the mold side. The peak at 368.2 eV corresponds to Ag<sup>0</sup> state rather than Ag(I), suggesting that the silver in blister copper is in a metallic state. Although we have not analyzed the chemical state of silver in anode slime, it is reasonable to guess that the majority of silver in the slime is metallic, as already reported [4]. A brief measurement of the electrical conductivity of the slime described later also implied that the slime is metallic rather than insulating.

All the above indicate that the metallic Ag contained in anode or anode slime disolves oxidatively through a redox reaction with the dissolved oxygen. Once dissolved, the resulting Ag<sup>+</sup> ions are reduced at the cathode, raising the content of Ag as an impurity in the electrolytic copper.

#### **Suppression of the Silver Dissolution by Contact with Pb or Cu** 

In order to verify our assumption that the oxidative-dissolution of Ag can be suppressed by galvanic contacting of Ag with Pb or Cu, we checked the rest potential of the metal Ag contacting with Pb in the electrolyte. We immersed Ag sheet and Pb sheets into the electrolyte without additives and the sheets were short-circuited by a lead wire. We performed a separate measurement for the Ag sheet contacting with Cu sheet. Figure 6 summarizes the time variations of the rest potential of Ag contact with Pb (left) and Cu (right) sheets. A set of rest potential data for single Ag, Pb, or Cu sheet immersed into the same electrolyte is shown for comparison. The rest potential of Ag sheet was negatively shifted by 20 or 40 mV, respectively, by contacting with Pb or Cu sheet, suggesting that the oxidative-dissolution of Ag can be suppressed by contact with Pb and Cu. 

To evaluate the effect that contact with Pb or Cu has on the suppression of silver dissolution, silver grains were put on a Pb or Cu sheet in the aerated electrolyte for two days, and the concentration of Ag<sup>+</sup> ion was measured using ICP-AES. When granular silver is immersed in the electrolyte without contacting Pb or Cu sheet, as noted earlier, the concentration of Ag<sup>+</sup> was about 400 ppm. In contrast, when silver particles were in contact with Pb or Cu sheet, the resulting Ag<sup>+</sup> concentration was below 1 ppm, demonstrating clearly that the silver dissolution is highly suppressed by contact with a different metal such as Pb or Cu. The reason is the potential shift of Ag in the negative direction as mentioned above.

#### **Suppression of Silver Dissolu

tion by Additives** 

The electrolyte used for the experiments described in the previous section contained no additives. However, additives such as chloride ion, thiourea, and glue, are present in the electrolyte in real processes, and may also act to suppress the silver dissolution. We thus conducted the same granular silver immersion experiment for two days under air aeration using electrolytes with these three additives. Without these additives the final Ag<sup>+</sup> concentration amounted to 400 ppm as mentioned before, but with these additives, it decreased to 170 ppm. After the immersion experiment, although the appearance of the particles immersed in the electrolyte without additives was not different from that before the experiment, a silver-gray color, the particle surface in the electrolyte with additives became black. In this case the composition of the surface analyzed by EDX was as follows: 60% silver, 35% chlorine, and 3% sulfur. It is considered that, at the surface of silver grains immersed in the electrolyte with additives, some of the oxidized Ag ( _i.e._ Ag<sup>+</sup> ion) reacted with chloride ions or the sulfur generated by decomposition of thiourea; the surface coloring was due to silver sulfide. In other words, silver dissolution was suppressed by the additives through a protective coating of silver chloride or silver sulfide formed on the surface. However, since the amount of silver dissolution was 170 ppm even with these additives, suppression by these additives is not as complete as that achieved by contact with different metals such as Pb or Cu. 

In order to consider the contribution of each additive to the suppression of silver dissolution, the same experiment was conducted with various combinations of the additives. While the granular silver surface immersed in the electrolyte containing only chloride ion or thiourea also turned black, the surface did not change when only glue was added. Moreover, the amount of Ag dissolved in the electrolyte containing both chloride ion and thiourea (without glue) was almost the same as that when all three additives were present (Table 2). From these results, we understand that the suppression of silver dissolution by chloride ion and thiourea is much greater than that by glue.

Finally, the effect of additives was compared with that of contacting with different metals. We conducted the immersion experiment for two days, putting granular silver on Pb or Cu sheet in the solution with additives, and, in this case, the amount of silver dissolved was less than 1 ppm. So, from this, it became clear that the oxidizative dissolution of silver is completely suppressed by contacting with Pb or Cu, regardless of the presence of the additives. 

#### **Measurement of Electric Conductivity of Anode Slime** 

As described above, we conducted

granular silver immersion experiments under various conditions. As a result, we succeeded in suppressing  silver dissolution by galvanic contacting of the granular silver with different metals, such as Pb and Cu, that are less noble than Ag. When applying this method in real operations, it would be effective to contact anode slime with Pb or Cu electrochemically. In real processes, there are two kinds of anode slime; one sticks to the blister copper surface and the other settles in the bottom of the electrolytic cells. The galvanic suppression of silver dissolution by contacting with Pb or Cu could be applied to the slime that settles on the bottom by placing a Cu or Pb plate in the bottom of the cell. As for the slime sticking to the blister copper surface, the suppression will be effective only in the case of a power outage when the blister copper is at rest potential. In each case, however, if the anode slime has no electrical conductivity, we cannot say that Ag is in contact with Pb or Cu electrochemically, and thus we cannot expect to see the suppression of silver dissolution. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

428 

We therefore investigated the electrical conductivity of anode slime. Anode slime was collected from the copper electrorefinery at Pan Pacific Copper (in Saganoseki) and pressed into a tablet (diameter 12 mm and thickness 3 mm) by a pressing machine. Two sheets of copper foil (thickness 0.05 mm) were press-fitted to both sides of the tablet, and the electric conductivity was measured. The conductivity was 1.3 Ч 10<sup>-2</sup> Ω<sup>-1</sup> m<sup>-1</sup> , meaning that anode slime has the same conductivity as a semiconductor. Although the conductivity is not of metallic level, it is high enough to establish an electrochemical contact between anode slime and a Cu or Pb sheet in real operations, as long as there is continuity, to suppress the silver disolution. 

#### **CONCLUSION** 

In this research, for the purpose of reducing the silver loss to electrolytic copper, and considering the suppression methods of silver dissolution, we investigated the mechanism of silver dissolution from the anode and anode slime during the copper electrorefining process. As causes of silver dissolution, the effect of complexation of Ag<sup>+</sup> ions with thiourea included as an additive in the electrolyte is small, while the effect of reduction of the dissolved oxygen contained in the bath is large. We found that the oxidative-dissolution of silver can be suppressed almost completely by galvanic contact of the silver with metals less noble than Ag, such as Pb or Cu. This is because when silver is in contact with lead or copper, the rest potential of silver is lowered by about 20 or 40 mV, respectively. 

The electrolytes used in real processes contain additives such as chloride ion, thiourea, and glue, for the purpose of making the electrolytic copper surface smooth and uniform. The use of these additives, especially chloride io

n and thiourea, also suppresses the silver dissolution by approximately half, through the formation of a silver chloride or sulfide layer on the surface of the silver. However, silver dissolution is suppressed nearly completely by contacting with Pb or Cu regardless of the presence of additives. 

In the real processes, there are two kinds of anode slime: one sticks to the blister copper surface and the other settles in the bottom of the electrolytic cell. Galvanic suppression of silver dissolution by contacting with Pb or Cu can be applied to the slime in the bottom by placing a Cu or Pb plate on the bottom of the cell. As for the slime sticking to the blister copper surface, suppression will be effective only in the case of a power outage when the blister copper is at rest potential. Thus, by suppressing the silver dissolution, we can reduce the silver loss to electrolytic copper.

#### **ABSTRACT** 

The AISI 316L type stainless steel is considered corrosion resistant in copper electrorefining electrolyte, both as permanent cathode blank material and in process equipment and piping. Damaged cathode blanks show increased surface roughness, corrosion pits and deeper grain boundaries. The test hypothesis was that too high chloride concentration and temperature can cause localized corrosion. A synthetic electrolyte with 180 g/l H2SO4, 45 g/l Cu, 15 g/l Ni and 10 g/l As was used. Test variables were temperature 50-70<sup>o</sup> C and chloride concentration from 40 ppm to 1000 ppm. Test method was cyclic polarization curve based on ASTM standard G61-86. No pitting or crevice corrosion was seen in the test series but highest chloride concentration resulted in wider active peak and higher passive current densities. In transpassive corrosion tests localized corrosion on grain boundaries and detachment of grains was seen. Two main possibilities for blank corrosion have been identified. High chloride concentration can cause active dissolution. T

he concentration of chlorides has to be at least 10 times higher than the normal chloride level. Polarization to transpassive potentials causes corrosion on grain boundaries and detachment of grains. The only possibility for transpassive dissolution is stray currents.

#### **INTRODUCTION** 

The common cathode blank material is stainless steel containing approximately 17% Cr, 12% Ni and 2% Mo, and this type has standard numbers EN 1.4404 and AISI 316L. The surface finish for stainless steel blanks has shallow grooves on grain boundaries that provide the necessary adhesion. The stainless steel AISI 316L is not very highly alloyed so it may corrode during idle periods in the electrorefining cell. The most likely forms of corrosion are pitting and crevice corrosion and intergranular corrosion. Less likely forms are general corrosion and stress corrosion cracking or corrosion fatigue. 

The corrosivity of the electrolyte depends on sulfuric acid concentration, chloride concentration and temperature. Deposits on the surface and stray currents can affect the corrosion of blanks. Based on 2007 world tankhouse data the electrolyte in refineries using permanent cathodes contains 42-49 g/l Cu, 160-190 g/l free H2SO4 and 36-56 ppm Cl<sup>-</sup> and temperature range is 62-68 °C [1]. The corrosion rate of AISI 316 type in 10% sulfuric acid (184 g/l) is approximately 0.1 mm/year at 60 °C [2,3] but in aerated sulfuric acid AISI 316 should be passive in concentrations and temperatures of copper electrorefining [4]. Addition of 25 mg/l Cu<sup>2+</sup> is enough to decrease the corrosion rate in copper refining electrolyte [3]. In electrolyte with 200-235 g/l sulfuric acid, T = 65 °C, general corrosion rate of AISI 304 and AISI 316 was less than 0.25 μm/year [5]. Copper enhances passivation, lowers dissolution rates in acid chloride-containing solutions, and decreases pit propagation [6-8]. 

AISI 316L has generally been found to be satisfactory for the tanks, piping and other equipment in a copper refinery. Cupric sulfate inhibits corrosion. However, AISI type 316L is not suitable for the heating coils where steam causes high temperatures [4]. Eastwood and Whebell refer to an Avesta report in [9] and state that in 30 days immersion in electrorefining electrolyte no uniform corrosion was detected on AISI 304, AISI 316 or duplex steel LDX 2101. No corrosion rate exceeded 0.01 mm/year. No localized attacks, such as pitting or crevice corrosion were observed. The results of Rojo and Gonzalez suggest that in PCR electrorefining AISI 304 does not corrode during anodic period [10]. 

High temperature and high chloride concentration cause corrosion problems for stainless steel. A standard test method for sensitization is immersion of stainless steel samples in boiling sulfuric acid and copper sulfate solution. The test solution in the method A of EN ISO 3651-2 (Monypenny Strauss test) contains 184 g/l sulfuric

acid and 25 g/l Cu. The test method suggests that electrolyte can have possibility to corrode grain boundaries. For AISI 316 type steel 200 ppm chloride ions counters the positive effect of oxidizing cupric ions [3]. Abe and Shimizu have found chloride enrichment to cause corrosion when organic residue coated the blank’s surface. This residue contained 2000 ppm chlorine and was considered to be enough to corrode the stainless steel blanks. They suggested removing organic residue on the surface so that chloride is not allowed to concentrate [11]. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013_

The aim of this work was to estimate the corrosivity of copper electrorefining electrolyte and determine the forms of corrosion that happen on the blank surface. The corrosivity was estimated by cyclic anodic polarization curves and accelerated potentiostatic and galvanostatic tests. The results indicated that corrosion of the blank material requires exceptional circumstances. Corrosion can happen when local chloride level increases or stray currents that dissolve the steel surface on transpassive potential range. 

#### **EXPERIMENTAL** 

The tendencies of AISI 316L type stainless steel for general, pitting and crevice corrosion were evaluated under copper electrorefining operating conditions. The purpose was to find out if corrosion happens, what are the most common forms of corrosion and how the solution conditions will affect corrosion. Cyclic polarization curves were done for pitting and crevice corrosion using Avesta cell. The transpassive dissolution and waterline corrosion were studied using normal three electrode cell and sheet samples. 

The test material was stainless steel type 1.4404. The main difference between 1.4404 and AISI 316L is slightly higher maximum Mo content. The samples were used in as-received condition with 2B surface finish. The samples were checked for scratches and cleaned with acetone, distilled water and ethanol, and dried with warm air. The base electrolyte contained 180 g/l H2SO4, 45 g/l Cu<sup>2+</sup> , 15 g/l Ni<sup>2+</sup> and 10 g/l As. The electrolyte was made of Pro Analysis grade chemicals and distilled water. Cu<sup>2+</sup> and Ni<sup>2+</sup> -ions were added as CuSO4 and NiSO4, and arsenic as As2O5. For adjusting chloride concentration 1% HCl solution was used. The solutions with gelatine and thiourea were made daily in order to avoid decomposition of additives. The concentration of the both additives was 2 mg/l. In pitting corrosion tests the solution was purged with nitrogen for 1 hour before the test. In transpassive dissolution and waterline corrosion tests no gas purging was used. 

Cyclic polarization tests were run using Avesta cell and ACM Instruments AutoTafel potentiostat. A copper sheet was used as counter electrode and Cu/CuSO4 as reference electrode. In waterline corrosion tests and accelerated potentiostatic and galvanostatic tests the samples were put in a small thermostatted glass ves

sel. The test electrodes were 37 x 50 mm pieces that were partly immersed in the solution. The waterline was marked and the surface area was 11.1 cm<sup>2</sup> . Figure 1a shows the Avesta cell and Figure 1b sample mounting in the static tests. The reference electrode was put between the samples. All potential values were measured versus a laboratory made copper-copper sulfate reference electrode. 

The pitting and crevice corrosion test method was based on ASTM standard G 61-86. It is a test method for conducting cyclic polarization measurements for localized corrosion susceptibility of iron-, nickel- and cobalt based alloys in a chloride environment. Initiation of localized corrosion is given by the potential at which the anodic current increases rapidly.

The polarization curve was measured from -20 mV vs. open corrosion potential to anodic direction using scan rate 10 mV/min. The scan was continued to 1000 mV and then potential scan direction was reversed and continued to the original starting potential. Potentiostatic tests were done to detect corrosion in prolonged experiments. The test conditions were set so that the sample was polarized to potentials on the start of transpassive dissolution and slightly above the critical potential.

Figure 9 – Damages developed on the blank when polarized to 870 mV at 70 °C with 100 ppm chlorides after 5, 24 and 30 hours _Proceedings of Copper 2013_ _Santiago, Chile_ 440 #### **DISCUSSION** Based on literature the AISI 316L type stainless steel is consi

dered corrosion resistant in copper electrorefining electrolyte, both as permanent cathode blank material and in process equipment and piping. Increased surface roughness, corrosion pits and deeper grain boundaries were found in used blanks. The test hypothesis was that too high chloride concentration and temperature can cause localized corrosion. 

No indication of pitting was found with cyclic polarization curves and optical microscopy. The chloride level and temperature had slight effects on pitting potential and passive current density, but a typical copper electrorefining electrolyte at T = 50-70 °C and chloride concentration 40-100 mg/l did not cause pitting corrosion. Pitting was not detected either when using 1000 mg/l chlorides. The pitting potentials and passive current densities did not differ from those measured in solutions with 100 mg/l. A clear change in the shape of the polarization curve was seen at 1000 mg/l chlorides, the size of the active peak was much larger. The organic additives used in the electrolyte have no significant effect on corrosion when the chloride concentration is on the normal level, _i.e._ 100 mg/l or less. When the solution contains high concentration of chlorides the additives seem to have protective effect as the active peak becomes smaller. 

The cyclic polarization curves had very much different shape in crevice corrosion tests. The high current densities on the passive range suggested corrosion, but no indication of crevice corrosion was found after the tests. The critical potentials were the same in pitting and crevice corrosion tests. Crevice corrosion cannot be excluded but it requires increase by orders of magnitude in chloride concentration on the steel blank surface. This could happen on dirty blanks covered with wax. 

No indication of waterline corrosion was found when the sample was partially immersed in the electrolyte as long as the sample was not polarized. The effect of stray currents was studied by polarizing the sample using potentiostatic methods. In these tests the sample potential was 800-870 mV. Small polarization to active or passive range did not cause visible corrosion. Polarization to potentials slightly above the critical potential caused clear corrosion on grain boundaries and in longer tests detachment of grains. In optical microscope lost grains appear as small pits with sharp edges. 

The results show that normal electrorefining electrolyte does not cause corrosion under immersion. The only clear corrosion damages were seen on samples polarized to the transpassive range. So far there is no clear explanation to damages seen on used cathode blank surfaces. Of the corrosion forms found in the literature, general corrosion, crevice corrosion and transpassive dissolution remain as the most probable, but all these corrosion forms require a specific set of conditions to happen. General corrosion of stainless steel is 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013_ 

_Santiago, Chile_ 

441 

possibl

e in the case that the passive film is lost. This can happen at very high chloride concentration when passive film is damaged and surface potential is on the active range. Crevice corrosion can happen in localized areas where solution can concentrate. The main difference to general corrosion is that the aggressive solution develops in localized shielded areas, _i.e._ under wax, deposits etc. Transpassive dissolution requires external polarization to potentials over 850 mV vs. Cu/CuSO4. Polarization to this potential range requires anodic current density higher than 0.01 mA/cm<sup>2</sup> or 0.1 A/m<sup>2</sup> . It is not known if there are leakage currents in the tankhouses that can polarize a cathode to high anodic potentials. 

#### **CONCLUSIONS** 

No pitting or crevice corrosion was seen in the cyclic polarization curves at temperatures 50-70 °C and chloride concentration up to 1000 mg/l. High chloride concentration resulted in wider active peak and higher passive current densities. Transpassive dissolution tests with external polarization produced localized corrosion on grain boundaries and detachment of grains. 

Two main possibilities for blank corrosion have been identified. High chloride concentration can cause active dissolution. The concentration of chlorides has to be at least 10 times higher than the normal chloride level. Polarization to transpassive potential range, above 850 mV vs. Cu/CuSO4 causes corrosion on grain boundaries, deeper grooves and detachment of grains. The only possibility for transpassive dissolution is stray currents. 

The corrosion damages seen in the tests were not same as seen in damaged blanks. Some investigated blanks had deeper grain boundaries than in the original state but it is not known if this has been caused by transpassive dissolution. The detachment of grains produces sharp edged damages on the surface. The origin of round pits seen in damaged cathode blanks was not clarified.

#### **ABSTRACT** 

A new system for reducing the anode scrap in a conventional electro-refining plant was investigated at laboratory scale. #### **CONCLUSIONS** 

The use of electrolytic copper for making the anodes to avoid variation in the electrolyte quality allows getting results based on the electrical and mechanical performance of the refining system. 

A relevant technological change for copper electro-refining has been evaluated at laboratory scale, showing promising results. The use of anode based on the Earless® technology has shown a significant reduction in the scrap generation and in the energy consumption. The use of experimental work at scale 1:10 for all type of anodes allowed to make reliable comparisons between their performances. 

When the performance of anodes based on the Earless® technology is compared with the performance of traditional anodes type Fure, there is a decrease in the generated scrap from around 22% to around 10% in both types of Earles®s. Both efficiencies, anode dissolution and copper deposition, were improved in all the experiments with Earless® anodes. The SECR showed a decrease of the energy consumption of around 18% for Earless® A and of 8% for Earless® B, however, the second one presents a strongest supporting point of the anode to the stainless steel case, which avoids risk for anode falling in the cell. 

The quality of the cathodes generated during the Earless anode processing was identical at those generated from processing anodes type Fure, i.e., there is not effect of the Earless technology in the quality of the cathodes produced.

#### **ABSTRACT** 

An ion exchange pilot plant, located at the University of Santiago of Chile, was tested for antimony control in the electrolyte of Chuquicamata Refinery. In the pilot plant were used three different resins: MX-2, UR-3300S and Duolite C-467. The results showed that th

e best behavior for antimony extraction follow the sequence UR3300S >Duolite C 467 > MX 2. A model with the experimental results was used as comparative tools to increase the knowledge of this process. 

Keywords: Antimony, IX, Modeling, Copper, Electrorefining. 

#### **INTRODUCTION** 

In the last times, Chuquicamata Division has experienced a significant and sustained increase in the content of impurities, mainly As, Sb and Bi, in the concentrates produced from the exploitation and processing of the Chuquicamata mine as well as products recirculation, which has affected the chemical quality of the anodes produced in concentrates Smelter, additionally with the entry into operation of the new Division Ministro Hales, whose product, the calcine copper concentrate with high content of antimony will be processed entirely in the facilities of the Smelter and Refinery Chuquicamata Division, increasing Sb content in anodes and Refinery electrolytes. 

This problem of Sb and Bi in concentrates and calcines, impact the cathode quality and has been addressed in many studies and engineering: Conceptual Engineering "Complex Concentrate Treatment and Increase DCN Smelter and Refinery Capacity" (API N04FP47) and in Basic Engineering "Impurities Treatment Feasibility in anodes and cathodes DCN" where technological options have been proposed to process concentrates in Codelco Chuquicamata, recommending a global solution to solve the problem of chemical quality of the electro-refined cathodes. 

Thus for electrolytic refinery was determined installing an ion exchange plant connected to electro refining circuits, enabling control of Sb in the electrolyte in a concentration not exceeding 0.3 g/L.  In this regard, the Refinery of Chuquicamata

Divisiуn has performed in the laboratory of  Electrometallurgy and Corrosiуn of the Metallurgical Enginnering Departament of the University of Santiago of Chile laboratory pilot tests with different resins to preparing a report with the behavior of the resins when was in contact with real electrolyte of Chuquicamata. However, because it is a new technology is needed gather a lot of information to help you get a better appreciation of this technology in both aspect, the loading and elution. 

In the processes for obtaining de copper by pyrometallurgy a fundamental stage is the electrorefining of impure copper anodes (98-99.8% de Cu). In this stage by applying a potential difference the copper present in the anode is dissolved electrochemically in the electrolytic solution, and is deposited on a stainless steel or pure copper cathode. At the same time, some of the impurities contained in the anode (As, Sb, Bi, S, Fe, Zn, Ni, Co) are dissolved in the electrolytic solution and the rest of those impurities (Ag, Se, Te, Pb) do not go into the solution and precipitate as “anode slime”. In turn, as a result of matter transfer mechanisms, physical contamination of the pure copper

cathodes occurs (occlusion of solids), affecting the electric properties of the copper and the quality of the pure copper cathodes<sup>(1)</sup> . 

Control of the impurities present in the electrolyte is done mainly by purging the electrolytic solution. However, the impurities that have the greatest incidence on cathode contamination and on operational problems are As and Sb compounds. There is a known ratio between arsenic and antimony (As/Sb ≥2) that prevents the formation of floating slime that can cause physical contamination of the pure copper cathode, leading to an As and Sb solubility curve from which it can be concluded that as the arsenic in solution increases, the solubility of antimony decreases. However, increased Sb in copper sulfide ores and its concentration in the electrolytic solution in spite of keeping the (As/Sb ≥2) causes this Sb “equilibrium” difference to form a compound (Sb2O3) that precipitates throughout the system, clogging ducts and physically contaminating the cathodes. 

This situation has made refineries take short-term measures to remove the excess antimony. Considering the above and reviewing the literature, there is a large variety of publications that highlight the benefits of using ion exchange resins to remove the antimony present in the electrolyte of copper refineries, particularly the work of Dreissinger and Izatt<sup>(2)</sup> . Industrially, this ion exchange process has been studied on the pilot scale in the Tamano, Nippon Hitachi, Saganoseki, Noranda, and other refineries. 

In Chile studies have been made<sup>(3)</sup> and are continuing at both the laboratory and pilot scales of ion exchange plants aimed at defining parameters for designing ion exchange plants at the industrial scale for extracting antimony. In view of the economic perspectives of the ion exchange techniques in mining as such and of their repercussion on the quality of the copper cathodes, it is of interest for the design and control of the process (control of flow, height of bed, initial solute concentration, etc.) to have a model and simulation of the ion exchange process. 

#### **Basics of Ion Exchange Resins** 

Ion exchange operations are mainly substitution chemical reactions of an ion in solution by another in the insoluble resin. The mechanisms of these reactions and the techniques used to carry them out are similar to those of adsorption, and in most practical engineering cases ion exchange is considered as a special case of adsorption. 

As in previous studies, the same as in adsorption, it is necessary to determine a mechanism that will control the ion exchange process for practical design purposes. Thus, it is found that the rate at which the ion exchange takes place depends (the same as adsorption) on the following transport phenomena that occur as the ion exchange progresses<sup>(4)</sup> :

2.

Internal diffusion of ions through the solid to the exchange site. 3. Ion exchange. 4. External diffusion of the released ions to the surface of the solid. #### **INTRODUCTION** 

During the copper electrolytic process, the 15 group elements in copper anode (arsenic, antimony and bismuth) dissolve in the electrolyte to form slightly soluble compounds comprising As, Sb and Bi [1]. Some of the compounds are suspended in the electrolyte and thus so-called “floating slimes”. Since the floating slimes adversely affect current density and crystal growth by adhesion on copper cathode, it is necessary to suppress the formation of the floating slimes. 

The recent enlargement of amount of throughput of waste resources and the increase of impurities in copper ores and concentrates raises increasing of the concentration of the 15 group elements in copper anode [2]. This trend increase the amount of floating slimes and consequently requires more frequent electrolyte purification to suppress the formation of the floating slimes, which results increase of the refining cost. Therefore, it is urgently desired to take countermeasures to the problems concerning the floating slimes. 

For considering and preventing the formation of floating slimes, the solubility product of floating slimes is one of the most important thermodynamic properties. Although the identity of the floating slimes has not been clarified, it is considered that SbAsO4, BiAsO4, Sb2O5, and/or other compounds comprising As, Sb and Bi constitute main part of the floating slimes. In this study, the solubility product of SbAsO4 and BiAsO4 is investigated as a first step. The empirical value of the solubility product of SbAsO4 and BiAsO4 is estimated by Braun _et_ . _al_ . to be 1.4 g<sup>2</sup> L<sup>-2</sup> and 0.8 g<sup>2</sup> L<sup>-2</sup> , respectively [1]. However, they did not consider the equilibria between aqueous species in electrolytes. Thus, their data are applicable only in the limited conditions. Consequently, there are few thermodynamic data allowing prediction

of the formation of SbAsO4 and BiAsO4 in the copper refining electrolyte. In this study, antimony arsenate, SbAsO4, and bismuth arsenate, BiAsO4, were synthesized by hydrometallurgical method and the solubility products of them were determined through dissolution experiments. #### **EXPERIMENTAL** #### **Synthesized arsenates** The arsenates used in the dissolution experiments were synthesized by hydrometallurgical method. #### **CONTROL OF BISMUTH IN TANK HOUSE ELECTROLYTES AT THE ASARCO REFINERY** 

Luis Navarro, Tracy Morris and Weldon Read, _Asarco 7001 State Highway 136 Amarillo, Texas 79106, U.S.A._ 

Neil E. Izatt<sup>*</sup> , Ronald L. Bruening and Steven R. Izatt _IBC Advanced Technologies, Inc. 856 E. Utah Valley Drive American Fork, Utah 84003, U.S.A. *nizatt@ibcmrt.com_ 

#### **ABSTRACT** 

An effective removal system for the separation of dissolved Bi from Cu electrolyte to reach desired Bi levels has been developed by IBC Advanced Technologies, Inc (IBC).  This system is being operated at Asarco in Amarillo, Texas to produce high purity electrolytic Cu. Control of Bi concentrations is necessary because Bi levels exceeding 1 ppm in the final Cu cathode product do not meet ASTM specifications and result in brittleness making the product unsuitable for wire production.  The Bi removal system is based on IBC’s Molecular Recognition Technology (MRT) process.  This process employs proprietary non-ion exchange resin materials, termed SuperLig®, to effect the separation.  Key benefits of the MRT process for Bi removal include (1) easy control of Bi levels in tank house electrolyte with a low environmental impact, (2) avoidance of brittle Cu, and (3) flexibility to handle “dirty” Cu concentrates as feedstock.  This paper describes the Bi MRT plant at the Asarco refinery, the operating process, and the results.  Limitations of alternate technologies for Bi control are discussed, particularly with respect to their environmental concerns compared to the MRT process.  Benefits of the MRT system to Cu refineries where Bi problems exist are presented.

#### **INTRODUCTION** 

A major challenge in the smelting and refining of Cu is the production of high purity product from feed stock containing a diverse range of metal impurities that are deleterious to the final Cu commodity.  Pyrometallurgical technologies alone are not able to separate these metal impurities to the extent required.  Several hydrometallurgical technologies including bleed streams, crystallization, solvent extraction, and ion exchange have been used in refineries to meet this challenge with varying degrees of success [1,2].  Specifications for high purity Cu are increasing as the need for this metal in new high tech devices increases.  Failure of the Cu product to meet specifications results in severe economic loss due to the facilities, labor and time required to re-process the Cu while often using the same inadequate impurity metal remova

l processes.  Metal impurities found in Cu ores include Pb, As, Bi, and Sb.  During processing, these impurities are found in the electrolyte and their concentrations gradually increase with time necessitating use of some means to maintain their concentrations at acceptable levels.  The most critical impurities, which cause grain boundary cracks in wiredrawing are Bi (severe effects), As (deleterious), and Sb (deleterious) [2].  Traditionally, a variety of methods including bleed streams, controlled As addition, crystallization, solvent extraction, and ion exchange have been employed to maintain acceptable levels of these metal impurities [2]. 

Environmental concerns associated with use of these methods are significant. New chemicals are added to the system increasing the number of impurities present. Additional steps and processes are needed to separate the target metal impurity, often with potential health hazards to workers.  Following separation, the impurity plus the additional chemicals must be disposed of usually in landfill or waste receptacles resulting in potential environmental problems.  Altogether, maintenance of acceptable levels of impurity metals in Cu electrolyte presents significant challenges. 

One of the largest Cu refineries in the world is operated by Asarco at Amarillo, Texas. The main feed for this ACR operation is produced at the Hayden smelter in Arizona.   During operation of the Hayden smelter, a variety of metals are carried as impurities in the copper anodes due to the diversity of ores and residue products, used as raw materials in the mix.  This paper will deal primarily with Bi impurity in Cu electrolyte, the means employed to control its concentration, and the use of MRT to recover Bi in an environmentally safe manner as a valuable by-product. 

#### **CONVENTIONAL METHODS FOR ELECTROLYTE PURIFICATION** 

The Bi potential is very close to that of Cu, making it possible to plate Bi on the Cu cathode which adversely affects the quality of the resulting Cu product.  Also, as the concentration of Bi in the electrolyte increases, precipitation can occur causing quality issues. Therefore, concentrations of Bi and other impurity elements must be controlled inside the tank house.  Constant input fluctuations of Bi and other impurities coming 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

477 

from the smelter make control of impurity levels in the electrolyte very difficult but necessary in order to meet ASTM standards or other customer specifications **.** Over the period January 2009 through April 2013, the amount of Bi processed in Cu anodes at ACR ranged from ~1360 to ~5900 kg per month with most values being ~2700 to ~3600 kg per month. 

Several methods for electrolyte purification have been studied. The method chosen by some other companies in North and South America is to adjust the mole fraction ratio of As/(Sb+Bi) (mol/mol) in order to convert Sb and Bi into the insoluble species, antimonious and bismuth a

rsenate (SbAsO4 and BiAsO4) [2].  These precipitates report at the bottom of the tank house cell mixed with the anodic Cu slimes. This method has the potential to cause environmental issues if not controlled carefully including the use of respirators inside the tank house, a practice that should be avoided due to the extra heat stress this can cause in a hot region like Amarillo, TX.  Disposal or processing/treatment of the residues can attract unwanted attention from environmental agencies and cause public concern since As and many of its compounds are potent poisons [3]. 

A conventional practice used at ACR is to bleed a certain volume of Cu electrolyte from the tank house and treat it in liberator cells using insoluble Pb anodes and Cu starter sheets as cathodes. In the first step of this process, Cu is plated making a product that can either be used inside the refinery to produce final product, or as a mix with anode scrap to produce new anodes. In the second step, some of the As, Sb and Bi impurities are co-deposited with Cu, the rest is precipitated as a sludge, and then both are shipped back to the Hayden Smelter. This process gives the possibility of producing nickel sulfate and black acid, however at the present time, due to the high cost involved in starting this process, neither black acid nor nickel sulfate is produced at ACR. A disadvantage of this process is that the smelter does not deplete the metal impurities completely, causing a recycle of some amount back to ACR with attendant labor, time and shipping costs. 

Other methods for removal of impurities [2] are based on adsorption, ion exchange, solvent extraction, and MRT.  ACR has used MRT successfully for several years to control Bi in tank house electrolyte.  This method has the advantage of higher selectivity and efficiency in comparison with other adsorption methods. The MRT process will be described on the following pages. 

#### **MOLECULAR RECOGNITION TECHNOLOGY** 

In MRT procedures, specially designed ligands such as organic chelating agents or macrocycles, chemically bonded by a tether to solid supports such as silica gel or polymers, are used to achieve highly selective metal separations.  The assemblage of ligand, tether, and solid support is termed SuperLig®.  MRT processes [4,5] use “lock and key” or “host guest” chemistry as a basis for their high selectivity.  Such MRT products are packed into fixed-bed columns that, in commercial operation, are built in skid-mounted modular form, and are fully automated for continuous operation.  Feed 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

478 

solution is passed through the column and the target metal is removed from the solution in a highly selective solid phase extraction (SPE) process. 

MRT products can be designed to bind selectively with ions based on multiple parameters such as size, coordination chemistry, and geometry. In contrast, separation methods based on conventional technologies generally recognize di

fferences between ions based only on a single parameter (e.g., charge, solubility, size).  MRT products can bind ions selectively even when the ions are present in highly acidic or basic solution and/or in solutions containing high concentrations of competing ions.  High species selectivity, high binding factors, and rapid reaction kinetics result in efficient separations. The simple elution chemistry features a wide choice of eluent formulations to ensure compatibility with particular plant requirements.  Since small volumes of eluate are used, highly concentrated eluent solutions are produced. The MRT process has wide applicability ranging from in-line incorporation in flow charts of primary ore processing operations to the removal of impurities from low-grade feed stocks.  The MRT process operates on a system cycle basis.  A complete cycle consists of a loading phase; preelution wash phase; elution phase in which the target metal is eluted from the column with a small amount of eluent, forming a solution concentrated in the product; and a postelution wash phase.  The product is recovered and the cycle begins again with the loading phase. 

Notable features of MRT are that new reagents are not added during the procedure, the target metal can be recovered in pure form following separation for resale or environmentally safe disposal, separations are made on-line at or near ambient temperatures, impurity concentration levels from g/L to < mg/L can be treated, and a wide variety of impurity metals can be processed [6]. 

#### **USE OF MOLECULAR RECOGNITION TECHNOLOGY FOR BISMUTH REMOVAL AT ACR** 

The composition of the electrolyte in the tank house is not always constant since it depends on the type and composition of dissolved metals coming from the original ore body from which the anode Cu was produced.  Production of high quality Cu cathodes in tank houses requires low and controlled impurity concentration levels in the electrolyte, because impurities can have adverse effects on the physical and electrical properties of Cu.  Bi can contaminate the cathode due to electrolyte or slimes occlusion or direct precipitation [2]. 

In order to achieve the desired Cu cathode quality, ACR in 2009 developed a new electrolyte purification procedure by modifying an ion exchange process which had been established in 1993 to remove mainly Sb.  This ion exchange process, not in operation in 2009, was converted into a Bi removal process based on the MRT approach.

#### **PROCESS DESCRIPTION** 

Initially, one column of the new Bi removal system packed with SuperLig® 83 was used.  One year later, a single column was found to be incapable of handling the amount of Bi coming into the refinery.  The capacity of the process was then increased by adding a second column. 

The MRT process for bismuth removal consists of the following steps (Figure 1): (1) electrolyte feed from the tank house is loaded on the column

s and Bi is selectively removed by SPE to the SuperLig® 83 material, (2) the loaded column is washed with hot water to remove residual electrolyte, (3) a small quantity of eluent solution (9 M H2SO4) is fed to the column removing Bi as a pure concentrated product, and (4) the column is washed with hot water to ready it for step (1). In step (2), a hot water wash is used. Hot water does not remove all of the Cu, which may be desired in some Biremoval operations. If removal of all Cu is required, a dilute H2SO4 wash may be substituted for the hot water wash in step (2). In the actual operation, electrolyte is drawn from any one of the six commercial modules or from the stripper module and passed to the electrolyte purification plant (EPP) where it enters into a receiving tank. From there the electrolyte is filtered through a 1 micron mesh and fed into the columns packed with SuperLig® 83. During this step, Bi is selectively removed from the electrolyte while Bi-free electrolyte is continuously returned to the selected operation module. When loading is complete, the column is washed with two bed volumes (BV) of hot water (4 L water/kg SuperLig® 83, followed by elution with ~3.1 BV of 9 M H2SO4. Part of the eluate, ~2.2 BV, is sent to the Bi precipitation tank and the remainder is recycled back into the eluent tank. After precipitation is triggered by dropping the temperature below 42o C, the product is sent to a filter press to recover bismuth sulfate. On a periodic basis, a 6 M HCl wash is performed to remove Pb and Sb that have built up in the SuperLig® 83 product. Pb and Sb cannot be removed effectively with 9 M H2SO4. Some other eluent solutions have been studied due to concern about using HCl in the tank house environment, i.e., 9 M H2SO4 in combination with thiourea or commercial salt, and have showed some efficiency in improving the removal of these metals, but more study needs to be performed. . The purification plant is not located inside of the tank house, but adjacent to it, eliminating any potential contamination of the tank house electrolyte. The process is designed to handle 3100 kg Bi per month, running both columns at 100% SuperLig® capacity. Cycle time depends on the Bi feed concentration, flow rate, and column size. #### **ABSTRACT** 

Approximately 160 m<sup>3</sup> /day of electrolyte bleed from the Atlantic Copper Refinery Tankhouse is sent daily to the Electrolyte Treatment Plant to control the copper content and impurities (As, Sb and Bi) in the electrolyte. #### **INTRODUCTION** 

The electrolytic copper refinery of Atlantic Copper in Huelva (Spain) was commissioned in 1970 with an initial capacity of 40,000 t of cathodes per year. #### **SEARCHING FOR AN ALTERNATIVE PROCESS TO A NiSO4 PLANT** 

#### **Background** 

A long-known alternative for Ni recovery from decopperized electrolyte is its selective precipitation by dosing sodium carbonate (Na2CO3). Copper and nickel carbonates precipitate while the pH is increased (pH 5 for CuCO3 and pH 9-10 for NiCO3) [4]. Nevertheless, the high consumption of soda ash to neutralize the H2SO4 in this stream led to the conclusion that this was not a competitive process in comparison with NiSO4 production. 

In 1963, a new process, known as 'acid retardation', for separation of strong acids from metal salts was presented [3]. The process held considerable promise for purification of waste acids generated in pickling metals and leaching ores. The primary appeal of the acid retardation process is that the acid sorbed by the ion exchange resin can be recovered with a simple water elution. Consequently, the economical recovery of a chemical as cheap as sulfuric acid can be contemplated. Although a few early attempts were made to exploit the process commercially, it was not until 1977, when

Eco-Tec introduced a system called the APU (Acid Purification Unit) for purification of sulfuric acid anodizing solutions, that the process became viable. The reason is that it only processes small volumes of acid water in each cycle of sorption / desorption while conventional columns, with a size of 1-3 m, are able to handle large volumes per cycle. _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 489 APU technology uses a technique called Recoflo® ion exchange, whose main characteristics are [9]: Short beds: 7.5 – 60 cm Small particulate resin (75-150 µm) There is no free space on top of the column Countercurrent regeneration Figure 5 depicts the evolution of the design of ion exchange columns until the development of the Recoflo® technology. #### **ABSTRACT** 

The liberator cells department at Amarillo Copper Refinery has the objective of reducing metal impurities in the copper electrolyte to achieve high quality cathodes via electrowining. Insoluble le

ad anodes are used and the copper is depleted from the electrolyte and then electrodeposited to copper starter sheets. This paper discusses how it is possible to precipitate a Nickel Carbonate product when the de-acidified electrolyte is treated using sodium carbonate. #### **INTRODUCTION** 

The electrolytic refining of copper consists of an electrolytic cell filled with a sulfuric acid based electrolyte and pairs of copper anodes and cathodes. When a current is applied, copper in the anode dissolves and is plated onto the cathode.  Impurities within the anode that are more noble than copper do not dissolve and end up at the bottom of the cell and are referred to as slimes. The remaining impurities will dissolve and gradually concentrate in the electrolyte; if they are not removed they can reach a concentration that will affect cathode purity [1,2]. 



Figure 1 - Schematic diagram of the copper electrorefining process 

ASARCO operates one of the largest copper refineries in the world near Amarillo, Texas. Even though the feed for this refinery is mainly produced at one single source, the Hayden smelter in Arizona, it is very difficult to predict the type and concentration of different metal species that will be present in the final product. This is due to the diversity of concentrates and residue products used as raw materials in the smelter feed mix and the limited capability to remove impurities during the smelting process. 

#### **CONVENTIONAL METHOD FOR ELECTROLYTE PURIFICATION** 

Considerable importance should be given to control impurity concentrations in the electrolyte during the electrolytic refining of copper to avoid cathode contamination in order to meet ASTM standards or other customer specifications. Nowadays, several methods for electrolyte purification have been studied. [3,4] 

A conventional practice used at the Amarillo Copper Refinery to reduce impurities and to control copper concentration in the electrolyte, is to bleed a certain volume of copper electrolyte coming from the tankhouse and then treat it in a two stage copper removal circuit, also called 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

499 

“liberator cells”. There the copper electrolyte is circulated through a series

of electrowinning cells using insoluble lead anodes and copper starter sheets as cathodes. In the first stage of this process, the Cu plates to the starter sheets allowing the production of a copper cathode that can either be used inside the refinery to produce final product (rod or cake), or as furnace feed with anode scrap to produce new anodes. In the first stage the copper concentration of the electrolyte is depleted by half to ensure that no other impurities are plated along the process. The second step reduces the copper concentration even further. As the copper concentration decreases in the electrolyte, the deposition potential gradually increases making it possible to plate some other metals onto the cathode and to precipitate others as sludge. After the installation of an Acid Purification Unit (APU) supplied by Eco-Tec in December 2011, the parameter of decopperization for the second stage was modified, rising from below 0.5 g/L to a minimum copper concentration of 3 g/L after the treatment. This reduces the precipitation of some of the As, Sb and Bi impurities and also the co-deposition of these impurities with copper and by that enhance the amount of As left available in the electrolyte. 

An APU gives the possibility of recovering sulfuric acid that can be used as make up in the tankhouse or as a possible reagent in the leaching of anodic copper slimes.  It also gives the possibility to recover nickel carbonate by treating the acid-free solution through a series of neutralization steps. This process eliminates the production of black acid and the use of evaporators with their associated high amounts of energy consumption, and also 70% of the arsenic has been reported to be returned with the sulfuric acid [3].
