#### **HEAVY METALS PRECIPITATION IN ACIDIC STREAMS** 

Heavy metals content in aqueous solutions can be effectively removed to low concentration levels by precipitating the metals into an insoluble form. Metals are typically precipitated as: 

1. Hydroxides: Most common precipitation method, typically follows the reaction (  ) (1) 

Caustic materials are added to raise the pH forming insoluble precipitates; sodium hydroxide and calcium hydroxide (lime) are the most commonly used alkalis. Lime has the advantage of acting as a coagulant during the precipitation process, but it may react with sulfates producing a hard precipitate and resulting in scale formation. Metal hydroxides are amphoteric reaching a minimum solubility at a specific pH, but they can go back to solution if pH is raised passing the point of minimum solubility. 

2. Sulfides or sometime sulfates: Metal sulfides are typically very insoluble. Therefore metals can be precipitated by adding sulfide ions (S<sup>-2</sup> ). It has the advantage that metal sulfides have much lower solubility than the corresponding metals hydroxides so by this method lower residual metal concentrations can be achieved. Sulfide precipitation is always conducted under alkaline conditions to promote sulfide ion formation. In contrast to metal hydroxides, metal sulfides are not amphoteric, so they are not soluble at both low and higher pH after the point of minimum solubility. 

3. Carbonates: Sodium Carbonate is added to the acidic solution to raise the pH and allow -2 

the presence of carbonate ions (CO3 ) promoting the formation and co precipitation of insoluble carbonates. High pH’s also promotes the precipitation of the metals as hydroxides, but values above 10 promote the formation of metal hydroxyl complexes that can increase metal solubility and reduce the precipitation effectiveness. 

Carbonate precipitates settle and can be dried more easily than the corresponding hydroxide precipitates. 

The method selected for this research was the carbonate precipitation using sodium carbonate since it is already successfully used in other refineries, previous experience on the difficult of filtering hydroxides precipitants and also due to commercial reasons on selling the final product. #### **EXPERIMEN

TAL PROCEDURE** The metals coming out of the APU process are in a stable, dissolved aqueous form and are unable to form solids. The goal of the carbonate precipitation is to adjust the pH of the solution so that the metals can form insoluble precipitates. Once the metals precipitate they can be separated by filtration. The goal of the experiment is to first raise the solution pH where the iron, copper, arsenic and other metals impurities can precipitate, then filter the solution, collect the solids and then raise the pH in the filtered solution high enough for nickel carbonate to be formed and can precipitate. This should be done in 2 stages since pure Nickel Carbonate needs to be obtained and the others impurities can be returned to the Hayden Smelter in order to be processed due to its copper content. Before doing so it was necessary to determine the initial concentration of sulfuric acid, Copper, Nickel, Arsenic, Iron and Bismuth in the byproduct stream from the APU. For this several gallons of solution were collected directly from the process. Once the byproduct solution was collected and analyzed, a known amount of volume was poured in a glass beaker and then placed on a stirring plate together with an on-line pH meter system to continuously get reading of the pH and sodium carbonate was added. #### **RESULTS** The initial experiments first started off by just adding sodium carbonate to a 300 mL solution of the APU byproduct while it was continuously stirred, this helped to determine how much soda ash would be needed to raise the pH from the initial value to a final value of 11, the agitation of the solution very difficult after reaching pH 9. The following experiments were to raise the pH unit by unit followed by a filtration after reaching every pH unit, then record the weight of sodium carbonate used, filter the solution and collect an aliquot and the filtrate to obtain chemical assays for both samples. #### **ABSTRACT** 

It’s now possible to operate entire Electrowinning or Electrorefining processing plants Without Short Circuits. Research in the design of capping boards and contact system calculations have been integrated and synchronized to create entire sections of refinery’s that are devoid of even the possibility of short circuits. This design is adaptable to every type of contact system in the industry, including symmetrical and nonsymmetrical electrodes and single, double, triple or quadruple contact bars on the same insulator. Our “Without Short Circuit” systems’ capping board design guarantees your production rates during the stripping process are fully maintained. Symmetrical electrode capping boards have been successfully redesigned into a Single bus bar insulator. Mechanical strength studies and simulations of electrical fluidity have been performed - using CAD 3D technology - to optimize efficiency of the electric current within the contact system, which incorporated into the Without Short Circuit design, reduces resistivity compared to existing contact systems. Research has yielded a chemical formulation that resists sulfuric acid concentrations above 80%. Our standard bus bar insulators are considered permanent, with operational lifetimes of up to 20 years or more with no maintenance and without increasing sulphatation during refining.

#### **INTRODUCTION** 

This presentation briefly describes the result of more than 37 years of Research & Development. Based on the empirical dat

a accumulated and a trial-and-error process, this research has proved that using our insulators instead of other standard capping boards, the lifetime of operation can reach 20 years, and - when refining without short circuits - the level of crystalline compaction of the refined copper is significantly improved. 

#### **History** 

Our company was founded by my father in 1966 under the name Technical Plastic TR ltd - then in 1988 we changed the name to Pultrusion Technique Inc. 

Investigations into capping board technology started in 1976 at CCR Noranda in East-Montreal. Back then, the process used was almost exclusively electro refining, the electrowinning process was rare, and mainly used for the liberators. 

The amp level was limited to 10,000A. There were some secondary factors for which they could not go higher, but mainly, it was due to the fact they were using wood as an insulator. The wood would rapidly get impregnated with water and sulfuric acid and loose its electrical insulating properties. 

However, the main purpose for using capping boards was to protect the top of the concrete cells. 

#### **EXPERIMENTAL** 

#### **Introduction of our capping board** 

In order to help improve production rates, we offered CCR Noranda a capping board made of ultra-high molecular weight polyethylene (UHMWPE), which was put into operation in early winter of 1976. 

Our capping board lasted 6 months. Since the operational lifespan of a wood board was 10 to 21 days, i.e. a regular cycle of plating on the cathode, the engineers were very impressed. However, when the summer heat came, our board melted. 

Not discouraged, my father engineered the first composite capping board made with a multi-ingredient recipe of isophtalic polyester high heat distortion resin blends, Fiberglas™, a specific filler blend and an impact resistant isphtalic resin. When the part was still in good condition after one year in service, the engineers bought 3 more. 

When those 3 were also in good condition after 2 years of uninterrupted service, they increased the number to 36. Two other companies: Amax and Kennecott (located in Baltimore), followed suit, and began using our capping boards on a regular basis. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

511 

#### **Research and development** 

In the summer of 1979, I chose capping board technology as the thesis for my bachelor of engineering – and, as a result, operational lifetimes of our capping boards increased to an average of 4.5 years. Yet, the main complaint from engineers was still the lifespan. 

So, with the determined goal in mind of increasing the quality of our products and meeting the needs of the industry, our company embarked on a continuous and ongoing research and development program that has led to a bus-bar insulator that now boasts operational lifespans of up to 20 years - without maintenance and without any kind of interference in the production process. 

Even so, this 7<sup>th</sup> generation o

f our bus-bar insulator technology has an even more appealing quality: the ability to enable an entire refinery to operate **without short circuits** . 

#### <u>Resistance</u> 

The reason why our insulators last so long is primarily due to the intense research program we have implemented to study their behavior. 

The parts are best described as an electrical insulator with high dielectric resistance and very high heat resistance - functioning within an extremely corrosive environment and subject to intense mechanical stresses and impacts. 

Contrary to what we had originally believed, when I observed the behavior of our competitors’ products, I realized that the accelerated degradation and eventual destruction of their parts was due primarily to poor electrical insulating properties, not poor chemical resistance. 

Understanding that synthetic chemical resins that have a high dielectric resistance have poor chemical resistance, and those with very good chemical resistance, like vinyl ester, have poor dielectric resistance - I decided to create a chemical formulation for bus bar insulators based primarily on electrical resistance instead of chemical. 

But, these resins are incompatible, so an intense research program into surfactant behaviors was implemented to make them synergic. Also, resin curing levels were found to have a significant impact not only on dielectric resistance and permeability, but also Barcol hardness; so these curing levels were studied intently. 

Research into these fields yielded excellent results, enabling the discovery of resin formulas that boasted operational lifespans of approximately 10 years. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

512 

#### <u>Precision and a place for each anode and cathode</u> 

In the 80’s, a standard capping board was a straight flat board. Then, the industry realized that keeping the anodes and cathodes in place provided major advantages and this technology quickly began to be applied. 

For us, that meant we had to make a new type of resin work with a completely revised manufacturing process. The goal was to control shrinkage during the curing process of the insulator in order to maintain the strict tolerances between the seats where the anodes and cathodes would now rest – and to ensure that the one-piece bus bar insulator adheres to these precise tolerances over the entire length of the cell and over its entire operational lifespan; which had now increased to 15 years. 

#### <u>Trials</u> 

Due to these impressive results, we were invited to participate in 2 important research projects for electrorefinery and electrowinning process improvements. The first was for an electrorefinery and consisted in producing the insulator for a single contact system, called Optibar™. 

It was on this project that we obtained – for the first time – a very high polycrystalline compaction level within the refined copper, due mainly to the unusual uniformity of the plating process when refining is

conducted in an environment without short circuits. 

The Optibar™ insulator technology was tested in Chile at the Chuquicamata refinery #2, for a period of 6 months. Unfortunately, a legal battle for ownership of the patent forced Codelco to abandon its use. The Optibar™ technology also had problems with its single contact system due to spacing difficulties. 

In electrowinning, there are other productivity inconveniences. Mainly, during the copper stripping process, an additional one third of the section that is being stripped is not plating, since stripping operations correspond to approximately one third of total production time, this has a major impact on overall productivity. 

We were then invited to participate in the production of an insulator for the 4 contact system of the Finnish company Outotec. Satisfied with our product, they purchased hundreds of insulators from us over the years.

#### **Electricity** 

#### <u>Anodic corrosion on cathodes and cathodic corrosion on anodes</u> 

There are always two distances to calculate when engineering an electric insulator: 1-the most direct or shortest distance between the two poles and 2-the contour distance. 

Parts made out of pultrusion are very popular as insulators within all kinds of electrical installations and distribution networks. However, the porosity level of pultruded parts used in the electrical field must be extremely low compared to levels acceptable in the chemical field; due to the fact we are trying to stop the displacement of electrons instead of the displacement of large corrosives molecules. 

Therefore, we implemented another major Research & Development project in order to develop synthetic insulators that would satisfy the stringent requirements of high voltage insulation. 

Fiberglas™ is acid and fillers are basic. Using surfactants in a solution containing both products is very touchy and complex. 

When trying to decrease porosity, many of the problems encountered are related to the Fiberglas™ and fillers’ degree of resin impregnation. Other difficulties that were carefully studied were the extraction of bubbles from the resin, which are introduced by the Fiberglas™ and fillers. 

Another important factor is the behavior of these bubbles. Only a few microns wide, a high percentage of air bubbles in Fiberglas™ composites change shape. They are no longer round but needle shaped, with a needle bubble vs. round bubble ratio at times higher than 15 to 1. 

Furthermore, this cylinder shape is not uniform. Clinging to the Fiberglas™ fibers, they become quite twisted and warped. This sort of situation is one of the main causes behind the creation of osmosis in composite parts. 

Standard composite materials all have a certain level of porosity. It is also a particular property of all synthetic resins to absorb water. In the case of capping boards, when they absorb water, sulfuric acid dissolves into that water which,

by osmosis, is then followed by metallic and sulfuric salts. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

514 

The sulfuric acid and these metallic and sulfuric salts embark on a path of migration into the capping board, which allows electric currents to flow through the insulator and along its surface, causing anodic corrosion on the cathodes and cathodic corrosion on the anodes. These electro-corrosions attack the different metal components where surface tensions are highest, which is on: 

- The nickel in between the stainless steel and the plated copper of the hanger bar cathodes 

- On the welding of the cathodes and anodes 

- On the polishing of the cathode plates and others. 

#### <u>Interpenetrating polymer network</u> 

We asked that some of our bus bar insulators used in production be returned to us for R & D purposes. We discovered that the fillers we use have a great influence on acid resistance, and we worked to improve that resistance. 

One main characteristic obtained, was to change the filler behavior from hydrophilic to organophilic. These organophilic properties in turn changed the behavior of our filler from hydrophilic to hydrophobic, which gave our insulators a high propensity to repulse water. In repulsing water, we decrease the impregnation of sulfuric acid. 

Also, resin curing levels were found to not only have a significant impact on dielectric resistance, but also permeability and Barcol hardness; for which we have been able to achieve results as high as 80. Competitor products vary from 35 to 42. 

By applying our synthetic insulators technology with our synergy of surfactants technology and then incorporating the synthetic alloy resins technology - we obtained an interpenetrating polymer network within our bus bar insulators that has now enabled us to achieve average operational lifespans of more than 18 years. 

This 7<sup>th</sup> generation of technological advances resulted in the pleasant surprise of totally stopping the electrical corrosion previously produced on the cathodes and anodes due to osmosis. 

We have now totally stopped the anodic corrosion on the cathodes, and the cathodic corrosion on the anodes, which has increased the operational lifespan of electrodes in hydrometallurgical electrowinning and refining plants using our bus bar insulators by 2 to 4 times compared with those that do not. We were able to verify these figures by studying a cathode provided by Xstrata that had been in actual operation. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

515 

It is our firm belief that it is better to offer a product with an exceptionally long operational lifespan, which reduces shut-down times and increases production rates - rather than offer a cheap, low quality capping board that must be frequently replaced. 

Our research continues… 

#### **Short circuit structure** 

Our Without Short Circuit technology can be applied to both electrorefining and electrowinning using symmetrical or asymmetri

cal electrodes. The principal is very simple, the creation of a short circuit within a refinery is mainly based on two factors: the speed of the electricity, which is around two-thirds the speed of light and the fact that ionic metal density is not uniform in an electrolyte solution. 

Electricity travels from the first or positive pole to the second or negative pole, using the shortest distance and the lowest resistivity travel path, which is a fundamental principal of electrical behavior. The flow of current always takes the path of least resistance over the shortest distance. 

Precise positioning of large quantities of anodes and cathodes is very important to avoid short circuits in one cell, single piece, full length contact bars; so deviations in anode and cathode positioning, slight warpage of the plates or physical displacement of the electrodes are all factors that, independently or put together, open up the possibility for the creation of short circuits. 

Since, the distance between the anode and the cathode is the shortest, the electromagnetic force between them is inversely proportional to the square of the distance; so, when those distances lose their uniformity – as previously mentioned – the electromagnetic forces and variations of ion density are proportionally increased. A structure for short circuits is now in place. 

Short circuits are a major problem in hydrometallurgy. I have learned that, near Calama Chili, a 5 year study with infrared spectroscopy in a major electrorefinery of around 2800 cells showed they were experiencing an average of 5000 short circuits per day; and this at 24,000A with a standard center to center distance of 120mm. 

Imagine short circuit problems, when you have 64,000A, 8 meter long electrowinning cells, all equipped with single piece bus bar contact systems. 

Throughout the entire length of the cells, each with parallel and continuous contact systems, running simultaneously in both directions - between one cell and another or within the same cell, excellent conditions for the creation of major short circuits exist. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

516 

#### <u>Electrolyte</u> 

The distribution density of metallic ions within an electrolyte solution could be compared to the distribution density of water molecules in the sky. They have a tendency to group into “clouds” with different densities and volumes, even if there’s turbulence. 

Within an electrolyte, as the current encounters clouds of increased metallic ions, more electric current flows through this area, capturing more metallic ions and – in turn – drawing more current. This process continues exponentially until a full blown short circuit occurs. 

#### <u>Technological principal</u> 

The main objective of our Without Short Circuit design is to prevent the displacement of the electric current, or – better said – forcing the current to pass where we want it instead of letting it choose the shortest distance or the point o

f least resistance.

#### **ABSTRACT** 

A modern tankhouse relies on high performance material handling, fully automated process control systems, quality assessment data and consistent operations reporting to ensure high efficiency of operation and stable quality of final product.  In 2012, Outotec’s and Uralelectromed’s specialists have developed comprehensive tankhouse process automation solution called Tankhouse Information Management System (TIMS), which has been implemented at UMMC’s (“Uralelektromed”) new 150.000  tpa copper electro refinery in Verkhnyaya Pyshma, Russia. 

TIMS collects process data from different systems and material handling equipment into a central database, providing material tracking and process key performance indicator calculations. TIMS automates daily production reporting and provides various analytical views of the process which can be used at higher level in business control systems. 

As a result an essential part of the new tankhouse operation information is provided by TIMS. Systematic and accurate reporting is based on real-time information which requires minimal manual work by the personnel. #### **CFD SIMULATION OF COPPER ELECTROREFINING PROCESS AND ANALYSIS FOR THE TANKHOUSE OPERATION AT NAOSHIMA SMELTER & REFINERY**

#### **ABSTRACT** 

Copper market has been requesting its smooth appearance on the LME Grade A Copper in addition to its composition. It is considered that nodular growth on cathode surfaces is inhibited by preventing the adhesion of anode slime particles to cathodes and supplying a

dditives optimally to cathodes. The way of circulating electrolyte, such as “bottom inlet to top outlet”, “side inlet to top outlet” etc., may affect both the slime behavior and the additive supply to cathodes. The authors have simulated flow patterns in the cell generated by several different ways of circulating electrolyte and analyzed the amount of slime particles reaching cathodes and the delivering time of fresh additives to cathodes using the computational fluid dynamics (CFD) model. The calculation results have revealed that the electrolyte circulation of “side inlet to top outlet” which Naoshima Smelter and Refinery has adopted has some advantages, such as inherent flows that contribute to the reduction of slime particles reaching cathodes, and the uniform time to deliver additives to every cathode, which can minimize the cell flow rate necessary to keep smooth appearance of cathodes. Detailed advantages of “side inlet to top outlet” are discussed in comparison with other conventional ways of electrolyte circulation. 

Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile 

542 

#### **INTRODUCTION** 

The copper electrorefining is an essential process not only to produce high purity electrolytic copper but also to collect precious metals as anode slime. Mitsubishi Materials Corporation’s Naoshima Smelter and Refinery has operated the copper tankhouse since 1969. Copper market has, recently, been increasingly requesting the smooth appearance of the electrolytic copper as well as its composition. 

It is considered that the nodular growth on the electrolytic cathode surfaces is caused by the adhesion of the anode slime particles to the cathodes and the inadequate supply of additives, such as glue, thiourea, chloride ion, etc., to the cathodes. It is well-known that both glue and thiourea are consumed by the electrochemical deposition of copper on the cathode surface, and also degraded due to high electrolyte temperature and strong sulfuric acid. The way of electrolyte circulation may affect the electrolyte flow pattern in cells, which is directly related to both the movement of slime particles and the additive supply to the cathodes. It is thus important to clarify how the difference in the circulation ways affects the electrolyte flow pattern. 

The present study has numerically simulated the electrolyte flow pattern as well as the cupric ion concentration field in the cell with the computational fluid dynamics (CFD) model. The CFD model accounts for both the natural convection induced by the electrochemical reactions and the forced convection caused by the electrolyte circulation. According to the calculated electrolyte flow field, both the amount of the anode slime particles reaching the cathodes and the delivering time of fresh additives to the cathodes have been numerically analyzed. 

#### **TANKHOUSE OPERATION AT NAOSHIMA** 

There exist two different copper electrorefining cells, called as “the ordinary cells” and “the 13th block cells of th

e east wing (E13B cells)” at the Naoshima copper tankhouse. The E13B cells were originally operated for the production of the starter sheets. Since the new electrolytic plant for the starter sheet was established in 1999, the E13B cells have been converted to copper electrorefining cells in order to increase the production of the electrolytic copper. 

The outstanding feature of Naoshima copper electrorefining process is the way of the electrolyte circulation. Figure 1 shows the schematic description of the electrolyte circulation way of the “side inlet to top outlet”, which has been adopted at Naoshima Smelter and Refinery. Contrary to the conventional electrolyte circulation way, the electrolyte is fed to the cell through holes on two pipes placed above the bottom of the cell, and it then overflows through the top outlet. 53 holes with 10 mm in diameter opened alternately on two pipes are designed to feed the electrolyte directly toward every cathode.

Figure 1– Schematic diagram of “side inlet to top outlet” circulation 

#### **CALCULATION MODEL** 

In the present study, calculation models have been developed according to the tankhouse data at Naoshima Smelter and Refinery. Figure 2 shows a schematic description of the electrolytic cell modeled in the present study. 



Figure 2– Schematic diagram of the electrolytic cell calculation model 

The dimensions of the cell are 5.4 m long and 1.2 m wide. In the case of the ordinary cell, the bottom of this cell is slanted from 1.2 to 1.35 m in depth. On the other hand, in the case of the E13B cell, the bottom of this cell is slanted from 1.3 to 1.45 m in depth. Thus, the E13B cell is deeper than the ordinary cell. In the cell, there exist 54 anodes with 0.98 m in height and 0.96 m in width, and 53 cathodes with 1 m in height and width. Anode spacing 

Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile 

544 

between centers is fixed to 97 mm. It is assumed that both the anode and the cathode are geometrically flat plates hanging vertically and they do not have any distortion. 

During the electrorefining process, the anode becomes thinner with time due to the electrochemical dissolution of copper, whereas the cathode becomes thicker with time due to the electrochemical deposition of copper. In the present study, four computational models have been developed in order to examine the effect of the thickness changes of both the anode and the cathode, as shown in Figure 3. Here, _L_ represents the inter-electrode spacing. It is assumed that copper cathodes are produced twice during one anode life in the present study. The process to produce the first electrolytic copper cathode is called as “1st crop operation”, and the latter process as “2nd crop operation”. The thicknesses of both the anode and the cathode in calculation models are set to correspond to “1st crop initial state”, “1st crop final state”, “2nd crop initial state”, and “2nd crop final state”.

The “bottom inlet to top outlet” circulation has been most conventionally adopted for copper electrorefining cells worldwide, although there may be some differences in detail. The electrolyte enters the cell through the bottom inlet located at one end, and it then overflows through the top outlet located at the opposite end. #### **Calculated electrolyte flow and concentration fields**

Figure 5 shows the calculation results in the inter-electrode space, which are obtained in “1st crop initial state” calculation model with “side inlet to top outlet” circulation in the ordinary cell. Both the concentration profiles and the vertical component of the fluid velocity profiles in the inter-electrode space of no. 26 cathode (See Figure 4) are plotted in Figure 5- (a) and 5-(b), respectively. Due to the electrochemical deposition of copper on the cathode surface, the concentration of cupric ion becomes depleted near the cathode surface, which induces the upward buoyancy force in the cathodic concentration boundary layer (CBL). Vice versa occurs near the anode surface. Calculation results have indicated that the concentration difference within the CBL is about 20 g/l, and the maximal peak values of both cathodic upward and anodic downward natural convections have the almost same velocity of around 1.5 cm/s in the present operational condition. Although the details are not shown in this paper, the calculation results have suggested that the electrolyte flow pattern in the inter-electrode space does not change according to the change of the inter-electrode spacing _L_ . #### **Numerical estimation of the delivering time of fresh additives to cathodes** 

Based on the calculated electrolyte flow fields in the cell, the delivering time of fresh additives to the cathodes from the inlet can be numerically analyzed. In the present study, the delivering time has been estimated by the concept of “the mean age of air” [4]. Figure 9 compares the delivering time of fresh additives toward every cathode in the cell among three different operational conditions. In the case of the “bottom inlet to top outlet” circulation, the electrolyte with fresh additives can be delivered to the cathodes in a short time near the inlet side of the cell. However, it can also be seen that it takes much time near the outlet side of the cell in comparison with the case of the “side inlet to top outlet” circulation. Contrary to the conventional “bottom inlet to top outlet” circulation, the “side inlet to top outlet” circulation has the characteristics of the uniform time to deliver additives to every cathode in the cell. 

In 2007, Naoshima Smelter and Refinery had faced a problem with the rough appearance of the cathodes produced in the E13B cells. The measure against the problem was the renewal of the electrolyte circulation pump for the E13B cells so that the cell flow rate be increased from 35 to 40 l/min. Since 2008, the appearance of the cathodes produced in the E13B cells has improved, and both the ordinary and the E13B cells have produced smooth cathodes with high current efficiency of over 97 % although the conventional starter sheet method has been adopted. The present numerical study can explain why the appearance of the cathodes produced in the E13B cells has improved as follows. 

Figure 10 compares the calculated mean delivering time of fresh additives to cathodes between the ordinary and the E13B cells in the case of the “side inlet to top outlet” circulation. When the same cell flow rate of 35 l/min is applied for both the ordinary and the E13B cells, it takes much time to deliver fresh additives to the cathodes in the E13B cells in comparison with the ordinary cells. It can be seen that the delivering time of fresh additives to the cathodes in the E13B cells can be reduced by increasing the cell flow rate from 35 to 40

#### **Numerical estimation of the amount of the anode slime particles reaching cathodes** 

Based on the calculated electrolyte flow field in the cell, the amount of the anode slime particles reaching the cathodes can be numerically analyzed. In the present study, the behavior of the anode slime particles has been numerically simulated with the discrete phase model (DPM). In this model, the slime particle trajectory is calculated by integrating the particle force balance equation where both the drag and buoyancy forces of the slime particle are considered. The anode slime particles were sampled from the bottom of the Naoshima copper electrorefining cell, and the particle size distribution and the specific gravity were measured. In the present study, 6.56 g/cm<sup>3</sup> is employed as the specific gravity of the anode slime particle, and the slime particle is assumed to be spherical. The “trap” boundary condition is applied on all cathode surfaces and the cell bottom surfaces, whereas the “reflect” boundary condition is applied on other wall surfaces. In this study, two kinds of DPM simulations have been carried out. One is the case in which the anode slime particles fall away from the anode surface, and the other is the case in which the anode slime particles are swirled up from the cell bottom. The amount of the anode slime particle to be trapped on the cathode surfaces has been numerically estimated by each DPM simulation. 

Figure 11 shows the relative comparison of the amount of the anode slime particles reaching the cathodes among three different operational conditions. The amount of the anode slime particles reaching the cathodes is normalized by that in the case of the Naoshima ordinary cell with the “side inlet to top outlet” circulation.

It can be seen that the amount of the anode slime particles reaching the cathodes in the case of the “side inlet to top outlet” circulation is clearly less than that in the case of the “bottom inlet to top outlet” circulation. The vortex flow characteristic of the “side inlet to top outlet” circulation prevents the slime particles from reaching the cathodes. On the other hand, in the case of the “side inlet to top outlet” circulation, it is concerned that rather large velocity from inlet holes on two pipes placed above the bottom of the cell might swirl up the slime particles from the cell bottom. However, its contribution to the total amount of the slime particles reaching the cathodes is quite small, as shown in Figure

11. Although the details are not shown in this paper, we observed whirling motion of fine particles below the electrodes, which verifies the existence of the vortex flows. The present numerical simulation has suggested that the “side inlet to top outlet” circulation can reduce slime particles reaching the cathodes compared to the conventional “bottom inlet to top outlet” circulation. 

#### **CONCLUSIONS** 

The present study has numerically calculated the electrolyte flow field as well as the concentration field of cupric ion in the cells of Naoshima Smelter and Refinery operated by Mitsubishi Materials Corporation. Based on the calculated electrolyte flow field, both the amount of the anode slime particles reaching the cathodes and the delivering time of fresh additives to the cathodes have been numerically analyzed. 

The calculation results have revealed that the electrolyte circulation of “side inlet to top outlet” which Naoshima Smelter and Refinery has adopted has distinctive advantages, such as inherent vortex flows that contribute to the reduction of the slime particles reaching the cathodes, and the uniform time to deliver additives to every cathode in the cell. These advantages may contribute to the current tankhouse operation at Naoshima Smelter and Refinery with high current efficiency.

#### **INTRODUCTION** 

Due to slow dynamics of the copper electro-refining process and ever tightening requirements for more sustainable, cost-efficient and safe production, the task of producing cathode copper with high quality and efficiency is not simple. Being the last phase in mine to metal production chain furthermore increases the demand for the capability and robustness to manage the changes in anode quality, electolyte composition and other disturbances emerging up-stream or within the process. 

A modern copper electro-refining plant, shown for instance in Figure 1, is highly automated process, where both discrete and continuous automation play a critical role. While material handling systems controlled by programmable logic controllers (PLC) ensure high machine safety and integrity, capacity and efficiency, the process control system (DCS / PCS) stabilizes the electrolysis and auxiliary processes. 

The chemical quality of anodes supplied to the tankhouse is tracked with anode batch analysis sampled and analysed at the smelter. Inspection of anodes’ physical quality parameters, such as dimensions, weight and taper are performed automatically by the anode preparation machine, but the surface quality is determined by operators’ visual evaluation. Rather sparse, once per day, sampling of electrolyte for laboratory analysis is allowed by the slow process dynamics. The final chemical quality of cathodes is determined in a laboratory with samples taken from the final cathode deposits. The surface quality of the cathode metal and maintenance requirement of permanent cathode blanks is visually observed and graded by operator judgment as cathodes pass through the cathode stripping machine.

Despite the high automation level of material handling or basic process automation, significant amount of manual operator work is still required in order to maintain high efficienc and quality or to recover the process from disturbances. Huge process area with aggressive environment, hundreds of similar cells and thousands of electrodes and typically lack of real on-line measurement systems to support observa

tions makes process disturbances long to be identified and removed. These events can cause significant annual losses through off specification cathode, low current efficiency, high scrap rate, malfunction of equipment and extra labor required to correct the problems (e.g. hand stripping of cathodes, intensified short circuit removal). 

This paper presents proven systems designed by Outotec to increase operations transparency of a copper electro-refining plant. The ultimate target of these systems is to improve the energy and operations efficiency and quality by responding to above mentioned challenges. 

#### **QUALITY INSPECTION OF ANODES AND CATHODES** 

#### **Anode Quality** 

Typically the quality of anodes supplied to a tankhouse is the major contributor and source of various problems observed at the process. Therefore it is very important to establish quality control procedures as systematic as possible to monitor and manage the anode quality. The importance is even more emphasized at tankhouses receiving anodes from several suppliers. Anode quality is measured from two perspectives. 

Chemical quality defines the contents of the elements of interest for the tankhouse in order to control the process. It is a key source of information to plan and optimize the production, waste management, economics, solution purification and precisious metal plant. Chemical analysis is conducted by taking a laboratory sample of each anode batch casted at the anode casting plant. The results are typically available before the batch is fed to tankhouse and can therefore be used for process control. This requires tough that anodes and batches can be tracked from casting to tankhouse and that the sampling is representative for the batch. 

Physical quality defines that anode dimensions, weight, form and surfaces match the specification which is designed to guarantee high efficiency, availability and low waste. Therefore it is critical that each anode supplied to a tankhouse is inspected for the in order to minimize the difficulties in loading and unloading of anodes, uneven scrap weight or current distribution, or short circuits between anodes and cathodes for instance. While most of the physical quality measurements are done automatically at the anode preparation machine the evaluation of the surface quality of an anode is still performed visually by the operators. Also, the measurement of anode’s dimensions, width, height and thickness over the full anode body including lugs has not been available on-line. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

556 

Surface quality inspection includes mainly the analysis of the anode surface evenness and outside mould copper on the air side of an anode. Occassionally due to various reasons and conditions in the casting process anode surface ends up having uneven areas sticking out from the anode surface, which are sometimes called blisters. These blisters, being large or covering the anode surface widely enough, a

re known to produce many problems discussed earlier during the loading of anodes or cathode growth cycle. Therefore being able to reject anodes for entering tankhouse with too excessive blister formations is very beneficial. 

#### **Cathode Quality** 

Maximizing the production of good “A” grade cathode that exceeds customer’s specification is critical because of customer satisfaction and premiums.  Lower “B” grade cathodes are often very problematic as a single “B” class cathode in a stack can deteriorate rest of the cathode bundle into lower class. Impact can even be more dramatic, if lower “B” class cathodes are mixed with high quality cathodes as inspected for accepted quality. 

Typically cathode quality and condition is justified by operator’s visual inspection of the cathode surface for nodulation and by chemical analysis representing set of cathodes. The most common reason for nodule formation on the cathode is uneven current distribution between anodes and cathodes. This is normally caused by bent cathode blanks, misalignment of anodes or cathodes, poor contacts between electrodes and bus bar. Nodulation can also occur due to too high current density, unsuitable electrolyte composition, wrong dosage of additives or electrolyte flow problems. High nodulation level on a cathode surface carries always increased risk of high impurity levels in the cathode. Because operator’s main task is to maintain high production availability, systematic task of cathode quality monitoring can be difficult to carry out in practice, and is always vulnerable to human factor. 

The condition of permanent cathode blanks used in the process has a significant impact of the overall efficiency and quality of the plant and require continuous monitoring. There is always a risk to return blanks back to process that are bent, have not previously been producing enough copper or have broken edge strips. It causes increased probability for extra work during the cathodes growth cycle, decreased cathode quality, decreased the current efficiency and production and increased downtime of the crane and stripping machine.

#### **ABSTRACT** 

In copper electrorefining additives are used for a smooth electrodeposition of copper cathodes. The classical additives glue and thiourea show some disadvantages like the relatively fast decomposition during electrolysis and the incorporation of sulfur from thiourea into the cathodes. Only new additive systems avoiding thiourea can help to reduce the sulfur content in the copper cathodes. Additionally the decomposition of glue and thiourea forces a continuous dosing of the additives. 

Our investigations show that alternative additives can be used in copper electrorefining indeed. Polyethylene glycols (PEG) act strongly polarizing and can substitute glue. Current density potential curves show that Bis-(3-sodiumpropyl)disulfide (SPS), dimethylthiourea, methionin and cystein have a stronger depolarizing effect compared to thiourea. 

Electrolysis experiments with PEG and SPS proceeded without short circuits at a current d

ensity of 500 A/m². However, the cathodes were rough and nodulous. Smoother cathodes were produced when using glue and thiourea or glue and SPS. In the first case the sulphur concentration in the cathodes ranged from 4 to 10 µg/g and in the second case only from 0.3 to 1.5 µg/g. SPS is considerably more stable than thiourea. Thus, there is no need for continuous addition during electrolysis.

566 

#### **INTRODUCTION** 

Today approximately 75 % of the world copper production derives from electrorefining. In recent years some copper producers have increased the current density from 300 to 380 A/m² and at the same time they have considerably improved the chemical purity of the deposited copper. Amongst others this was made possible by improved control of the effective additive concentrations in the electrolyte, which enabled dosing of the additives according to their actual consumption. A combination of glue, thiourea and chloride is used as additive system in nearly all copper electrorefining tankhouses. Within this system glue acts polarizing and thiourea slightly depolarizing. In spite of a large number of investigations the mechanism of this additive system has not been fully clarified so far. 

Despite their high effectiveness these classical additives are known to have disadvantages as well. Due to the relatively high decomposition rate of glue, continuous dosage during electrolysis is strictly required. Because the glue is made from animal bones, the electrochemical effectiveness depends on the raw material and the production process and can vary for different lots. 

During the electrolysis process sulfur originating from thiourea is partly incorporated in the copper cathode. The sulfur concentration in the cathodes increases with an increasing amount of thiourea. On the other hand cathodes produced without thiourea are rough and have noldules which contain high concentrations of impurities due to inclusions of electrolyte and anode slime. Therefore a decrease of the sulfur content in cathodes can only be achieved if thiourea is substituted by other depolarizing compounds. Our investigations show also that the additive system glue, thiourea and chloride is not sufficiently effective at current densities above 500 A/m<sup>2</sup> [1]. Therefore, a further increase of the current density will require a systematic research for alternative inhibitor systems in copper electrorefining. 

#### **EFFECT OF GLUE, THIOUREA AND CHLORIDE DURING COPPER ELECTROREFINING** 

In the field of electrometallurgy glue and gelatine are used e. g. as additives during the deposition of copper and zinc from sulfuric acid electrolytes. Both substances have a straight chain structure formed by peptide linkage of amino acids such as glycin, pyroline and alanine. Oxygen atoms in glue and gelatine act as the radicals for adsorption by utilizing their lone pairs of electrons [2]. The adsorption behavior of glue and gelati

ne on the cathode surface is quite different between high and low molecular weight polymers because the higher molecular polymers have a large number of radicals and adsorb tenaciously. Glue and gelatine cause a shift of the cathodic polarization towards the negative direction during copper deposition from sulfuric acid electrolytes and therefore act as inhibitors. Nakano et al. [2] investigated the influence of molecular weight and gelatine concentration on the cathodic polarization in chloride-free solutions. The investigations showed that the polarization increased with an increase of the 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

567 

concentration and the molecular weight. During electrolysis the polarization decreased due to the decomposition of gelatine molecules. According to [3] the average molecular weights of different glue types ranged from 285,000 to 544,000 and so they are considerably higher than those of gelatine. Our investigations showed that under the same conditions glue has a clearly stronger depolarizing effect than gelatine. 

The adsorption of glue at the cathode is affected by polarizable NH-groups after the following mechanism [4]. The electroadsorption of the polar glue molecules on the cathode occurs mainly at locations with high field strength like edges, nodules and needles. The glue molecules form an isolating layer and the growth of the needle is stopped. After the normal copper layer has grown up to the peak of the needle the glue is desorbed and can be adsorbed again on another place with high field strength. Thus glue is relatively rapidly decomposed as a result of acidic hydrolysis especially at higher electrolyte temperatures. Half-life of glue under the conditions of copper electrorefining at 50 °C is about 150 minutes and at 65 °C it is just about 50 minutes [4]. Therefore at higher electrolyte temperatures larger amounts of glue must be added to obtain the same inhibitory effect. 

The partial coverage of the cathode surface with glue increases the effective current density, which in turn produces the increased cathodic polarization. A too low glue concentration leads to a nodulated surface, since not all tops can be covered with glue. In contrast, at a too high glue concentration, the larger part of the cathode is covered with glue and thus blocked for copper deposition. At the few free places, a very high effective current density will prevail then, which may lead to strong dendrite formation. Therefore a defined glue concentration, mostly ranging from 0.5 to 1.0 mg/l, must be maintained during electrolysis. 

Thiourea or thiourea combined with glue and chloride acts normally slightly depolarizing. There are different mechanisms of thiourea action described in the literature [5, 6]. Thiourea shows a tautomerism between thion and thiol structure. 



Thiols can form disulphides by oxidation. Thiourea reduces divalent Cu ions to monovalent Cu ions while Formamidindisulfide is formed. Cu(I) is bonded

on thiourea complexes and becomes reduced to Cu at the surface. 



According to another theory thiourea and Cu form hardly soluble CuS at the cathode surface, which blocks the growth of already existing crystals and increases the number of seed crystals. In contrast to glue the decomposition of thiourea during copper electrolysis takes place predominantly electrochemically at the cathode. The inclusion of 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

568 

sulphur from thiourea results in cathodes containing 2 to 5 µg/g sulphur whereas the sulphur concentration rises with increasing thiourea content. The optimum thiourea concentration mostly ranges from 1 to 3 mg/l and should be kept as low as possible. A further reduction of sulphur concentration in the cathodes is only feasible by substitution of thiourea. 

The electrochemical effect of the chloride ions is mostly explained by the formation of complexes with thiourea or the formation of sparsely soluble CuCl. The usual chloride concentration in the electrolyte is between 20 and 80 mg/L. Chloride increases the polarizing effect of glue and gelatine markedly [8] and moreover chloride acts polarizing even if glue and thiourea are absent. 

During copper electrorefining smooth and thus chemically pure cathodes can only be produced if glue, thiourea and chloride are dosed in optimal concentrations. The dosage is complicated because these components are consumed relatively quickly and the analytical determination of glue and thiourea within the electrolyte is difficult. The active glue concentration can only be determined by measuring the cathodic polarization, which is also influenced by other parameters. In addition, our investigations showed that the positive effect of the system glue, thiourea and chloride is lowered at current densities above 500 A/m² due to unstable conditions. Therefore the search for alternative additives is necessary which should fulfil the following requirements: 

- Deposition of smooth and pure cathodes which means that the additives should not be included in the cathode; 

- High chemical and electrochemical stability under the conditions of copper electrolysis; 

- Well defined chemical composition and therefore defined electrochemical efficiency; 

- Optimum efficiency within a large range of current densities and especially at high current density.

It could be shown that thiourea acts polarizing if combined with PEG and thus does not improve the cathodic deposition. SPS is normally used in combination with PEG

and chloride. Investigations concerning the effect of SPS in copper electrorefining have not been published so far. Several investigations were performed concerning the effect of SPS combined with PEG and chloride in copper electroplating. In the additive system PEG-SPS-Cl PEG acts as inhibitor and SPS as catalyst. Several models were described relatied to the effect of SPS during copper deposition [11-13]. First tests show that at this current density without addition of additives the cathodes were very nodulous, which caused short circuits during some experiments. The additives were dosed in intervals of 1 to 4 days. Despite of many optimization tests it was impossible to deposit smooth cathodes using PEG and SPS at a current density of 500 A/m<sup>2</sup> . The cathodes were either nodulous or fine grained depending on the additive concentration (Fig. 6). The rough cathode surface induced electrolyte inclusions. Therefore the sulphur concentrations of the cathodes ranged mostly from 50 and 500 µg/g. 

Another test series was performed under the same conditions, on the one hand with the classical additives glue and thiourea and on the other hand with glue and SPS. Compared to the tests with PEG the cathodes were generally clearly smoother (Fig. 7). In the experiments with glue and thiourea both additives were dosed continuously over the test duration. The sulfur concentrations in the cathodes ranged from 4 to 10 µg/g and were thus considerably lower than in cathodes produced in tests with PEG. 

Also in experiments with glue and SPS the glue dosage occurred continuously. The dosage of SPS was performed either only at the start of the test or at most once a day whereas only very small amounts were necessary. Cathodes with relatively smooth surfaces contained only 0.3 to 1.5 µg/g sulphur. Thus the application of the new additive decreases the sulphur concentration in the cathodes. Obviously SPS becomes either not incorporated into the cathodes or it becomes incorporated in only very small amounts.

### **DETERMINATION AND CONTROL OF BISMUTH CONTAMINATION IN COPPER ELECTROREFINING** 

Shijie Wang and Daniel Kim _Rio Tinto Kennecott Utah Copper 11500 West 2100 South Magna, UT 84044, USA_ <u>wangs@kennecott.com</u>

#### **ABSTRACT** 

Bismuth is the most critical impurity to cause copper grain boundary cracks during wiredrawing.  Thus, control of bismuth in the copper electrorefining process is an important topic for most copper refineries in the world.  Due to a fact that copper anodes at Kennecott Utah Copper (KUC) contain a significant amount of bismuth, it is very critical to determine, minimize, and control bismuth contamination in the copper production.  This article presents the methods and techniques used in a study of bismuth contamination.  It also summarizes the observed contamination mechanism identified at KUC. 

#### **INTRODUCTION** 

Bismuth contamination in cathode is the principal factor affecting the quality of electrorefined copper at the Kennecott Utah Copper (KUC).  Bismuth is widely known to cause copper grain boundary cracks during wiredrawing [1].  Thus, the London Metal Exchange (LME) and the American Society for Testing and Materials (ASTM) specifications for bismuth content in copper are low (2.0 ppm and 1.0 ppm, respectively). Due to a fact that the KUC anodes have the most reported high content of bismuth [2], controlling bismuth is critically important for the production of LME and ASTM grade copper cathode. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

578 

#### **EXPERIMENTAL** 

In industrial electrorefining practice, copper cathode quality is normally affected by 1) impurity co-plating with copper, 2) entrapment of electrolyte and/or 3) suspended slimes inclusion.  To determine and control bismuth contamination, a series of tests, viz., double spacing cell, clean copper anode, flocculant addition, including Hull cell plating, slimes settling and flocculant testing as well as DOE tests from different anode type in Tankhouse, were conducted.   To understand the mechanism by which Bi is transported from the anode to the cathode, contamination of cathodes by bismuth were examined using industrial data from KUC. The effect of operating variables on contamination, including anode composition, electrolyte composition, electrolyte temperature, addition agent practiced, and electrolyte bleeding rate were examined using 10 years of KUC data. To confirm the mechanism of suspended slimes inclusion, laboratory testing includedcyclic voltammetry and characterization of anodes, cathodes and slimes characterization using SEM and electron microprobe analysis were also carried out [311]. 

#### **RESULTS**

To investigate the effect of electrode spacing on cathode contamination, two regular tankhouse cells were employed.  Anode to anode centerline spacing was adjusted from the typical 98 mm to 196 mm, as shown in Figure 1.  The cells were operated under normal tankhouse condition. produced smooth copper cathodes with 0.13 – 0.28 ppm bismuth (Bi). During the same period, regularly spaced cells in the section produced copper cathodes with 1.39 – 1.52 ppm Bi. Since the current density was the same for all cells in the section, the cathode potential should have also been the same. This result indicates that contamination by slimes particles is most likely and not co-plating of bismuth. #### **DISCUSSION** 

#### **Cathode Contanimation Theory** 

#### <u>Bismuth in Anode</u> 

Anode composition plays a vital role in cathode quality.  As, Bi, and Sb are found in commercial anodes either in solid solution with copper or secondary oxide phases with copper and/or lead.  In KUC bismuth-rich copper anodes, bismuth is present mainly as Cu-Bi-As oxide, Cu-Pb-As-Bi oxide, Cu-Bi oxide and Cu-Pb-As-Bi-Sb oxide inclusions, occurring along the copper grain-boundaries.  During the electrorefining of the copper, some arsenic and bismuth dissolves.  However, the majority of the dissolve bismuth react with the electrolyte to form BiAsO4, which retains the morphologies of the original 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

589 

bismuth-bearing oxide grains (Cu-Bi-As oxide, Cu-Pb-As-Bi oxide, Cu-Bi oxide and CuPb-As-Bi-Sb oxide).  The maintenance of arsenic in the electrolyte is used to control bismuth in the electrolyte.  The result is the formation of BiAsO4 in the slimes.  By limiting the concentration of Bi and Sb in the electrolyte the formation of floating slimes and the electrochemical deposition is thought to be prevented.  The presence of BiAsO4 in the Kennecott anode slimes is observed in all of the slimes examined.  These BiAsO4 were found in the cathode indicating the transport of Bi from the anode to the cathode is mainly by inclusions of slime particles. 

It is not believed that BiAsO4 forms away from the anode based on the results using clean anodes (300 ppm As, 28 ppm Sb, 34 ppm Bi).  When clean anodes were loaded in electrolytic cells, the quality of the cathodes were very good (0.14 ppm Bi) thus indicating that the electrolyte was “not bad”.  It appeared that, although the electrolyte contained 50-55 ppm of bismuth, there were no slimes (i.e., BiAsO4) adhered to top of the cathode forming top nodules and contaminated them indicating that floating slimes we

re not being generated. 

#### <u>Laboratory Copper Electrorefining</u> 

Characterization of impurities in copper cathode products indicates that bismuth contamination during normal copper electrorefining in the Tankhouse occurs by the physical inclusion of bismuth containing slime particles and not electrodeposition.  In order to detail the correlation between bismuth concentration in the electrolyte and the resulting electrodeposit, laboratory electrorefining tests were conducted in synthetic electrolytes, examining the effect of bismuth electrolyte concentration and slime particles on cathode purity and deposit structure produced by electrorefining. 

From these experiments, no bismuth metal was detected in any copper cathode product produced.  It was thus concluded that copper cathode quality upsets was primarily caused by extreme high anode impurities and the mechanism of copper cathode contamination was suspend slimes inclusion. 

#### <u>Suspend Slimes Control</u> 

Thus at Kennecott Utah Copper, it appears that cathode contamination comes from slimes generated on the anode surface breaking free and “floating” to the surface of the cathode where it becomes included in the electroplating copper.  This mechanism was confirmed by looking at samples of cathode and their embedded impurities using an Electron Microprobe.   Physical observation of the slimes and slimes fall, as illustrated in Figure 24, also confirmed that slimes with higher concentrations of arsenic and low concentrations of lead were very fine whereas slimes with higher lead concentrations along with the high arsenic concentrations had a thicker, more stable slimes layer on the

The key to maximizing good cathode quality in high impurity level conditions is to not disturb the slimes layer on the anode surface.  This conclusion is verified by the double cell operation in the Tankhouse; also supported by data showing 1<sup>st</sup> harvest cycle cathodes averages lower bismuth concentrations than the 2<sup>nd</sup> harvest cycle cathodes.

As slimes transport is important to bismuth contamination, an effort to accelerate sinking of the suspended slimes using flocculation was attempted to clarify the electrolyte within the cell.  Flocculation has been commercially practiced in Union Miniere (Belgium), LG Nikko (Korea), Magma (USA) and Phelps Dodge (USA) [16]. Floucculants, such as Magnafloc 351 and Betz 1160, are recognized effectively for fine suspended slimes settling, which, ultimately, would improve copper cathode quality in the Tankhouse.  But from the study at the KUC, modification in dosage rate is needed and requires further testing. 

#### **Anode Composition Correlation** 

Copper electrorefining in a tankhouse is a complex process with no less than 20 independent variables relating to electrolyte and anode compositions and basic physicochemical aspects.  One critical variable is anode impurity content, which must be controlled to avoid cathode contamination and to meet stringent customer demands. 

It was confirmed by a DOE study [12] that the minimum Bi in cathode correlates to minimum Bi, As, and Pb in anode.  It was also verified by the DOE test done in the Tankhouse that anodes containing low Bi, low As, and reasonable high Pb were beneficial to copper cathode quality.  Several iterations were run comparing factors (i.e. lead in anode, arsenic in anode, bismuth in anode and current density) to bismuth in

#### **CONCLUSIONS** 

A comprehensive study with a series of experimental tests as well as industrial investigations was conducted to understand, control and minimize bismuth contamination in copper.  The significant findings and creative recommendations from the study are: 

1. Copper cathode is normally contaminated by 1). Impurity co-plating with copper, 2). Entrapment of electrolyte, and 3). Suspended slimes inclusion.  Since bismuth and antimony

electrolyte concentrations are kept low, entrapment is typically slimes encapsulation. 

2. All the cathode samples studied were very uniform and fined-grained.  Slimes particles, such as BiAsO4, Cu2(Se,Te), PbSO4 and BaSO4, were detected as inclusions in the cathode in all samples. 

3. BiAsO4 and Cu2(Se,Te) are the most abundant impurity species in the cathodes. The slimes particles are generally present in clusters, together with micro-cavities, embedded in the cathode copper matrix. 

4. Based on experimental testing and mineralogy studies, it is concluded at KUC that bismuth contamination is caused by suspended slimes, such as BiAsO4, inclusion. 

5. Bismuth would increase in the cathode with increasing bismuth in the anode.  If more arsenic in the anode leads to less oxidative phase or “cement” in slimes, then high arsenic could promote more slime detachment and/or reducing the effective size of slime particles leading to more suspended slimes and entrapment. 

6. If higher lead in anodes leads to less dissolution of complex oxides.  This could cause large slime particles formed during electrorefining and result in less arsenic dissolution and more “cement” in the slimes. 

The recommended continued work with the biggest impact on stabilizing the production of grade 1 copper cathode is to: 

1. Improve the ability to physically track anodes from the smelter to a particular cathode produced in the refinery. 

2. Develop more understanding and a better mass balance around recycled impurity streams.  Identify where removal of bismuth from the system will have the biggest impact. 

3. Improve the modeling of concentrates moving forward from the mine so that periods of high impurities can be better managed through the downstream systems (smelter recycled streams, refinery operations, etc.). 

4. Operate a test cell at the Refinery to further optimize the Tankhouse ability to process “high impurity” anodes.
